paragraphs.text: A book [?] containing the [?] of the Lord, and also [?] their interpretations; and besides these [?], the teachings that agree with them and follow from them.

PROLOGUE TO THE PRESENT COMPILATION. That Antiochus renounced the whole world in every way and lived quietly for no short time in the monastery of the great Sabas at Jerusalem. Living thus by himself, he was still and came to know the things that bring salvation, according to the commandment that says, "Be still and know." In this way he gathered the wealth of the Spirit and did not hesitate to share it richly with those in need. Instead he bore fruit a hundredfold and multiplied the talent, so that, as a faithful, wise and good servant, he might be blessed by the Master who loves the good. This Antiochus, then, lived in the times when the beastlike purpose and bloodthirsty onslaught of the Persians had pitifully dragged away every land [?] toward the rising sun that was subject to the Roman sceptre. He seized on this very thing as a fitting [?] occasion and composed a sacred book from the divine oracles, as he himself shows most clearly in it [?] …
… naming it, and setting it forth publicly for the greatest [?] of those who have read it from then until now …

FROM ANTIOCHUS, MONK OF THE LAVRA OF ABBA SABAS, TO EUSTATHIUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF ATTALINE IN THE CITY OF ANCYRA IN GALATIA, CONCERNING THE HOLY [?] FATHERS THERE, AND A PRAYER OF CONFESSION. [?] MONASTERY OF ATTALINE. You have written to me, honoured Father Eustathius, that you have endured much affliction. For fear of the Chaldaean storm that now prevails, you have moved from place to place and from country to country, and you have known hunger and thirst, not for bread and water but, as it is said, for hearing the word of the Lord. Because you can neither carry the weight of books nor easily find what you need in the places where you are staying, you told my littleness to compress the whole divine Scripture, Old and New, into a short form. It was not to become a burdensome load for us, and yet nothing that serves the benefit and salvation of the soul was to be left out. I readily obeyed your command and at once arranged everything you asked for from the divine Scripture into one hundred and thirty chapters. These are joined together and yet kept distinct from one another, so that the reader will not suffer confusion and muddle. I have sent them to your Godliness. When you receive them, send up fitting glory and thanks to God, who perfects his power in weakness. Repay us with your acceptable prayers, so that we may spend the rest of our life in a way that pleases God. If, as is likely, you find any fault, pardon both my lack of learning and the haste of the commission. You also sent me another request, honoured Father: to tell you about the holy fathers of our Lavra, and whether the things you said you had heard from many people about their way of life and their slaughter are true, since they are hard to believe and go beyond anything one hears. I thought it necessary first to tell you briefly

what concerns them, and then to add the contents of the divine [Scripture]. As for their virtuous way of life, this is not the occasion to recount it, nor is it a task for my tongue. I say only this: they were truly divine men, if indeed one should call them men and not angels. They had grown old in asceticism, in stillness and in labours for piety from their youth. They were aged and venerable, grey in hair and in understanding, good, humble-minded, orderly, self-controlled, truthful, blameless, just and God-fearing. They kept away from every evil deed, lacked no good thing, and were filled with divine love. Some of them were past fifty and sixty years of age and had never once left the Lavra. Some did not even go out to the church [?], and had not seen the city since [?] they became monks. They were adorned with every kind of virtue, angels on earth and men of heaven. That is why they won such an end and received the prize of victory. The Ishmaelites fell upon our Lavra one week before the holy city was taken, and they plundered all the sacred vessels of the church. Most of the fathers withdrew at once, but the steadfast servants of Christ stayed in the Lavra, unwilling to leave the place. The barbarians seized them and tortured them mercilessly for many days, thinking they would find money, though these men owned nothing of this world. In the end, having failed in their aim, they flew into a frenzy and hacked them all limb from limb. But the blessed ones rejoiced, and with radiant faces they gave up their souls to the Lord with thanksgiving, as men who had long desired to depart and be with Christ. Their bodies lay unburied where they had been thrown for many days, and then we arrived from Arabia. When Abba Nicomedes saw the pitiful sight of the fathers, he fainted and was carried off almost dead, so to speak. But the most holy Modestus came and gathered all the bodies of the saints. He washed them, weeping many tears, embraced the holy and steadfast remains, and laid them in the tombs of the fathers. When he had completed the customary rite over them, he spoke over them the saying of Isaiah: "Righteous men are taken away, and no one takes it to heart; the righteous man is taken away from the presence of wickedness; his burial shall be in peace." And: "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord, and no torment shall touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, but they are at peace, and their hope is full of immortality. Having been disciplined a little, they will receive great good, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself, and like a whole burnt offering he accepted them, and [?] ² "The holy remains": holy relics.

in the time of their visitation they will shine forth." Having said this about our holy fathers, he urged all of us not to abandon our place but to endure nobly in our trials. He told us to remember the Lord, who says, "Narrow is the gate and hard the way that leads to life," and the Apostle, who says, "Through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of heaven." We heeded his exhortation and stayed in the Lavra for about two months. Then came another report of barbarians, and in fear we fled to a monastery near the holy city, about twenty stadia away, called the monastery of Abba Anastasius, which had no one in it at that time. After we had spent about two years there, the most holy Modestus whom I have mentioned urged us again to return and live in our own place. Persuaded by his good counsel, some of us returned at once and lived in the Lavra. Others came a little later, for fear of the Saracens who were our neighbours. And some of us stayed in that monastery itself together with Justin, its most holy abbot. He had renounced the world in the Lavra and spent very many years there, and he was so distinguished in many virtues that he was even honoured with the rank of priest. By the grace of Christ, this most God-fearing Justin gathered a large community in that monastery. He keeps the rule of the Lavra and the rest of its order without any change, and in all Palestine, or in any other community, one could not find such a spiritual order. It flourishes and grows every day, and like Isaac it goes on and becomes great. So we rejoice, rightly judging from this that the seed of our holy father Sabas shines like stars in every land. As for us, the lowly ones, by the grace of God and the zeal of the most holy Modestus we live in stillness more than in former years. We give thanks to God and glorify him, who puts to death and makes alive, and who alone does great wonders. For his goodness had compassion on us and brought our place to great progress, as far as the times allow, on account of his holy servants who truly served him there before us. His goodness also gave us a father and shepherd worthy of his providence: the most holy Thomas. He has spiritual knowledge, is adorned with every kind of virtue, and has practised the life of stillness from early youth. He is gentle, loves the brethren and is full of compassion, lowly in heart and most fervent in prayer and in the rule. Therefore during his leadership God has also increased the number of his disciples. The number of the fathers who were slain comes to forty-four names. Their memory is kept on the fifteenth of May. And by the grace of Christ and the zeal of our most holy father

Modestus, the other monasteries of the desert are also inhabited again. Here, then, honoured father Eustathius, is the brief account I have given your Godliness about our saints and the Lavra. I also bring you other good news, which gladdens [?] your soul and the soul of every Christian who hears it. The most holy Modestus cares not only for the monasteries of the desert but also for the city and all the surrounding region, for God works with him in everything. He is truly our new Bezalel or Zerubbabel, filled with the Holy Spirit. He has rebuilt the venerable churches of our Saviour Jesus Christ that had been burned: the holy Cranion, his holy Anastasis, the august house of the precious Cross, the mother of churches, his holy [?], and the other venerable houses. Because of this we have good hopes for the future too, especially those who come from foreign lands to venerate the holy places, and all glorify God. To him belong all glory, honour and worship, now and always and to the ages of ages.

PRELIMINARY REFLECTION BY ANTIOCHUS THE MONK. The wise Solomon says in the Song: "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number." As far as we are able, we say that the sixty queens are the approved books, that is, the sixty canonical books of the Old and New Testaments. The eighty concubines are the books that are not approved, which are called apocryphal. They are called concubines because they have no open standing and are illegitimate. The maidens are the sayings of the Church's teachers of the new proclamation, because their word is pure. For maidens are called pure. Scripture says: "Let them seek a young virgin for the king," and they found the Shunammite

to warm him [?]. That is, heavenly thoughts and the words of those who sing [?]: "My heart grew hot within me, and as I meditate a fire will be kindled." For "Shunammite" means "heavenly." And: "Grain for young men, and fragrant wine for virgins." For those without guile are fed by the rain of heavenly bread, which endures to eternal life, and their drink comes from the bowl of the true vine. And: "The sayings of the pure are holy," and, "The sayings of the righteous are pure," as Scripture says. They are called innumerable because the word of their teaching is abundant and without measure. From the loom of these sixty queens, then, we have taken a few threads, and I have made a girdle to warm those who read with faith. A loom has many parts, yet it produces a tunic woven in one piece. In the same way, all the prophecies of the divinely inspired Scriptures came to their end in the tunic of the Master's dispensation, which he took from the holy, glorious and ever-virgin Mary. That tunic was corruptible, because it was subject to the same passions as ours, but he made it incorruptible, so that he might free us who are held by corruption and transform us into incorruption. By "girdle" I do not mean that Jewish one which Jeremiah hid and which rotted at the river Euphrates. I mean the girdle of the new grace, which the Lord showed us when he girded himself and wiped the feet of his disciples. He did this so that, cleansed from the filth of the old leaven, they might become a new lump. Then their feet would be beautiful, as the feet of those who bring good news of peace, and they would tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. With the beauty of this girdle Christ has clothed his Church. It covers our blemishes and the nakedness that came from Adam's transgression, as it is said: "You tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness." We put this girdle on from the divine Scriptures. For when we search them we find eternal life, our Lord Jesus Christ himself, our true God. But now the time calls us to add the chapters we have mentioned, to the glory and praise of the holy Trinity, the source of life: the Father, I mean, and the Son and the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

On Faith. With the Lord working with us and confirming the word, let us begin with the discourses on faith, and then go on to the others in order. First one must believe in God, that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him. For faith will stand forever. And: "The righteous shall live by faith." The one who is truly righteous by faith has a faith that is active, a faith that grows, a faith fully assured, a faith that shines in good works, so that the God of all may be glorified. Faith is the beginning of union with God. The perfect believer is a stone of God's temple, made ready for the building of God the Father. He is lifted up to the heights by the crane of Jesus Christ, which is the cross, with the Spirit as its rope. Faith is what hoists a person up, and love is the road that leads up to God. Such a person becomes a God-bearer, that is, a Christ-bearer, a temple of God and a bearer of holiness [?], adorned in every way with the commandments of Jesus Christ. Nothing is ranked above the beginning of life that comes through faith and love. But I mean an active faith, since faith without works is dead in itself. The works of faith are love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, humility and boasting in the Lord, and trust in God; to crucify the flesh; to rest from all one's works, as God rested from his own; to take up one's cross and follow; to live by the Spirit; to obtain the Spirit [?] … whom he may devour. Resist him, firm in the faith [?]. Paul says: "In him, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise." And again: "Above all, take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming darts of the Evil One." And again: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for. For by it the elders [?]. … These all [?] in faith." And again: "The righteousness of God [?] through faith, for all who believe." And again: "That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through

faith." And elsewhere: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. But to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness." And he adds: "That is why it depends on faith, so that it may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all the offspring, not only to those who are of the law but also to those who share the faith of Abraham. It was not written for his sake alone, but for ours also, to whom it will be counted, to us who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." And to Timothy: "Pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, with all who call on the Lord." And: "Without faith it is impossible to please God." And John: "This is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and that by believing you may have eternal life." And our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, says: "Whoever believes in me, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water." He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive. And again: "Who, then, is the faithful and wise servant?" And elsewhere: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." And to Martha: "Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live." And to the disciples: "Truly I tell you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these." And: "Whoever believes in me has eternal life." And again: "Believe in God, and believe also in me." We have now, I think, set out enough testimonies from the divine Scriptures about faith. By faith we mean the faith directed to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity, in whom we also believe. It is also necessary to set out the passages and testimonies of divine Scripture on this subject, for the enlightenment of readers. Throughout the whole of theological teaching, then, we see the Godhead sacredly hymned in two ways. It is hymned as a Monad and a Unity, because of the simplicity and oneness of its indivisibility, which is beyond nature, and by this, as by a unifying power, we are made one. And it is hymned as a Trinity, because its superessential fruitfulness shows itself in three hypostases. So we say that the theologians apply all the divine names to the superessential and consubstantial Trinity: names such as God, Lord, Holy, Good, Light, Life, Truth, Almighty, All-powerful, Lord Sabaoth (which means "of hosts"), and all the other names the theologians sacredly hymn. This can be learned from the Godhead itself as it teaches about itself: "Why do you ask me about what is good? No one is good but one, God." And to those in the vineyard: "Because I am good." And: "Your good Spirit." And to Moses: "I [?] 16. ³ Heb. [?] 1, 2, 15.

am He Who Is." And John: "That which was from the beginning," and, "He who is coming." And: "The Lord Almighty is his name." And: "The Spirit of truth, who is [?], who proceeds from the Father." And to Thomas: "I am the truth and the life." And: "Sanctify them in your truth." And: "Your word is truth." And: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father." And again: "When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all the truth. He will glorify me, because he will take what is mine and declare it to you." And again: "All that the Father has is mine; that is why I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you." And again: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will." And: "It is the Spirit that gives life." And: "The Lord is the Spirit [?]." And: "All things are from God, and through him and in him all things were created." And: "All things came into being through him." And: "You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created." And: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth." To sum up, the divine Word himself said: "I and the Father are one," and, "All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine." And again, he ascribes everything that belongs to the Father and to the Son himself jointly and in union to the divine Spirit as well: the reverence due to the divine working, and its [?] and unfailing cause. He does this when he says [?]: "… baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." All these passages show, then, that all theology is both united and distinguished. It is not right either to divide what is united or to confuse what is distinguished. What is united belongs to the whole Godhead: the Super-good, the Super-divine, the Super-essential, the Super-living, the Super-wise. With these go all the names that speak of it as cause [?]: the Good, the Beautiful, Being, the Life-giving, the Wise, and every name given to the cause of all good things from the gifts that befit its goodness. What is distinguished is the superessential name and reality of the Father, of the Son and of the Spirit. Among these no interchange, and no commonality at all, is brought in. [?] Since we have received the knowledge of God through faith, let us not ignore the grace given to us, which the Lord has truly [?]. For this reason the Lord received ointment on his head: that he might breathe incorruption upon the Church. So let no one be anointed with the foul smell of the unbelief [?] of the ruler of this age. Let us not turn aside from the straight road, so that we may be able to lay hold of the eternal good things and of everlasting life, in Christ

On Hope. From faith let us go on to hope, which comes second to it. Watered by faith, hope bears fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold and some a hundredfold. For nothing stands higher than a hope that is firmly founded. Love is named third but is in fact first of all the virtues, and we will speak of it later. The first was Enosh, son of Seth, a righteous man born of a righteous man: he hoped to call on the name of the Lord God. For all who are led by the hand through hope in God are brought up to him and are lit by the radiance of the everlasting light. When King David had grown old and was not warmed by his own righteous deeds, he asked for a virgin to keep him warm, the Shunammite. "Shunammite" means "heavenly." But the king did not know her; that is, he did not corrupt his heavenly hope. See what Scripture says: "If two lie together, they keep warm." If faith has hope, it has its proper work, and it is warmth to the one who has it. As blessed Peter says: "Gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and set your hope fully on the grace that is being brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ, as children of obedience." And the son of Sirach says: "Who ever hoped in the Lord and was forsaken? Or who held fast in the fear of him and was overlooked?" And the Psalmist says: "Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord." And: "Let all who hope in you rejoice." And again: "In him my heart hoped, and I was helped, and my flesh flourished again", and from his own help [?]. And he led others by the hand, saying: "Hope in him, all you assembly of peoples; pour out your hearts before him, for God is your helper." And: "Hope in the Lord and do good." And: "Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act." And Isaiah says: [?]

"We have hoped in the name of the Lord, and in the remembrance of him is our desire." And again Paul: "For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope, for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience." And again: "We who have fled for refuge have strong encouragement to lay hold of the hope set before us, which we have as an anchor, sure and steadfast." And he adds: "The ploughman ought to plough in hope, and the thresher to thresh in hope of a share." And in the Gospel according to Luke it says of Simeon: "It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord's Christ." He did not let his hope die. He kept waiting for the longed-for Redeemer and Saviour of the world, and when he joyfully received him in his arms he said: Release me, Master, to depart to your kingdom, for which I long. For I have received my hope, the Lord's Christ. To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Feasting. About feasting the author of Proverbs says: "If you sit down to dine at the table of rulers, consider carefully what is set before you, and put out your hand knowing that you must provide such things yourself. But if you are rather greedy, do not desire his dishes." And another writer says: "Are you seated at a great table? Do not open your throat over it. Remember that an evil eye is a wicked thing. Do not stretch out your hand wherever he looks, and do not jostle him in the dish. Judge your neighbour's feelings by your own, and be thoughtful in every matter. Eat what is set before you like a human being, and do not chomp, or you will be hated. Be the first to stop, for the sake of good manners, and do not be greedy [?], so that you do not give offence first. And if you are seated among many, do not reach out your hand before they do. How little is enough for a well-bred man!" And Moses says: "Take heed to yourself, lest when you have eaten and are full you forget the Lord your God." And Paul: "Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God." And: "...and not for disputes over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats vegetables." And he adds: "The one who eats must not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats. For who are you to judge someone else's servant? It is before his own master that he stands or falls." And again: "The one who eats

eats to the Lord, and gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat does not eat to the Lord." And: "Do not hinder the work of God for the sake of food." And he adds: "All things are indeed clean, but it is wrong for a person to eat in a way that causes stumbling." And: "Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves. But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because it does not come from faith." And: "Food will not commend us to God. We are no better off if we eat, and no worse off if we do not." And the author of Proverbs says: "Do not be deceived by filling your belly. For a soul that is full scorns honeycombs, but to a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet." And the Apostle, declaring foods clean, says: "...which God created to be received with thanksgiving by believers and by those who know the truth. For everything God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word and by prayer." And: "To the pure all things are pure." And: "When you come together to eat, wait for one another." The law also says: "When you have eaten and are full, bless the Lord your God." And David said in thanksgiving: "You have put gladness in my heart, from the fruit of grain and wine and oil." And again: "For he satisfied the empty soul and filled the hungry soul with good things." And the good Lord, wishing us to be humble-minded, says: "When you sit down to a meal, do not take the place of honour, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited by him, and the one who invited you both comes and says to you, 'Give this man your place,' and then in shame you start to take the lowest place. But when you sit down to table, go and recline in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, 'Friend, move up higher.' Then you will be honoured in front of all who are at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." This is enough for understanding and benefit. But it is good also to recall Job, for he says: "If I ate my morsel alone and did not share it with the orphan, for from my youth I brought him up like a father..." And again the Lord says: "When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or your neighbours, in case they invite you in return and you are repaid. But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. You will be repaid by God at the resurrection of the righteous." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Gluttony. Everyone needs to do violence to the belly and master it, but especially those who wish to serve God. For moderation is best in everything. Eating without restraint is like an overloaded ship. The body needs nourishment, not luxury; frugality, not surfeit; sufficiency, not extravagance. The first of each pair benefits both body and soul, producing health, strength and good condition. The second harms both: it not only ruins health but also gives birth to the most painful diseases. A clear proof is that ascetics who embrace frugality are wiser, more self-controlled and healthier than those who have chosen a soft way of life. And there is more: whoever masters the belly also weakens the passions. Whoever is overcome by food increases his pleasures, for just as a lot of wood raises a great flame, so a great quantity of food raises desire. Costly food delights the gullet, but it feeds the sleepless worm of licentiousness. Just as land that has gone to waste brings forth thorns, so the mind of a glutton sprouts shameful thoughts. A gluttonous monk becomes nothing but a beast of burden for his belly, and he counts up the feasts of the saints, while the abstinent monk imitates their lives. The glutton takes pride in nothing but a broad and roomy belly, the storehouse of his precious dung. What is more, the Spirit who dwells in the gluttonous man is grieved, and since he cannot bear the stench he departs from him. As smoke drives away bees, so the glutton drives away the grace of the Holy Spirit. It is better, then, to pass by the spiced dishes of the belly and meet the body's needs with plain food, so that we do not become like the belly-enslaved people in the wilderness. "For the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play," it says. By eating and drinking without measure they forgot God's commandment and ran aground in the madness of idolatry. So the apostle Paul rightly writes about their successors: "Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things." And again: "Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both the one and the other." And again: "If your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not let your food destroy the one for whom Christ died." And he adds: "For such people do not serve our Lord but their own belly, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the innocent." And again: "For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace." And: "For it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace,

not by foods." And again: "For the kingdom of heaven is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." It is not luxury and self-indulgence, which, as has been said, are food for worms. For luxury is nothing but a banquet for creeping things. So James too, reproaching the slaves of the belly, wrote: "You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence; you have fattened your hearts as for a day of slaughter." And the Lord says to the unbelieving Jews: "Truly I tell you, you are looking for me not because you saw signs, but because you ate some of the loaves and were filled." And he goes on: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man gives you." To him be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.

Drunkenness is much more grievous than gluttony, and divine Scripture strictly forbids it. Indeed it is wrong to take pride in it, as some worldly-minded people boast of getting drunk. For heavy drinking produces nothing but derangement of mind and poverty, and it leaves the body wasted and flabby. It is good and acceptable, then, to take a little wine because of bodily weakness. When the earth is watered by moderate rain, it sends up the seed sown in it clean and multiplied, but when it is drenched by heavy rains it bears only thorns and thistles. In the same way the earth of the heart, if we use wine in moderation, yields its natural seeds clean; but if it is soaked through by heavy drinking, it bears all its thoughts as nothing but thorns. And there is more: it makes the drunkard a laughing-stock to fools and an object of mourning to the wise. For divine Scripture says that Noah, a righteous man, drank wine and became

drunk, and lay naked. It was not that the righteous man was given to wine; he simply had no experience of using it. Foolish Ham laughed at him, but his sensible sons covered him. So let us flee the demon of drunkenness, brothers, so that he does not make a mockery of us. Let us rather make ourselves secure with sobriety, so that a person may be whole, together with his ruling mind. As the author of Proverbs commands: "Do not be a wine-drinker, for every drunkard will become poor." And again: "Who has woe, and who has uproar? Who has quarrels, and who has disgust and idle talk? Who has wounds for no reason? Whose eyes are bloodshot? Is it not those who linger over wine? Is it not those who look out for where drinking parties are held?" And he adds: "Do not get drunk with wine, but keep company with righteous men." And another writer says: "Do not play the hero over wine, for wine has destroyed many." And again: "Whoever is pleasant company at drinking-bouts will leave disgrace in his own strongholds." And again: "Do not be a wine-drinker, for luxury does not suit a fool." And again: "Wine is licentious and drunkenness is insolent; no one who mixes with them will be wise." And the prophet Hosea says about the people of old: "The heart of my people received wine and drunkenness." And Isaiah, lamenting over those who linger over wine, said: "Woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink, who stay up late, for wine will inflame them." And again: "They have gone astray through the drunkenness of wine." Joel too cries out: "Wake up from your wine, you drunkards; weep and wail, all you who drink wine to drunkenness." Weeping and wailing are laid on the lovers of drink. And truly drunkenness belongs to the most shameful of people and to those who have gone astray, as Job says when he was oppressed by certain people: "Let them stagger like a drunkard." But those who wish to live soberly walk on the straight road without straying, for they listen to the Apostle when he says: "Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery." And again: "Drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God." And: "The widow who lives for pleasure is dead even while she lives." And he adds: "So do not be foolish, but understand what the will of God is." For all shameful passions spring up from drunkenness, as David also says: "Night was my light in my delight." That is: it was night all around me, wretch that I was, and I did not know it. He calls luxury night. For according to the Apostle, mist and darkness belong to those who are drunk. I will gladly pass over the story of Lot's daughters. The Lord confirms what has been set out and commands everyone: "Take care that your hearts are not weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness." To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

On Self-Control. Self-control befits everyone, but especially those who wish to please God. By self-control we mean not only control over food but control in the comprehensive sense, that is, abstaining from everything forbidden. Whoever practises self-control, then, must be self-controlled in all things, as the Apostle says. If any one of a person's limbs is removed, the whole remaining form of that person is disfigured. In the same way, whoever neglects a single virtue destroys the whole beauty of self-control. So we must work hard not only at the bodily virtues but also at those that can cleanse our inner self. For the work of self-control is to abstain from every irrational pleasure and to do nothing contrary to the will of God's commandments. Self-control is a bridle that chokes the impulse of desire towards food, money or glory. For nothing good can be born without patience and the most general self-control. "By your endurance you will gain your souls." So whoever wants to achieve self-control must pray continually. "Pray without ceasing," he says. Prayer and self-control keep the mind away from worldly pleasures and hold it back from all wrongdoing. By "flesh and blood" the Apostle meant the passions of the flesh, which drag the mind down to their way of thinking, when he said: "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." This flesh is food for demons: "When evildoers came near me to devour my flesh." So whoever wastes away his flesh through self-control starves the demons and makes them weaker in their war against him. As has been said, then, we must practise self-control through all the senses: through sight, hearing, smell, tongue and belly, and touch, through a seemly gait, and the rest. For whoever is self-controlled must rise above every shameful pleasure and desire. Those who love self-control are plainly sound in body and healthy in mind. Their souls are gladdened by delight in God, and their minds turn away from earthly things and reach out for the things above. Because they are strangers to all indulgence, they are found to hate the passions and to love God. Their prayer to the Lord is pure, and they honour God together with the angels. Scripture also says: "Do not go after

your desires; restrain yourself from your appetites, and do not delight in great luxury." And: "Do not be insatiable for every delicacy, and do not throw yourself on a great many dishes. For with a great many foods comes sickness... but whoever takes care will add to his life." And blessed David, showing the perfection of self-control, says: "I was struck down like grass and my heart withered, for I forgot to eat my bread." And: "Because of the sound of my groaning my bones cleave to my flesh." And again: "For I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping." And Paul says: "Put to death your members that are on earth." And again: "Let us cleanse ourselves, brothers, from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, so that we may become temples of the living God." And Peter: "To your faith add virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge self-control, and to self-control endurance." We must therefore always be sober and watchful, and seek and think on the things above, according to the Lord's commandment, which says: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like men waiting for their master to return from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may open the door to him at once." And he adds: "Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will gird himself, have them recline at table, and come and serve them." To him be glory forever. Amen.
On Fasting. A monk who wishes through pure fasting [?] himself ... [?] (Ezek. 16:50 [?])

...from there he finds rest. For the one who fasts is like the flower of the palm called halation [?]: dull-coloured on the outside, but snow-white within and [?]-fruited. In the same way the one who fasts looks gloomy on the outside, but being full of light within, he speaks with God boldly. "For," it says, "though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day." Fasting, then, is not only eating late but also eating little. It is not eating every other day [that is ascetic discipline], but not eating much. For ascetic discipline is a frugal table with a single kind of food. But a fast is irrational if it waits for the appointed time and then, at mealtime, rushes to the table without restraint [?], binding [?] the mind together with the flesh to the pleasure of what is set out. In self-control over food it is also necessary to observe this: one must never come to loathe any food. That is accursed and altogether demonic. For we do not abstain from foods as if they were evil — God forbid! — but so that, by drawing ourselves away from pleasant foods, we may chastise the inflamed members of the flesh in due measure. When the body is healthy it should be chastised as is fitting, and when it is sick it should be fed up moderately. For the body that is in the contest should not be [?], but should have as much as is enough to be able to contend. First of all the law commands: "Whoever makes a vow shall keep himself pure from wine and strong drink, and shall eat nothing that comes from the vine all the days of his life, for he shall be holy to the Lord." And Daniel says: "I was mourning for three full weeks. I ate no rich bread, no wine entered my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil." Having wasted himself away like this by going without food, and not craving anything to eat at all, he became a man of the desires of the Spirit. He was counted worthy to behold unspeakable mysteries and to speak with [?] the archangel Gabriel. Likewise the fare of the three youths came from the seeds of the earth, and their self-control and love for God turned the fire of the furnace into dew. Moses received the law through forty days of fasting. Elijah too became an eyewitness of God's glory through as many days of fasting. Hannah received Samuel through prayer and fasting. And the Apostle brought his body into subjection "in labours, in sleepless nights, in fastings." The prophet Joel also says: "Sanctify a fast, proclaim a service, cry out: Alas, alas, for the day of the Lord is near." And shortly after: "And now says the Lord our God: Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping and with mourning; rend your hearts and return to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and compassionate." [Note:] Not halation but elatē, which is also called spathē in

[...] is, long-suffering and abounding in mercy, and relenting over your evils.” And again David: “But I, when they troubled me, put on sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting.” And: “My knees grew weak from fasting, and my flesh was changed for want of oil.” For true fasting is not only wasting oneself away, but also giving the cost of what one would have eaten to a widow or a poor man, so that the one who has received mercy, once filled, may pray for him, and his sacrifice may become acceptable to God. As Isaiah also says: “When you fast, break your bread for the hungry.” Our good Master, wishing to teach us by deed, first fasted himself. And about the man possessed by a demon he says: “This kind can come out by nothing except by prayer and fasting.” And he adds: “When you fast, do not be like the hypocrites.” And: “Blessed are those who hunger now, for they shall be filled.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

[?] and is of no benefit; but this man carries the image of wealth about like an idol. And just as for those who are slaves to their belly the belly becomes their god, so gold becomes god for him. This demon becomes a moth in a man's bones, devouring him through anxiety and sleeplessness. And indeed this passion is rightly forbidden in the divine Scripture, since, as has been said, it is the faithless and the hopeless who suffer from it, or rather the lovers of pleasure and idolaters. For they do not set their hope on God but on royal [?]; and having turned aside from the straight road, they are swept over cliffs and into pits of destruction, as Scripture says: “He who loves gold will not be justified.” And again: “Nothing is more lawless than a lover of money, for such a man puts even his own soul up for sale.” And: “Many have been brought to ruin on account of gold.” So too Judas, through love of money, was not only wrecked and cast out of the company of the apostles, but also became the betrayer of the Master, and perished by hanging. Truly love of money is the abomination of leprosy, as was shown through Gehazi. Yet it does not cling to one who is willing to be rid of it, for it is not natural but a matter of choice, and such a man can quickly be cleansed by crying out to Jesus: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” But for the unwilling it is “a stumbling block to those who are infatuated with it.” “Blessed, then, is the man who has been found blameless and has not gone after gold,” according to Scripture. For James, threatening lovers of money, says: “Your gold and your silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and will eat your flesh like fire.” And again: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you.” Much like these, Habakkuk the prophet, reproaching lovers of money, says: “Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own.” He spoke well in saying “what is not his own,” for wealth belongs to all [?]. And David, agreeing with them, said: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and grew strong in his vanity.” And Job: “Even if a sinner gathers silver like earth and prepares gold like clay, the righteous will obtain all these things.” And, confident in his own blameless life, he said: “If I made gold my strength; if I rejoiced when great wealth came to me” [?]. “Better, then, is a little for the righteous than the great wealth of sinners.” Paul also testifies that love of money is the root of all evils. For the lover of money is both without sympathy and without mercy. But our Saviour and Lord, knowing that the passion of love of money is the destruction of the soul, offers the fitting cure, saying: “Do not acquire gold or silver or copper for your belts.” And he adds: “Truly I tell you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty,” as [?].

On taking bribes. The bribe-taker, the greedy man, the lover of money and the usurer are one four-horse chariot, with arrogance as their charioteer and leader. He has been cast down by the Lord, yet he drives along all who follow him into his own destruction. It is not right, then, for those of sound mind to be driven by the enemy, lest they be dragged down with him into the pit of punishment; rather, they should be led to life by the Apostle, who says: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content. For those who wish to be rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil.” He, then, who fears the commandment of the Apostle, or rather of him [...]

[...] again: “The bribe-taker destroys himself, but he who hates the taking of bribes will live.” And again: “He who receives gifts in his bosom unjustly does not prosper in his ways.” “A good name, then, is more to be chosen than wealth.” And David, beseeching God, said: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is full of bribes”—calling bribe-takers ungodly, lawless and men of blood. And again: “The fool and the senseless will perish, and leave their wealth to strangers.” This is as much as to say: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?”—calling those who trust in wealth fools, because life in the flesh is so uncertain. And again: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to greed.” And Job, showing his purity, says: “If indeed I have touched bribes with my hands.” And our Lord and Saviour commands, saying: “Take care, and guard yourselves against all greed, for a man's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

On stinginess. Stinginess springs from smallness of soul, or rather from faithlessness and hopelessness. For if we do not trust him about the visible good things that his goodness richly provides us every day, but waver, how shall we trust him about the invisible, eternal and abiding good things that he himself promised to give us, “which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered the heart of man”? Rightly, then, does the divine Scripture reproach us: “A faint-hearted man, who will bear him?” Let us, then, entrust to him the needs of the body, we who plainly trust him with those of the spirit as well [?]. So let us hand over to him the care of all things, for he cares for us and knows what we need before we ask him. For the God of the simple is simplicity, as Wisdom also says: “He who walks in simplicity walks in confidence.” And again: “To the faithful belongs the whole world of riches, but to the faithless not even an obol.” And: “The blessing of the Lord is on the head of the righteous.” And: “Every simple soul is blessed; and he who sows righteousness will receive a sure reward. For the Lord will not let the soul of the righteous starve. But he who trusts in his wealth will fall.” And: “Property hastily gained with lawlessness dwindles, but he who gathers for himself with godliness will be increased.”

Moses too says: “If there is among you a needy man of your brothers, you shall not close your hand against him, but you shall lend him as much as he lacks.” And the Psalmist: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, to deliver their souls from death and to keep them alive in famine.” “The rich have become poor and gone hungry, but those who seek the Lord will not lack any good thing.” And: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.” And another: “He who has mercy on the poor is blessed.” And: “A merciful man does good to his own soul.” Likewise the Apostle: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. Let each give as he has decided in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” And the good Lord, the lover of souls, says: “Look at the birds of the sky: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” And he adds: “So do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

On those who lend. Lending is a duty, especially to brothers who share our faith and are fellow heirs, as the law also declares, for it says: “To your brother you shall lend”—that is, to one who is under the law—“but to a stranger you shall not lend”—that is, to the lawless. So says the law. The writer of Proverbs agrees, saying: “He who shows mercy will lend to his neighbour.” And: “He who strengthens his hand keeps the commandments.” And again: “Lend to your neighbour in the time of his need, and do not hold back from doing good to the needy whenever your hand is able to help. Do not say, ‘Go away and come back, and tomorrow I will give.’” Much the same the Psalmist urges, saying: “Good is the man who shows mercy and lends.” And again: “All day long the righteous man shows mercy and lends, and his seed will be a blessing.” And again: “The sinner borrows and will not repay, but the righteous has compassion and gives.” One must understand the aim of the divine Scripture: lending has been commanded as a way of showing mercy to one's neighbour, as it is written: “For the commandment's sake help the poor man; lose your silver for a brother's sake.” And again: “How beautiful is mercy in a time of affliction!”

If you help your fellow member of the body, you will have him come forward at the resurrection as a witness to your compassion, and not groaning against you. For this is not without profit. Let us not, then, become inhuman for the sake of gold and silver and spices, whose rust and moth will be a testimony against you; let us listen to Paul when he says: “He who shares, in simplicity; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” And: “Contributing to the needs of the saints.” And elsewhere: “Let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works for pressing needs, so that they may not be unfruitful.” The prophet Zechariah also says: “Judge righteous judgment, and show mercy and compassion, each to his neighbour.” And John: “Whoever has the world's goods and sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?” In keeping with these, the Lord who provides for our salvation commands, saying: “Give to everyone who asks of you, and do not turn away from him who wishes to borrow from you.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

The people of this world will not stop going to law until they have taken the property of the defendants with something extra, especially when they collect the interest before the debt itself, so that their “justice” becomes the beginning of great injustice. That is why usurers are called accursed and merciless, for they are abominable before God and men. And the very idea of interest is altogether forbidden to Christians. As the prophet says of the unjust city: “Interest and deceit have not departed from its streets.” And of the righteous man: “He did not put out his money at interest.” And again: “From interest and injustice he will redeem their souls.” And the writer of Proverbs: “He who increases his wealth by interest and usury gathers it for him who is kind to the poor.” And another: “Interest upon interest, and deceit upon deceit.” I know some who, for the sake of gain from interest, lost the principal along with their soul. Rightly, then, does the law command, saying: “You shall not charge your brother interest on money or food or anything.” And again: “You shall not put out your money at interest.” And: “You shall not give your food for profit.” And Ecclesiastes declares this about those who grow rich from interest or from injustice: “There is a grievous sickness that I have seen under the sun: wealth kept

by its owner to his own harm; and that wealth perishes in an evil distraction; and indeed all his days are spent in darkness and mourning and much anger and sickness, and their toil goes to the wind.” Likewise the Apostle, exhorting Timothy, said: “Command the rich in this present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of wealth, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy; to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may lay hold of eternal life.” Obeying the divine Scripture, then, brothers, let us depart from terrible greed and from this abominable device of interest; for interest is yoked together with deceit. Let us rather emulate the noble zeal of blessed Zacchaeus, saying with him: “Behold, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold,” so that we too may hear from our Master and Saviour, who knows our hidden things well: “Today salvation has come to this house.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

On greed. The Lord says: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will despise the one and hold to the other, or he will hate the one and love the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon.” “For having been set free from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness.” And: “You cannot serve God and Mammon”—which means wealth, as it says: “If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it.” For “woe to the sinner who walks on two paths”; since, according to the law, if one part is leprous and another clean, the whole is unclean. The greedy man, then, is never sated in his love of money. For when he has acquired much, he craves still more; and when he has made that his own as well, he desires yet other things again; and [?] he never ceases from this vain craving. And he does not know that in proportion to the attachment a man has to [?], so far does he share in apostasy from God. Such a man does not expect the end of his life, nor does he understand that he is a sojourner in this life and that what he has acquired is not his own. And so he is numbered among the fools; for he is a partner of that rich man whose land yielded abundantly. And Scripture rightly says of such people: “As Hades and destruction are never filled, so the eyes of men are insatiable.” Wishing, then, to heal this disease of greed, blessed James writes, saying:

“Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your wealth has rotted, and your garments have become moth-eaten.” And David addresses such people: “Surely man walks about as a phantom; yet he is troubled in vain; he heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” For hoarders are always found labouring in vain and toiling for others. “For those who wish to be rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil,” and into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge men into ruin and destruction, according to the Apostle. And again he commands us to flee greed, “which is idolatry, on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.” It is right, then, to cast off the senseless boasting that comes from wealth, by hating one's own desires—which is to hate one's own soul and to renounce all things for the sake of the glory of the Gospel of God. For he who lifts his thoughts away from all greed can see the schemes of the devil. When the mind has come out of bodily cares, it sees in like measure the cunning of the enemies. The writer of Proverbs also says: “Treasures will not profit the lawless, but righteousness delivers from death.” And: “A good name is more to be chosen than great wealth, and good favour than silver and gold.” “He who hoards grain, may he leave it to the nations.” And: “He who drives up the price of grain is cursed by the people, but blessing is on the head of him who shares.” And: “He who trusts in his wealth will fall, but he who helps the righteous will rise.” And the Lord says of the man who wanted to pull down his barns and build bigger ones: “Fool, this night the angels demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” And he adds: “So is everyone who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. DISCOURSE [?]. On distraction. Concerning distraction Ecclesiastes teaches us plainly as follows: “I gave my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the sun; for God has given an evil distraction to the sons of men, to be distracted by it.” And a little further on: “And I looked upon all my works that my hands had done, and on the toil I had toiled to do them, and behold, all was

vanity.” And again: “To the man who is good in his sight he has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, and to the sinner he has given distraction” (“has given” must be understood in the sense of “has permitted,” because of man's free will) “to add and to gather; for this too is vanity. All came from the dust, and all return to the dust.” And he adds: “Better is a handful of rest than two handfuls of toil.” And again: “In which I gave my heart to know my sin, and to see the distraction that is done on the earth; for neither by day nor by night does his eye see sleep.” And the whole life of the ungodly is spent in anxiety, for distraction is the beginning of evils. Since the divine Scripture has clearly shown us that a life of distraction belongs to the ungodly, we ought to flee from it—especially we who have supposedly renounced the world and are pursuing the angelic life. For quiet free from business is more precious than distinction in affairs, especially since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him.” And again: “That we may lead a calm and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.” Our much-longed-for Lord teaches us the same thing through Martha, saying to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” For Mary chose the good portion. So too through the parable of the sower, when he says: “Some fell among the thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them.” And in explaining it he adds: “This is the one who hears my word, and the care of wealth chokes the word, and it becomes unfruitful. But as for what was sown on the good ground, these are those who hear my word in a good heart”—that is, in quiet and calm—“and bear fruit to God, one thirty, another a hundred.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

On not loving the world. Men who, for love of Christ, have left parents and children and brothers, and have counted all the things of this age as refuse so that we may gain Christ: let us not seek glory here; let us not make provision for the flesh; let us not love what is temporary and perishable; let us not bury the talent in the ground; let us not seek a homeland here, but let us seek the one that is to come. Let us look to those who hated the world, and we shall see them with their minds transplanted to the eternal dwellings there—those who “went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted,” so that they might delight in the longed-for Maker of the world. Therefore

Let us too, looking to these wonderful men, follow in their footsteps, looking to nothing else — not to human glory, nor at all to the things of this age — so that we may be strong enough to obtain with them the good things prepared for those who love God. Let us flee, then, beloved, the world and the things in the world. "For the whole world lies in the power of the evil one," as the divine word has declared. A soul that has not been freed from worldly cares will neither love God sincerely nor loathe the devil as it ought, for it wears the cares of life like a heavy veil. If, then, we form the habit of despising the good things of this world, we can join the earthly appetite of the soul to its rational disposition, since the communion of the Holy Spirit arranges this for us. If, then, we are living in a foreign land, and our city is far away from this city, and we know the city in which we are going to live, why are we preparing fields and buildings and empty houses and costly furnishings in a land that belongs to someone else? Whoever prepares these things in a foreign city plainly does not expect to return to his own city, that is, to the Jerusalem above. Such reasoning belongs to foolish, double-minded and wretched people. He does not understand that all these things belong to another and are under another's authority, that is, the ruler of this age. So, as people living in a foreign land, we ought to prepare nothing more for ourselves than enough to suffice. For those who love their Lord and have him always in their heart believe in his promises and eagerly await them. It is good, then, instead of buildings¹ and money that are ours today but someone else's tomorrow, to buy relief for afflicted souls, as far as each is able, and to visit widows and orphans and not overlook them. Likewise in monasteries, and so to manage well what concerns ourselves, and to spend on them the wealth we have received from God in this life. For this is why our good Master provided these things to us: that they might be spent on this ministry, and that in return we might receive a treasure that never fails. It is far better, then, to buy fields and possessions of this kind, which last and go ahead of us to our mother city when we depart for it. So let us be free of care, beloved, for passing things, that we may attain the eternal; let us run past the world, that we may reach the world's Maker. Let us leave behind what is not ours, that we may enjoy what is ours (for the form of this world passes away like a dream), and if we make any use of this world, let us be as those who do not use it to the full, as blessed John also commands, saying: "Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not ¹ Perhaps read "possessions."

in him; for all that is in the world — the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life — is not from the Father but from the world." And: "The world is passing away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God abides forever." James also says: "Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God." And Paul: "Having put off the old self with its practices, and having put on the new self, which is being renewed." And he adds: "We brought nothing into the world, and clearly we can carry nothing out; but if we have food and clothing, with these we shall be content." Solomon too asks for these things, saying: "Give me neither riches nor poverty, but appoint for me what is needful and sufficient." And again [?]: "[What will it profit a man] if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will he give in exchange for his soul?" To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Forwardness. Forwardness is like a great scorching heat: people cannot bear its blaze, so they flee from it and run to the shade to cool themselves, and that shade is reserve and reverence. They desert the acrid smoke of forwardness and go over to the vapor of fragrant incense, which is stillness. They flee the stench of the garlic-eater and draw near to the one who is perfumed and sweet of speech, who pours forth a good word and gushes with the pure sayings of the Lord. For nothing so naturally destroys virtue as jesting, frivolity and idle talk. And [?]

again, nothing so renews a soul grown old as the fear of God, good prayer, meditating ceaselessly on the sayings of the Lord, always arming oneself with prayer, and pursuing the gain that comes from keeping vigil. For forwardness is abominable, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: "An abomination to the Lord is one who stares boldly; and the uneducated cannot control their tongue. If you flog a fool in the middle of the council and disgrace him, you will not take away his folly." And again: "A man's wisdom makes his face shine, but one with a shameless face will be hated." And in Proverbs: "Set your foot seldom in your friend's house, lest he grow weary of you and hate you." And: "Put reproachful words away from you." And again: "Whoever blesses a friend early in the morning in a loud voice will be thought no different from one who curses." And again: "Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from trouble." Let us strive, then, beloved, with all our strength not to give the passion of terrible forwardness room to lord it over us. For it is very grievous, it gives birth to all the passions, and it destroys all of a person's fruits and virtues; and it is hated by God as well. This is why God put Uzzah to death on the spot as accursed and unholy, when he dared to stretch out his hand to save the ark of God. Forwardness, then, and self-exaltation are displeasing to God and to people. David understood this clearly and said: "It is good for me that you humbled me, that I might learn your statutes." And: "Pierce my flesh with the fear of you, for I am afraid of your judgments." And Paul says: "A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, to beat me, so that I would not be too elated." And another says: "Who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will be bold before him?" This is why the Lord rebuked Peter when he spoke forwardly and said, "Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you," and told him: "Get behind me, Satan." But when the Lord asked him after the resurrection, "Peter, do you love me?" he answered with all reverence, "Yes, Lord, you know that I love you." To him be the glory. Amen.

Discourse 17. On Abstaining from Women. Abstaining from women is altogether fitting and appropriate for those who wish to lead a blameless and spotless life. For it is unfitting for those who have once fled the world to keep company with women or to be eager to meet with women. Some, on the pretext of compassion, suppose it is pious to live together with women. They do this recklessly and entirely on their own, and they become easy targets of reproach and the cause of many scandals. Though they behave so openly in this shameful way, they do not blush. What hidden evils would they not commit, if they pride themselves this way in open ones? How could they be brought to self-control, when they laugh at those who practice it? How will they stop when they are reproved, when they mock those who reprove them? How will they respect the divine oracles, when they think them myths? How will they fear the judgment, when by their works they proclaim that it does not even exist? How will they obey Christ, when they do not wish to keep his commandments but walk according to their own wills? This is not permitted to pious Christians. It is good, then, to desert from such company, for this is pleasing to God and to people. For the sight of a woman is a poisoned arrow. It wounds the soul and leaves its venom there, and the longer it lingers, the more it spreads corruption; but whoever is on guard will not fall into it and will not be wounded by its arrows. For as oil feeds the flame of a lamp, so meeting with a woman kindles the torch of pleasure; and as a spark that lingers in straw raises a flame, so the memory of a woman, if it stays, kindles desire. And just as with the fire-stones on the eastern mountain, the male and the female: when they are far from each other they burn no fire anywhere, but if the female comes near the male they kindle a fire and set everything ablaze, so also the rational male [?] … Let us flee from them, then, beloved, for meetings with them are poisonous and easily ensnare our souls. Let us hear, then, what divine Scripture declares about them. First the author of Proverbs says: "Sin began with a woman, and because of her we all die." And he goes on: "Do not give water an outlet, nor a wicked woman freedom of speech." And: "Do not fall for a woman's beauty."

And: "Do not desire a woman." And [?]: "Let your eyes look straight ahead, for a man's ways are before the eyes of God. Make straight paths for your feet; do not turn aside to the right or to the left. Turn your foot away from the evil way." And again: "Do not let desire for beauty conquer you; do not be caught by your eyes or captured by your eyelids, for a woman hunts the precious souls of men. With much talk she leads a man astray, and with the snares of her lips she drives him aground. He follows her, fooled like a silly bird, as an ox is led to the slaughter and a dog to the leash, not knowing that he is running for his life. So do not let your heart turn aside into her ways, for she has wounded and laid low many, and those she has slain are beyond counting; for her house is the way to Hades, leading down to the chambers of death." So says Solomon. And what of the Egyptian woman? She longed with carnal desire for the beauty of Joseph, a man of the utmost chastity; and when he did not consent, she pierced that pious man through with afflictions and distress by her lies, bringing him near death. Do you see how much affliction the Egyptian woman's fleshly persistence brought upon the righteous man? For this reason, then, it is in every way to our advantage to abstain from them. For meeting with them brings no profit to those who truly wish to gird their loins. Have you not heard about Samson the Nazirite, with whom the Spirit of the Lord went? Yet a woman destroyed so holy a man through wicked flesh and unlawful desire. This is why we are not permitted at all to sit with a woman, or to have any meetings with her whatever. Likewise, have you not been taught about David, whom God found to be a man after his own heart? Desiring a woman's beauty — I mean Bathsheba's — into how many evils did he fall! For when this truly holy man saw her bathing and was seized with desire for her beauty, how much wickedness did that greatest of men commit! He sinned against God not only by falling into adultery but also by ordering her husband to be killed. Do you see what a drama of wickedness David, the Lord's anointed, carried out because of desire? Let us learn from this not to desire. For if men so great were captured through women, how shall we who are weak escape, walking along with our own downfall and passing through the middle of the snare? Likewise Amnon was justly slain because of his sister Tamar. Likewise Solomon, who had wisdom and understanding and largeness of heart, wealth and great glory above all others — he too was ruined through a woman and became an apostate because of women. And the elders who sat as judges against Susanna, by persistently gazing at and studying another man's beauty, fell into the sea of desire and rose up against blessed Susanna. So much for desire. Jesus the son of Sirach also exposes a woman's wickedness for all to see: "All wickedness is small

compared with a woman's wickedness." And again: "I would rather live with a lion and a dragon than with a wicked woman." And the author of Proverbs: "Keep your way far from her; do not go near the doors of her house, lest strangers be filled with your strength and you repent at the end." It is good, then, to hold to the one who says, "Flee the world and the sight of them" [?]; for "everyone who looks at a woman with desire for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Not Lingering with Women Who Sing [?]. It does us no good to keep lingering with women who sing, for we are harmed by meeting with them — the so-called nuns. For the image of women seen begins to shake a man's heart, to draw his mind away from stillness and to drag it after them; and then the mind gapes idly at prayer, is distracted from glorifying God, and is taken up with anxious thought about them. For the habit of meeting with them becomes in a monk's heart like a worm in wood and a moth in a garment. If, then, you wish to remain chaste, flee meeting with them, and do not give them the liberty of being familiar with you. At first they show reverence and play the part, but later they shamelessly dare anything. Before you have met, they speak gently, eyes cast down; they weep constantly, put on a modest air and sigh bitterly. They ask about purity and listen with pleasure. At the second meeting they look up a little; at the third, you smiled, and she laughed freely. After that they even speak words that soften you toward the shameful passion. These become hooks for you, baited for death. It is better, then, to come near a burning fire than near a young woman, when you yourself are young. For when you touch fire and feel the pain, you jump back at once; but once a woman's words have made you slack, you will find it hard to withdraw. It is good, then, and pleasing to God and to people, to decline and not to keep lingering

[?] … we have no need of their vain and soul-harming company, lest grief arise in our souls. For the demon who loves sin devises many schemes against us: he prompts them to plead with groans and tears that we visit them continually and look after them for the sake of the Lord's reward. And when we give in to them, what we carry away as our reward is wounds in the soul that are hard to heal, and the most shameful thoughts. Then the heart, in turmoil, is tormented as if by executioners stretching it this way and that — the mind on one side and the passion on the other. It is vanity for us, then, as was said before, to have left parents and brothers only to acquire acquaintances that ruin the soul. For it is altogether unfitting for a man who wishes to live as an ascetic to eat and drink with a woman, to be waited on by a woman, to look after women, or to have any acquaintance with them at all. Likewise it is unfitting for women under the rule to pair themselves with men, so that no one may be scandalized because of us, but that we may give no offence to anyone. "Knowing," he says, "the fear of the Lord, we persuade people, but we are made manifest to God." Let us fear, then, as has been said, to scandalize anyone, hearing the Lord say that it would be better for a man to have a millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea than to scandalize one of these little ones. We must flee from them, then, as from the face of a serpent and from great sin, because for those who wish to live as ascetics, not only their company but even the thought of them is deadly. The author of Proverbs teaches us this when he says: "Do not give your wealth to a woman," nor your mind to later regret [?]. And another says: "Do not linger with a woman who sings, lest you be caught by her wiles." I think Isaiah too speaks of them: "Because the daughters of Zion were haughty and walked with outstretched necks and with winking eyes," and so on. And he adds: "And the Lord will uncover their form in that day." This happened, I suppose, at the coming of the Chaldeans. He also says elsewhere: "Do not gaze at a virgin, lest you stumble and incur the penalties for her." And again: "Wine and women will lead astray the hearts of the wise." And Ecclesiastes: "More bitter than death is to seek a woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net and whose hands are fetters; one who is good before God will be delivered from her, but the sinner will be caught by her." And he adds: "Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and walk blamelessly in your ways, and not in the sight of your eyes; and know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment." Likewise the Apostle: "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil." We, then, who seem to know the Scriptures and do not keep them, are liable to a heavier charge than those

who do not know them, according to the word of the Lord: "That servant who knew his master's will and did not act according to his will shall receive many blows." And he adds: "From everyone to whom much was given, they will demand all the more." To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

On Fornication. The many-branched passion of fornication springs up from meeting with women. For the flattering conversations of wanton women easily plant that terrible bait in a man's heart. Not only that, but the demon of fornication is twofold, establishing itself in both soul and body, and for this reason we must take up a twofold struggle against it. Bodily fasting alone is not enough for anyone to acquire perfect chastity and purity, unless there is also contrition of heart, earnest prayer to God, constant meditation on the Scriptures, toil and manual labor, which can restrain the disorderly impulses of the soul. Above all, humility of soul helps, for without it no one can overcome either fornication or the other passions. We must also guard the heart with all vigilance against filthy thoughts. "For out of it come," as the Lord says, "evil thoughts." If, then, we are to compete lawfully and be crowned, as the Apostle says, by conquering the unclean spirit of fornication, let us not trust in our own strength or asceticism, but in the help of God our Master. For a man does not stop being attacked by this spirit until he truly believes that it is not by his own effort and toil, but by God's protection and help, that he is delivered from this disease. It is good, then, for driving away the adversary and for purity of body, before sleep, upon [?] …

"Grant us, Master, as we go to sleep, rest for the body, and guard us from the dark sleep of sin; deliver us from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Grant us holiness in your fear, and deliver us from every dark and nocturnal sensuality. Stop the impulses of the passions; quench the burning of the body; put down the uprisings of the flesh; lull to sleep the passions of the body and the mind of the flesh. Grant us, O God, a watchful mind, a temperate thought, a sober heart, and light sleep free from every satanic fantasy; and rouse us for the night and morning services. Grant us to glorify you all night long, to hymn your magnificent name, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, forever."

It is good, then, as was said before, to escape the nets and hooks of women and to keep away from them. For the most wise Solomon, having learned this by experience, exhorts everyone, saying: "Do not pay attention to a worthless woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot, which for a time is smooth to your throat, but afterward you will find it more bitter than gall. So do not fix your eye on her." And again: "Do not pay attention to a worthless woman; for the feet of folly lead those who deal with her down to Hades with death. Keep your way far from her." And again: "Do not go to meet a woman who plays the harlot, lest you fall into her snares." And he adds: "Can anyone tie fire up in his bosom and not burn his clothes?
