Or can anyone walk on burning coals and not scorch his feet? So no one who touches her will go unpunished." And the law says: "You shall not commit fornication; you shall not commit adultery. Whoever commits adultery with his neighbor's wife shall surely be put to death." And David: "Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding." And the prophet Hosea, grieved over the people, said: "They were led astray by a spirit of fornication, and the people that had understanding embraced a harlot." And again: "They have played the harlot utterly; they loved dishonor." And again: "A spirit of fornication is in them, and they have not known the Lord." And the Apostle writes, saying: "Flee fornication. Every sin a person commits is outside the body, but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body." And he adds: "Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a price." And in those who are truly faithful, who have the Spirit of God, nothing carnal can exist — namely fornication, impurity, licentiousness and the rest. For the carnal will not inher[it] the kingdom of God …

[?] …will inherit. For those who do such things are already dead. And the author of Proverbs says: “Turn your eye away from a beautiful woman, for many have been led astray by the beauty of women.” And: “Do not sit carousing with her over wine, lest your soul turn aside to her, and your spirit slip into destruction.” And another says: “A woman’s fornication shows in the raising of her eyes.” “Know that you are walking in the midst of snares.” And again Paul: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Do you not know that whoever is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her?” And again: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” And he adds more weightily: “If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and that temple you are.” And again: “But let fornication and impurity not even be named among you. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor.” And again: “And the sanctification of the body, without which no one will see the Lord.” And the Lord says: “I tell you, whoever divorces his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery.” To God belongs glory forever. Amen.

On Chastity. Chastity is honored and praiseworthy, and has confidence before God and men, and it lies beyond the reach of envy. And even if some hostile people are in the habit of slandering those who wish through it to draw near to God, the truth is plainly brought to light, as in the case of Joseph, and of blessed Susanna in the story of Daniel. For she chose a temporary death rather than lose the crown of chastity. And the judgment of God (that is, Daniel, for that is how the name is interpreted) condemned the envious judges, declared the chaste woman free, and rescued her from death. So too Joseph, slandered by the Egyptian woman and shut up in prison, not long afterward came to govern Egypt. And the victory of chastity [?]

[?] …to learn the mystery of the faith, and to be shown to be a great wonder-worker. For the lovers of chastity not only have praise in this life, but they will also receive the crown of beauty and the tunic of chastity from the hand of the Lord; and they will say: “Let our soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the tunic of gladness; as on a bridegroom he has set a turban on me, and like a bride he has adorned me with ornaments.” These will shine in the kingdom of the Father, if they truly possess the other virtues as well, those that befit chastity. There life will appear to them, and length of days, calm and untroubled, from which pain, sorrow and sighing have fled. The perfectly chaste person guards himself on every side. For I have heard of a certain king among the pagans who, on seeing a priestess at Ephesus who appeared exceedingly beautiful, left Ephesus at once, fearing that he might be overpowered against his will and do something improper. And Cyrus the Persian would not even consent to look at Spania [?], who was reputed to have a wonderful and irresistible beauty. If, then, even [?] the precepts of outsiders bear witness to these things without the saving oracle, how much more should we, the disciples of Christ? It is necessary, therefore, to practice self-control, and to master not only speech but also sight. For continual gazing is the road that leads to the deed. And even if it does not go on to the act, it meanwhile defiles the mind and makes the one it has caught an adulterer. Who is so bold as to gaze continually at the beauty of others and say that he is not harmed at all? And if this is difficult, one must above all avoid frequent meetings with women. And that one must bridle the eyes, the blameless and chaste Job says, speaking with his friends: “If my heart has followed another man’s wife, if I have lain in wait at her doors, then let my wife also please another. For the fury of anger is unrestrained, to defile a man’s wife; for it is a fire burning on every side, and whomever it comes upon, it destroys from the roots.” And blessed Paul admonishes in his letter: “I appeal to you, therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.” And he says to Titus: “Older men are to be sober, dignified, self-controlled; older women likewise reverent in behavior, teachers of what is good, so that they may train the young women to love their husbands, to love their children, to be self-controlled and pure.” And again: “So that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age.” And to Timothy: “Honor widows who are truly widows.” And he adds: “She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day”; just as the holy Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, who lived chastely with her husband seven years from her virginity, as the

Gospel declares, and who, being a widow of about eighty-four years, did not depart from the temple, serving the Lord with fasting and prayers; and, being deemed worthy of prophecy, she came up at that very hour and gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke to all who were awaiting redemption in Jerusalem about the Lord, our God and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

Discourse 21. On Virginity. Virginity is close to chastity, but since it is higher both than chastity and than the other virtues, it rivals the angels and draws near to God by its purity. Truly great, then, is the possession of virginity, angelic and heavenly. A proof of this is that we do not readily find anyone in the divine Scriptures before the Law who was distinguished in this virtue. And under the Law no one could name anyone except the earthly angel and heavenly man, Elijah the Tishbite, and his disciple Elisha; perhaps also Jeremiah, and a few others among the prophets who can easily be counted; and the one who became great among those born of women, the mediator between the Old and New Covenants. For he was a true virgin, in body and in spirit; and because of the sincerity and purity of his life he was not only called the friend of the bridegroom but was also deemed worthy to baptize the Lord himself. And no one could point to more than these among those before the Law and under the Law who pleased God through virginity. Among the Greeks, and their so-called philosophers, not only has virginity never yet appeared, but they do not even believe that any human being clothed in a body could stand up to it; and rightly so, for how could they believe in virginity, who made gods of shameful passions and live like pigs in every kind of licentiousness and debauchery? And the Jews to this day neither embrace virginity nor pursue it. But when they see it flourishing among us Christians throughout the whole world, and practiced at every age, they waste away, as it is said: “The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and melt away.” Since our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was pleased to appear to the world from the holy, immaculate Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, and gave us authority over the devil, the virtue of virginity

is easily achieved by anyone who wishes: such is the virtue of virginity. That it is a great accomplishment, and that greater still are the good things laid up in the promises for those who love God, is obvious to all. But it is impossible for anyone to reach the height of such virtue without love of God and humility, as the all-blameless, all-praised and all-glorious Theotokos herself testifies when she sings: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,” revealing her love for God. And immediately: “For he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid.” And again: “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and lifted up the lowly,” and so on. And earlier, to Gabriel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” These words, then, plainly show that it was out of the deepest humility and love for God that the one full of grace wove for herself the spotless tunic of virginity. So it has been shown that the virtue of virginity is great. But whoever strips for this arena must compete according to the rules, as the Apostle says. For their wrestling is not against flesh and blood alone, but against the invisible powers. The young man, then—that is, one who has made himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom—and the virgin cannot be saved unless they are such in every respect, like true imitators of Christ. For to be called a virgin and not to have the virtues that correspond to it, proper and fitting to a virgin—such a virgin the Lord calls foolish. For since she has no light and no oil, she is shut out of the kingdom of heaven, deprived of the bridegroom’s joy, and will be counted among those who hate the bridegroom. For she thinks she is something when, being idle, she is nothing, and she deceives herself. Let each one test his own work and know himself, for religion is vain when people profess to have virginity and continence but have denied its power. For true eunuchhood and true virginity in the Lord is holy in body and in spirit, serving the Lord without distraction and with constant devotion in the Spirit of God, pleasing the Lord purely and without defilement, always anxious how to please him, and it is one spirit with the Lord, as it is written: “You shall be holy, for I am holy,” says the Lord. For the holy one is not holy in bare name only; the holy one is holy in everything, in body and in spirit. If, then, you have renounced the passions of the flesh, attend to the contest [?]

of true virginity. If you have chosen to make yourself a eunuch for the sake of the eternal kingdom, hold diligently to the contest of ascetic discipline, and watch for the assaults of the adversary, like a helmsman crossing the waves. Let yourself be guided by grace, and do not turn aside from the straight road. Strive to serve God without distraction and with your whole heart, and to please him in holiness of body and spirit, so that you may attain the glory of the virtuous life. Strive to compete according to the rules, so that you may enjoy the crown you have chosen and depart crowned to the Jerusalem above. For its sake you have renounced the mind of the flesh; ascribe the grace of your purity to God, because he did not deliver you into the hands of the desires of flesh and blood, and of the corrupting and impure people who busy themselves with them, but kept you safe with his own right hand. It is a great thing, then, to remain in purity for the honor of the Lord’s flesh without boasting. For if one boasts, he is lost. And, as has been said, one must also have the other virtues in proportion to virginity. For virginity is higher than all things: a virgin womb conceived God the Word. From this, recognize the glory of virginity. For those who are consecrated to God become imitators of Christ, for he says: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” In such dispositions the mind of the flesh has no place. One must therefore guard one’s heart with all vigilance, and a virgin must never at all be paired with a young man. And if there are reverent older women and something needs to be handed over, let them wrap their hands in their own garment. Likewise the men too, looking straight ahead with modesty, soberly and reverently in the Lord, should keep their distance with their right hands covered by their own garment. Above all, the virgin must adorn her lamp with the oil of good works, so that she may not be deprived of the bridegroom’s joy and gladness, according to the Lord’s parable: “The wise took oil in their vessels,” and went in with the [?] bridegroom; “and the doors were shut.” And they enjoyed his joy forever. To him be glory forever.

On Rashness. The law says: “If it has been testified against him, and he does not do away with it, he shall pay.” Sometimes at a banquet the vainglorious thought leaps forward, wanting to speak out of turn. The good thoughts testify against you, urging you to do away with the babbling thought. If, then, you do not do away with it by silence but allow it to come out, you will afterward pay the debt, handed over by justice to great sin. For the one who is rash in word or deed is also muddled, and he very much likes to lay down the law; for he always seeks to win the argument and to have his word prevail. Such a man is a stubborn fool, for he hears from the author of Proverbs: “Whoever trusts in boldness of heart is a fool; but the wise conceal their understanding.” And: “The mouth of the rash draws near to ruin; but whoever spares his lips will be prudent.” And again: “Whoever guards his mouth keeps his own soul; but whoever is rash with his lips will bring terror on himself.” And again: “Whoever answers a word before hearing, it is folly and disgrace to him.” And again: “If you see a man hasty in his words, know that a fool has more hope than he.” And: “The one who is rash in speech will be hated.” And James says: “If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well.” And again: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak.” And he adds: “If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, his religion is worthless.” And again: “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we will receive the greater judgment. For we all stumble in many ways.” And Paul: “So that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written, so that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another.” And: “Love does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave unbecomingly.” And he goes on: “For I think that God has exhibited us apostles last of all, like men sentenced to death.” And: “We are fools for Christ’s sake.” It is better, then, to be silent and to be, than to speak and not to be. Teaching is good, if the one who speaks also does what he says. There is, then, one Teacher, who spoke and it came to be; and the things he did in silence are worthy of the Father. Whoever truly possesses the word of Jesus Christ can also hear his silence, so that he may be perfect: so that he may act through what he says and be known through what he keeps silent. For nothing escapes the Lord, but even our hidden things

are near to him. Let us therefore fear the judgment of teachers. For the judgment is greater on those who speak and do not do, who teach what is falsely called knowledge, who rashly intrude into things, puffed up by the mind of the flesh—blind leading the blind, and both falling into a pit. For a man will be known by what comes out of his mouth. Of such the Apostle also says: “These are without self-control, brutal, haters of good, traitors, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.” And the rash Judas Iscariot said: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief [and he held the money-box and carried off what was put into it]. Or rather, being implacable, he spoke lawless words that suited his own mind. But the long-suffering Lord, who bears all things, said: “Leave her alone; she has kept it for the day of my burial.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

A person must force himself hard to master the passion of anger and to restrain the wrath of the soul through long-suffering, through gentleness, through prayer and humility, and in everything to keep himself [?]. For this demon of anger wages fierce war against a person in many ways, especially against those who wish to struggle. So when someone gathers fruits with much labor, whether through fasts and vigils, or through prayers and psalmody, or through acts of service, it scatters them all at once, especially if it sees someone turned a little aside from prayer. For this utterly wicked demon falls upon the person, and the fruits he has gathered over a long time it scatters in a single moment. And then the person is found drunk without wine—such people the prophet laments, saying: “Woe to those who are drunk without wine.” A person needs a great struggle, then, to drive out the passion of anger by earnest prayer. Whoever, therefore, wishes to reach perfection and longs to fight the spiritual contest, let him be a stranger to every failing of anger. For when the spirit of anger sits in our heart, it blinds the eye of the mind with dark disturbances; and then we can neither acquire discernment of what is beneficial, nor attain a grasp of spiritual knowledge, nor hold to the perfection of good counsel, nor become sharers in true

life. Nor will our mind become receptive to the contemplation of the divine light, nor shall we be sharers in wisdom; we cannot even acquire the saving counsels of discernment, nor will we be able to hold fast with a sober heart to the guidance of righteousness. We must not, then, for any reason whatever be moved with anger against a fellow believer, but only against our own passions and evil thoughts, which are eager to lead us astray from the true way. That is why the author of Proverbs commands, saying: “Put away provocation from yourself, for youth and folly are vanity.” And: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth.” And again: “Anger destroys even the prudent; and a harsh word stirs up wrath.” And: “A foolish son is his father’s anger; but a prudent servant calms a man’s wrath.” And again: “A stone is heavy, and sand is hard to carry; but a fool’s anger is heavier than both.” And again: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him”; but: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise in his own eyes.” And again: “A fool makes his anger known the same day, but the shrewd man keeps it to himself.” And: “A fearful word troubles a man’s heart.” And: “As water is stirred by the force of the winds, so the wrathful man is troubled by angry thoughts [?].” An irascible [?monk] is a wild boar of the desert: he saw someone and gnashed his teeth. And James teaches us, saying: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. For the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.” And again: “Where do wars come from, and where do quarrels among you come from? Is it not from this, from your pleasures?” And Paul: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath.” And again: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no place to the devil.” And again: “Let all bitterness and wrath and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.” Likewise David: “Cease from anger, and forsake wrath.” And: “Be angry, and do not sin.” And the Lord, the guardian of our souls, declared, saying: “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” To him be glory forever. Amen.
On Wrath. And concerning wrath: whenever temptation comes upon you, or contradiction, or provocation to stir up wrath against someone, remember prayer and the judgment that attends it,

[?] at once the disorderly movement within you will grow still. For anger, more than the other passions, tends to trouble and confuse the soul. Wrath and anger, these two, are the offspring [?] of one mother, who is called folly. For it says: “A fool vents all his anger.” And: “A fool makes his anger known that very day.” So whoever wants to be separated from the hostile mother who bore them, let him master himself in patience [?], with a gentle heart and supplication to God, and by denying himself; and he is quickly freed from her. And the son of wisdom becomes one who fears God and loves God. For “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.” And: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” For from fear one advances to the love of God. And Ecclesiastes says: “Remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh.” And in Proverbs: “A gentle man is a physician to the heart, but a touchy heart is a moth in the bones.” And again: “A yielding answer turns away wrath, but the quick-tempered man acts [?].” And again: “A sensible man bears much.” And: “A patient man is great in understanding, but the faint-hearted man is a fool through and through.” And: “An angry man is unseemly.” And again: “A fool vents all his anger, but the wise man doles it out bit by bit.” And again: “Do not be quick in your spirit to grow angry, for anger lodges in the bosom of fools.” And again: “A hot-tempered man kindles strife.” For an angry man cannot be justified. And again: “A sinful man will trouble his friends and stir up slander among those who are at peace.” And he adds: “Do not be a companion to an angry man, and do not lodge with a wrathful friend, lest you learn his ways.” And David says of such men: “Their anger is like the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears.” For just as the brood of the viper devours the mother that bore it, so does an angry thought. The prayer of an angry man is like loathsome incense, and his [?] like a harsh noise. And just as a lion in a cage keeps rattling the bolts, so the angry man kindles thoughts of wrath. And just as a violent wind does not shake a strong tower, so anger does not carry off a soul free of wrath. And the Apostle, admonishing us, says: “Put away [?]

On Sorrow. [?] Grieving at the wrong time comes from the envious demon. To draw the mind somehow away from its resolve to pray and to make a person fruitless, he sends this untimely sorrow upon him. So we must not welcome it, nor be vexed out of season and so fill up the joy of the Enemy. Instead we must come to our senses and escape the plot of that avenging demon of sorrow. For when this evil spirit takes hold of the soul and darkens it entirely, it does not allow it to say its prayers with eagerness, or to persevere in the benefit of sacred reading. Nor does it leave it gentle and easy to live with toward the brothers. It breeds hatred even for one's very profession of life. Sorrow throws all the soul's saving resolutions into confusion and renders it senseless and deranged, blocking every good encounter. It does not let it accept a word of counsel even from true friends, nor allow it to give them a peaceable answer. Seizing the whole soul, it fills it with bitterness and disgust, and persuades it to flee from people as though they had caused its turmoil. For it does not let the soul recognize that the disease lies stored up not outside but within. It is exposed when temptations come and through that exercise bring it into the open. Sorrow, then, is dejection of soul, a lion's mouth that easily swallows the one who grieves. Sorrow is a worm in the heart that devours the mother who bore it. A sorrowful monk no more knows the taste of honey than a man in a high fever. A sorrowful monk does not stir his mind to contemplation, nor does he ever send up pure prayer to God. He who has mastered the passions has mastered sorrow; but he who is defeated by pleasure will not escape its bonds. He who grieves constantly while pretending to dispassion is like a sick man feigning health. For as a sick man is betrayed by his complexion, so the man ruled by passion is exposed by his sorrow. He who loves the world will grieve much; he who despises what is in it will rejoice always. And as a furnace refines impure silver, so godly sorrow purifies a sinful heart. It is therefore very good and profitable for the soul to bear firmly every affliction, whether brought on by people or by demons, and to know clearly that we owe a debt of toil. We must

therefore resist this demon with prayer and patience. For he who wants to overcome temptations without prayer and patience will not drive them off, but will become more entangled in them. So we too, with patience, sing with David: “Why are you so sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.” For it is impossible for one who is being schooled by temptations to come through without sorrow. But afterwards such people are filled with great joy, especially if they arm themselves with prayer and patience, and with sweet tears and divine thoughts: all those who have cultivated toil and affliction in their hearts. For it is in afflictions that those who contend are crowned [?]. But if the mind grows slack in prayer, sorrow begins to devour a person's heart, as has been said, like a moth a garment and a worm wood, working its way into his bones. And the person is found gloomy in a darkness of thoughts. That is why Scripture exhorts, saying: “Put sorrow far from you, for sorrow has killed many, and there is no profit in it.” And: “From sorrow comes death.” And: “Sorrow of heart will bend one's strength.” And it adds: “Do not give your heart over to sorrow, but put it away; remember its end.” Lift this sorrow from yourself, then, and do not grieve the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, lest he plead against you before God and depart from you. For the Spirit of God, who has been given to this flesh, does not endure sorrow or distress. Put on cheerfulness, then, which always finds favor with God, and delight in it. For the cheerful man does good and despises sorrow, but the sorrowful man always does evil. First, he does evil because he grieves the Holy Spirit who was given to man [?]. Second, he then commits lawlessness by not giving thanks to the Lord. For the sorrowful man's prayer has no power to rise up to the altar of God, because sorrow sits in his heart. Sorrow mingled with prayer, then, does not allow the prayer to rise pure to the altar. For just as vinegar and wine mixed together do not keep the same pleasant taste, so sorrow mixed with the Holy Spirit does not keep the same prayer. It is good, therefore, to cast sorrow away from ourselves and to put on all cheerfulness. Let us therefore make every effort to be free of this sorrow, because it is of the world. “But godly sorrow,” as the apostle Paul said, “produces a repentance leading to salvation that brings no regret, while worldly sorrow produces death.” And the author of Proverbs says: “The blessing of the Lord is on the head of the righteous; [it makes rich,] and no sorrow of heart will be added to it.” And again: “A cheerful heart keeps one healthy, but a sorrowful man's bones dry

up.” And Paul says: “For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we suffered in Asia, that we were utterly weighed down beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of life. But God, who comforts the lowly, comforted us.” Let us too, then, say with David: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted; my eye is troubled by anger; for I was afflicted and brought very low; I roared from the groaning of my heart.” And: “I grieved in my musing and was troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the oppression [?] of the sinner.” But: “Save me, O God, for the waters have come in up to my soul; I am stuck in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold.” And: “Do not turn your face away from your servant; for I am afflicted, hear me quickly. For you are my refuge from the affliction that surrounds me. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my supplication.” And when you rise up out of sorrow, say with thanksgiving: “The Lord looked down from heaven to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to set free the children of those put to death.” And: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” Because: “In affliction I called upon him, and he heard me and brought me into a broad place.” And the Lord said to his disciples: “Truly I tell you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.” And he spoke in a parable of the woman in labor, that she has sorrow. And he adds: “So you too have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” To him who gives joy to those in affliction be glory forever. Amen.
On Listlessness. This demon of listlessness is terrible too. It is the fellow-worker and yoke-mate of the spirit of

sorrow, and it is exceedingly heavy. It falls upon the monk around the sixth hour. It fills him with anguish and makes him hate the place, and still more the brothers who live with him, and every task. It also gives him distaste for divine Scripture and sets him yawning endlessly. On top of this, it brings on great hunger, and he turns this way and that, waiting for mealtime. He picks up a book and reads a little, then puts it down again. He begins to rub his eyes and stare at the windows, then reads a little more. Then he counts the quires and looks for where the book's chapters begin. Finally he closes the book and goes to sleep; after a short nap he gets up again. He does all this because he wants to use up the hours until he hears the signal for the meal. When he hears it, he becomes all eagerness and is found quick to serve, and he reckons his own satisfaction a commandment. Then this demon of listlessness insinuates thoughts into him [?]: that unless he moves to other places, all his time and toil will have been in vain. Then it suggests that there is no other way for him to be rid of this sickness than to go out constantly and visit brothers, supposedly for their benefit, or for the sake of visiting the sick. And he becomes like brushwood in the desert: it lies still for a little, then is driven along by the wind again. And just as a plant that is constantly uprooted bears no fruit, so a wandering [?] monk will not bear the fruit of virtue. And as a waterless cloud is driven by the wind, so a monk without patience is driven by the spirit of listlessness. And when it cannot drive him out of his cell, it begins to distract him inside it at the hour of the synaxis: “This,” it says, “is badly placed for the other thing; there's no need for it to be here.” It does this to make his mind idle and fruitless in glorifying God. All these things are the work of idleness and sloth. For a listless monk never keeps to one task. He is sluggish in prayer but eager for idle talk. Whoever wants to overcome this demon, then, should set himself a measure in every task and not leave off before finishing it. Let him pray constantly and briefly, and the spirit of listlessness will flee from him. For this passion is overthrown by prayer, by refraining from idle talk, by handiwork as far as one's strength allows, by meditation on the divine oracles, and by patience in temptations. For if it finds us not armed with these weapons, it shoots us with its own arrows

and makes us wanderers and unstable, moving from place to place, caring about nothing else and looking out for one thing only: where there are drinking parties and feasts of the saints. For the mind of a listless man imagines and reckons up nothing but the distractions that come from these. And then it binds him to worldly affairs as well, and little by little lures him with these harmful occupations, until it drives him out of the monastic profession altogether. Rightly, then, does the apostle Paul, like a skilled physician wishing to cut out the causes of this disease from which listlessness is born, exhort us, saying: “Brothers, you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, for we were not idle among you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it; instead we worked with labor and toil night and day, so as not to be a burden to any of you.” And he adds: “Not that we do not have the right, but to give ourselves to you as an example to imitate.” So, beloved, it greatly profits us to persevere in handiwork. It not only drives listlessness away, but also lets us earn our food by it and help those in need. And let us constantly meditate on the words of David: “Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed, for the enemy has humbled my soul. He has made me sit in dark places like those long dead, and my spirit grew listless within me. But do not turn your face away from me,” O good one, “for to you I have lifted up my soul.” Hear me, Lord, for my soul is in straits, and a listless spirit has cried out to you. Do not let me be tempted beyond what I can bear, but “with the temptation provide also the way out,” so that I may be able to endure it. Deliver me from strange and evil thoughts. Turn me back to the straight way, to the knowledge of the truth. And grant me to serve you with a pure conscience and all boldness, with an undistracted heart, all the days of my life. Yes, Lord Jesus Christ, imprint and radiance of your blessed Father, who sowed your divine words in our hearts, who alone care for your servants, the physician who heals without charge, the only benefactor who is without arrogance, the only one who is merciful and loves humankind, the only Savior and the just one, who always are, who are in all things and present everywhere, encompassing and filling all things: Jesus Christ, God and Lord, shelter us who hope in you with your gifts and your mercy, you who know precisely the arts of our adversary, who is everywhere, and the assaults he plots against us. Lord, you alone help us in your holy visitation. And when you are relieved, say: I know, Master who love souls, that “when my heart grew listless, you set me high upon a rock, you guided me, for you became my hope, a tower of strength against the enemy.” From now on I will dwell in your tabernacle forever and be sheltered in the shelter of your wings, for you, my God, have

heard my prayers. “For my soul slumbered from listlessness, but you, Lord, strengthened me with your words.” If we pray like this with a sincere heart to the Lord who bears no grudge, we hear from him that “everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened,” and that “your faith has saved you; go with a peaceful mind.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Despair. The passion of despair is far more terrible than those before it, and hard to heal. For it leads a person into unbelief and hopelessness. Then he hands himself over to the accursed demons, and becomes food and a source of gloating for them. The faithful and hopeful person is the food of Christ (“For my food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father,” and his Father's will is that every person be saved). In the same way, the will of the wicked and murderous devil is to drive a person into despair and destroy him. We, then, who have put on Christ and are one body with him, hear from him: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” So let us strive through repentance to win over the God who bears no grudge, so that we may not hear the words of Jeremiah: “Does one who falls not get up again? Does one who turns away not turn back?” And again: “Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? For this people has turned away in shameless apostasy.” Since we have God as our helper, brothers, let us cling to him in everything and not depart from him. “Draw near to me,” he says, “and I will draw near to you.” For he cares for us, since he purchased us with his own blood. It is the mark of a great and noble soul not to despair in any misfortune whatever. For human life is a time of trial. But let us not depart from the Lord until he orders the tempters to depart from us. Let us be brought to life through patience and steadfast dispassion. For despairing is worse than sinning. Judas the traitor was faint-hearted and had no experience of war. So when he despaired of himself, the enemy rushed upon him and threw the hangman's rope around him. But Peter, the solid rock, was brought down by a great fall. Yet because he was experienced in war, he did not sink into despair, but offered the bitterest tears from a burning heart. And when the enemy saw this, he fled far away howling terribly, as though his eyes had been burned with fire.

So let us not despair of ourselves, beloved. Rather, let us brace ourselves and wall ourselves round with the light of faith, and cry out against the evil one with great boldness: What have you to do with us, you stranger to God, runaway from heaven, wicked servant? You have no claim against us. Christ the Son of God has authority over us and over all. It is against him that we have sinned, and to him we will make our defense. But you, destroyer, flee far from us! For we hold his precious cross as our pledge, and we trample on your head, you serpent. So let us always stand up boldly against the enemy and not give ourselves up to despair. For if the demons who begged the Lord not to be sent into the abyss obtained their request, how much more will one who has put on Christ be heard when he asks to be freed from spiritual death [?]? So let us not lose hope in ourselves, but stand firm in confession and say with compunction: Master, Lord of heaven and earth, King of the ages, be pleased to open to me the door of repentance. For in anguish of soul I implore you, the true God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the light of the world: look upon me in your great compassion and accept my supplication. Do not reject it, but forgive me, for I have been found guilty of many offenses. Incline your ear to my supplication, and pardon me all the evil I have done as a man overcome by my own will. For I seek relief and do not find it, because my conscience does not let me rest. I wait for peace, and there is no peace in me because of the depth of my countless iniquities. Hear, Lord, my heart crying out to you, and do not look at my wicked deeds, but look upon the anguish of my soul, and hasten to heal me, for I am terribly wounded. Give me a time to come to my senses, by the grace of your love for humankind. Deliver me from the most shameful deeds, and do not measure out to me in return or choose to repay me what my deeds deserve, so that I may not perish utterly. Hear me, Lord, for I am in despair. Bereft of all eagerness and of any thought of amending myself, I fall down before your compassion, that you may have mercy on me, who lie cast on the ground under the condemnation of my sins. Call me back, Master, for I am a captive, held fast by my deeds as if bound tight by a chain. For you alone know how to set prisoners free and to heal hidden wounds, which you alone know, since you know what is secret. For whatever evil passions are upon me, in every one of them I find you named: physician of the sick, door for those who lament outside, way for those who have strayed, light for those in darkness, redeemer of those led away captive. You always hold back your hand and do not let loose the wrath prepared for sinners, but through your great love for humankind you have given a time to recover. Appear [?] …

[?] me, Master, who have fallen so terribly, you who are swift in mercy and slow to punish. In your compassion be willing to stretch out your hand to me, and raise me up from the pit of my iniquities. For you alone are our God, who takes no delight in the [?] of sinners, who does not turn away the face of one who gazes on you in tears. Hear, Lord, the voice of your servant crying out to you. Shine your light on me, whose light has gone out, and send the moisture of your Holy Spirit, and grant me lasting eagerness, so that I may recover, I who have utterly despaired of myself. Turn my mourning into joy for me, Lord; tear off my sackcloth and gird me with gladness. Be pleased to let me rest from my evening works, and to obtain the morning rest like your elect, Lord, from whom pain, grief and sighing have fled away. Let the door of your kingdom be opened to me, so that I may enter it with those who enjoy the light of your face, Lord, and attain eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." If we come to him in this way with a humble heart, he accepts our prayer. So whenever the light appears we ought to hymn and glorify him, for he is the cause of all good things, their beginning, being and life. For those who have fallen away from it, he is recall and resurrection; for those who are slipping, renewal and transformation; and for those who stand, a foundation and security. Ecclesiastes also says: "There is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die, but the dead do not know [?] the dog that has been despaired of." Paul too, writing about the man who had fallen in Corinth, says: "On the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, so that such a man is not swallowed up by excessive grief. So I urge you to confirm your love for him, so that we are not outwitted by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his designs." Let us also, then, strive together with Paul, saying: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal flesh." And again: "The Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. For just as the sufferings of Jesus abound, so through Christ our comfort also abounds. If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which is at work in the patient endurance of the same sufferings that we also suf-

[?], beloved, the most evil counsel of the devil, namely despair: let it find no way at all into us. For despair is the devil's complete joy. Instead, let us come to our senses like the prodigal son, and return to the compassionate Father with shame and with joy, and say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; receive me as one of your hired servants. Bring me, the lost sheep, into your fold, so that the destroying wolf does not find me outside and devour me. For I know you, Master, the good shepherd, the harbor of the storm-tossed, the hope of the hopeless, the physician of those despaired of. [Bind up?], Master, with oil and wine the wounds I received from the robbers. For you yourself said, Lord: 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.'" If you too pray, he will raise you up like the paralytic and say to you: "See, you have been made well; sin no more." For the Lord himself spoke in a parable about the widow and the unjust judge, to show that we ought always to pray and not lose heart. And he adds: "Will not God vindicate his elect, who cry to him day and night, and will he be slow to help them? I tell you, he will vindicate them speedily." To him be glory forever. Amen. [2 Cor 4:8 ff.]

On Murmuring. Murmuring, whether with a plausible excuse or without one, belongs to the accursed. For the upright life, the one acceptable to God, is the life of those who do not murmur and who give thanks. The one who does not murmur is like clear water; the murmurer is muddy and stirred up. The one who does not murmur is thankful, the murmurer ungrateful; the one who does not murmur is lovable, the murmurer hateful; the one who does not murmur is beyond reproach, the murmurer deserves reproach; the one who does not murmur reviles no one, while the murmurer is found to be a reviler, brazen, and hateful to God. For this passion is born of folly and of the absence of the fear of God. And just as the Lord wills to save a man through a man, so Satan is eager to destroy a man through a man. We must not, then, cling to a malicious person who does not guard his tongue, or we may go off with him to punishment. It is good, then, to flee those with undisciplined tongues, those who stir up quarrels, and those troubled by inner and outer agitations; otherwise one is found a sharer and partner with the wicked in the wilderness and with the ungrateful Jews who murmured against God, as it is written: "And the people murmured against Moses. And Moses said: Your murmuring is not against us but against God." And again: "Why do you revile me, and why do you test the Lord?" Isaiah also says: "Those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet." And he adds: "Those who murmur will learn to obey." David likewise says of them: "They did not believe his word, and they murmured in their tents." And again: "Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is iniquity." Jude, the brother of James, also says: "These are murmurers, malcontents, walking according to their own desires, and their mouth speaks arrogant things." Let us, then, stop murmuring, and listen to Paul writing to the Philippians: "Do all things without murmuring and arguing, so that you may become blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish." Rightly, then, does Scripture say: "Healing of the tongue is a tree of life, and whoever keeps it will be filled with the Holy Spirit." And the author of Proverbs commands: "Beware, then, of useless murmuring, and keep your tongue from slander." And again: "Do not say: Why is it that the former days were better than these? For it is not from wisdom that you ask about this." The offspring of the murmurers, the scribes and the Pharisees, murmured against the Lord's disciples, after the custom of their fathers [?]. ("A man of understanding will not murmur." [?])

saying: "Why do you eat and drink with sinners?" Having it, then, as a tradition from their fathers, like bad heirs of a most shameful inheritance, they murmured against our Savior because he said: "I am the bread that came down from heaven." But the Lord said to them: "Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him." The first workers also murmured against the householder because of those who came at about the eleventh hour: "These worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat." And they heard from him: "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I choose to give to this last one the same as to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I choose with what is mine?" And exposing their envy and wickedness, he adds: "Or is your eye evil because I am good?" To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Slander. Slander and murmuring are close neighbors; both are branches of senselessness. The murmurer destroys himself, but the slanderer destroys both himself and those who listen to him. For by slander he wants to unsettle others as well and make them partners in his own folly, heaping up a double debt of sin for himself, since he becomes answerable both for himself and for those who are persuaded by him. And if we do hear evil words, let us blame ourselves and not the one who spoke them, for those who carry a word to us do so according to our own inclination. So when afflictions come upon us, we must not blame and slander others, lest we fall short of the just judgment of what is fitting; rather, let us blame ourselves, for this is pleasing to God. It is good, then, to slander no one, and not to listen gladly to anyone who slanders. Otherwise the listener too will be guilty of the slanderer's sin, if he believes the slander. For whoever believes it will hold something against his brother, and so he is guilty of the slanderer's sin. One must not say anything against an absent brother with the aim of discrediting him, which is what slander is, even if what is said is true; instead, one should turn away from the slanderer. Oh, how wicked slander is, a restless demon, never at peace, but [?]

always dwelling in dissensions. It is good, then, to put away the evil leaven of murmuring and slander, which has grown old and gone sour, and to pass over to the new lump of obedience and thanksgiving. For it is not fitting for us to resemble the murmuring and slandering people in the wilderness; rather, as children of grace, let us imitate the saints who lived under grace, becoming obedient and well-pleasing. For it is written of those people: "And they spoke against God and said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?" And: "Aaron and Miriam spoke against Moses and said: Has God spoken to Moses alone?" "And the Lord was angry with them, and behold, Miriam was leprous." The author of Proverbs also says: "Do not love to slander, lest you be cut off. For a man's own lips are a strong snare for him, and whoever is unguarded with his lips, going crookedly, will be tripped up." And again: "It is a man's glory to turn away from reviling, but the fool entangles himself in such things." And again: "A reviling man leads into the turmoil of strife; but whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from affliction." And: "Whoever loves life will spare his mouth." And again: "What your eyes have seen, speak; do not rush into strife, lest you regret it in the end." And Job to his friends: "You speak against me, not ashamed to press hard on me." And the Psalmist: "Whoever secretly slanders his neighbor, him I drove out." And again: "Your mouth abounded in evil, and your tongue wove deceit. You sat and spoke against your brother, and laid a stumbling block for your mother's son." "For you loved evil more than good, injustice more than speaking righteousness; you loved all words that devour, a deceitful tongue." And: "Whoever speaks unjust things did not prosper before my eyes." "For rulers sat and spoke against me." James exhorts: "Do not speak against one another, brothers; for whoever speaks against a brother and judges his brother speaks against the law and judges the law." And Peter: "So put away all malice and all deceit, hypocrisy, envy and all slander." Let us hate, then, beloved, this loathsome passion of slander, so that we may not become like the slandering Jews who said: "This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons." But the long-suffering Lord says: "If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Whispering. Again, the whisperer and the slanderer are partners in their most shameful trade. For the two have a single activity, one that leads to the road of destruction and is truly hateful to God and to men. The pollution of slander and whispering, living with them, shows their way of life to be stained and unclean. Let us not, then, persist in this forbidden and lawless conduct, lest we be found irreconcilable toward our own kind. The law also commands: "You shall not accept an idle report; you shall not join with the unjust to become an unjust witness." "Every evil word is an abomination to the Lord." The most wise Solomon says: "The whisperer and the double-tongued deserve to be cursed, for they have destroyed many who were at peace." And again: "A double tongue has shaken many; whoever heeds it will never find rest." And again: "The blow of the tongue breaks bones; for its death is an evil death." The prophet Habakkuk says: "Your men of peace have laid an ambush beneath you." And Jeremiah says: "Their tongue is a wounding arrow, and their words are deceitful." David, wanting them to turn away from this hostility, commands: "Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit." And knowing the harshness of their mind, he adds: "Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they have deceived. Judge them, O God." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "For all my enemies whispered against me; against me they plotted evil; they set a lawless word against me." But: "Let those who slander me be clothed with dishonor," and: "Let them wrap themselves in their own shame as in a cloak." And he prays: "Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue." But me too [?] from them: "Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others, so that I may be blameless." And the author of Proverbs commands: "Do not be called a whisperer, and do not lie in ambush with your tongue; for the whisperer defiles his own soul. For a man of shifting tongue will fall into evils." And again: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who master it will eat its fruit." And James: "If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, his religion is worthless." And he adds: "See how great a forest so small a fire kindles!" And: "The tongue is a fire, the world of iniquity. The tongue [?]

is set [?] among our members, staining the whole body and setting on fire the wheel of birth." Clearly this means the span of our life. For human life is a wheel that rolls on and is set aflame by Gehenna. Let us flee, then, brothers, from whispering, so that it may not rob us of paradise and send us off to the Gehenna of fire. For it was by whispering that the serpent drove Eve out of paradise. As a certain wise man says: "Blessed is he who has not slipped with his tongue." And again: "Blessed is he who is sheltered from the face of the tongue." And: "Better a slip on the pavement than a slip of the tongue." And Paul: "Lest there be among you strife, jealousy, anger, selfish rivalries, slanders, whisperings, conceit," and so on. And the Lord says: "The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth what is good, and the evil man out of the evil of his heart brings forth what is evil. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks." To him be glory forever

On Not Blaming Others. To blame others out of season and without examination is forbidden in divine Scripture, unless perhaps someone, out of love, wishes to use such reproach toward his neighbor to correct one who has stumbled. For whoever truly fears the Lord's commandment that says, "Do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned," looks at his own failings and overlooks those of his neighbor. For it is harmful for a person to neglect his own debts and pay attention to the failings of others. To blame others is plainly to present oneself as blameless, and so God turns utterly away from such a person. And if some affliction comes upon you because of your neighbor, accept it as your own and not as someone else's. But if you resist it with sullen outbursts and blame others, you are, without realizing it, fighting against God's command. If you accept it, however, it is clear that you are waiting patiently for the Lord. The author of Proverbs teaches us about this, saying: "Before you examine, do not blame on hearsay; first understand, and then rebuke. Before you hear, do not answer, and do not break in while others are speaking." For death and life are in the power of the tongue. And: "Say nothing in the ears of a fool, lest he mock your sensible words." And another: "A wise heart will receive commandments, but one who is unguarded with his lips, going crookedly, will be tripped up." Ecclesiastes also says: "Do not set your heart on all the words that the ungodly speak." And: "Even in your bedchamber do not curse

a rich man, for a bird of the sky will carry off your voice." And Paul writes: "Brothers, bear with one another and forgive each other, if anyone has a complaint against another; just as Christ forgave us, so you also must forgive. And above all these, put on love, which is the bond of perfection." Let us, then, obey Paul as he encourages us, so that we may not hear from Jude, the brother of James: "These are murmurers, malcontents, walking according to their own desires; and their mouth speaks arrogant things, flattering people for the sake of gain." For blaming suits no one except the Pharisees alone, since they justify themselves. That is why, when the Lord's disciples were hungry and began to pluck ears of grain and eat, the Pharisees said to the Lord: "Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath." The condemned were blaming the blameless. But the forbearing Lord said to them: "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the presence, which it was not lawful for anyone to eat except the priests alone?" And to teach them not to blame the innocent out of season, he went on to say: "If you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath." To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

On Contentiousness. Contentiousness and brazenness are bound together under the yoke of wickedness. For the contentious man is on a par with the one who throws off the reins. He always wants to fight against the truth, and he is often unsettled, assailed by the desire to lead. As it is written in the law, Korah, Dathan and Abiram rose up against Moses, and the Lord was angry with them; and the earth opened beneath them and swallowed them up together with their households. For those who seek office by their own power, without God, and who oppose the authority that is under God, are subject to such punishments. The Apostle also writes about certain people who oppose, as follows: "Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith." Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles, Elymas the magician opposed Paul and Barnabas, seeking [to turn away] the procon-

…to turn the proconsul away from the faith; and immediately he was struck blind. And again, writing to Timothy, the Apostle says: "Alexander the coppersmith did me a great deal of harm; the Lord will repay him. You too must beware of him, for he strongly opposed our words." And so he received the reward his contrariness deserved. And the prophet Micah, mourning the harshness of the people, says: "Their tongue was lifted up in their mouth. Woe is me, my soul, for the devout man has perished from the earth." And another: "Every wicked man stirs up quarrels, but the Lord will send a merciless angel against him." And again: "A man's wisdom will light up his face." And: "One whose face is shameless will be hated"; and "no one who utters unjust things will escape notice. For if a man is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?" Likewise Solomon: "The wicked man does evil with insolence, but those who know themselves are wise." Let us therefore fear the divine Scripture, brothers, and stop being reckless and contentious, so that it may not say of us too: "We tried to heal Babylon, but she was not healed." Let us listen instead to Isaiah, who says: "If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land." So let us make ourselves secure through humility and quietness. And following the divine Scripture, let us submit to the clergy, who put a stop to disputes. For a great weapon of the soul is the discipline that accords with God: to speak much to God and very little to men, and night and day to keep our eyes on the last day. And let us not become like the priests of the Jews, who were always in the habit of resisting God. For the chief priests, it says, came to Jesus and said: "By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority?" But the long-suffering Lord answered them gently, saying: "I too will ask you one question; if you answer me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things." To him be glory forever. Amen.

HOMILY 31. On Idle Talk. Idle talk is born of having time on our hands and not looking ahead to what is to come. For if we feared punishment and longed for the kingdom, we would never talk idly, especially since the Lord has declared that we shall give an account at the time of judgment for every idle word; and whatever brings no benefit to the soul counts as idle words. We must therefore restrain ourselves forcefully, so as to give idle talk no room. For whoever is easily overcome by small things is of necessity enslaved to great ones as well; but whoever disdains these will also stand firm against the great ones, in the Lord.

We must therefore guard the heart and the body with all vigilance and speak in a measured way, as mature people. This applies above all to us who are thought to instruct and guide those in the world, so that we may not hear: "You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" For idle talk is a sign of thoughtlessness, as is written in Proverbs: "My son, do not envy evil men, and do not desire to be with them." And he goes on to say: "An unguarded mouth causes disorder," and "the fool multiplies words." And again: "He who is lavish with words will be loathed. For with much talking one will not escape sin, but he who spares his lips will be prudent." And again: "Whether before friend or foe, do not relate other people's lives." And: "Unless it would be a sin for you, do not disclose it." And Job says to his friends: "Would that you kept silent; that would prove to be wisdom for you." And another: "Blessed is the man who has not slipped with his mouth." And again: "He who controls his tongue will live free of strife, and he who hates chatter lessens wickedness." The Preacher also declares: "The words of a wise man's mouth are grace, but the lips of a fool will swallow him up; for the [?] of his mouth is folly." And: "The fool multiplies words." And he goes on: "He who loves life will spare his mouth." Likewise the Apostle: "Let no rotten word come out of your mouth, but only what is good for building up, so that it may give grace to those who hear." Since we have so many testimonies, then, beloved, let us with all zeal keep away from idle talk, which is useless, or rather harmful to the soul, constantly bearing in mind, as has been said, the fearful threat of the Lord, who says: "Truly I tell you, for every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Meddlesomeness. Being a busybody and meddling in other people's affairs is unfitting for anyone who wishes to please God. For whoever wishes to lead an undefiled life in this world must be self-contained, that is, attend to himself and converse with God in quiet, with an undistracted mind and an intellect that does not meddle, in simplicity of disposition. For in this way the grace of the Holy Spirit will come upon him abundantly. It is written in Proverbs: "Things too deep

for you, do not search out, and things too strong for you, do not examine. Ponder what you have been commanded; for you have no need to see hidden things with your eyes." And again: "Milk the milk, and there will be butter; but if you squeeze the nostrils, blood will come out; and if you drag out words, lawsuits and quarrels will come out." And again: "Do not meddle in matters beyond your tasks. If you lack knowledge, do not lay claim to it. For if you have no pupils in your eyes, you will be without light." And Peter too says: "Know this first of all, that in the last days scoffers will come with their scoffing, following their own desires and saying: Where is the promise of his coming?" And he goes on: "Therefore, beloved, strive to be found by him spotless and blameless, and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation." Likewise Paul says in his letter: "For there are many insubordinate people, empty talkers and deceivers, who must be silenced; they upset whole households by teaching what they should not." And elsewhere: "For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: if anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat. For we hear that some among you are living in idleness, doing no work at all, but being busybodies." And the hypocrites too, meddling, said concerning [?]:

"What do you think? Is it lawful to pay tax to Caesar, or not? Should we pay, or should we not?" But the Lord, putting their meddling hypocrisy to shame, says to them: "Why are you testing me, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius. And he says to them: "Whose image and inscription is this?" They say to him: "Caesar's." He said to them: "Then give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they went away put to shame; for shame covers the meddler. [?] To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Contempt. To treat anything with contempt is a terrible and [?] thing, and above all things that pertain to God. So let us not give ourselves over to negligence and contempt, lest we fall under the curse of Jeremiah, [?] who says: "Cursed is everyone who does the work of the Lord negligently." For all things have [their proper order], as Paul also teaches us, saying: "Let all things be done decently and in order." After all, what was wrong with Uzziah burning incense to God? Or with Saul [offering sacrifice]? Yet their [?] was rejected. Each person must pay careful attention to himself and not presume to [?] beyond his own measure. [?]

so that we may not hear from Habakkuk: "The presumptuous man and the scorner, boastful and arrogant, will accomplish nothing." And elsewhere: "As I live, says the Lord, those who glorify me I will glorify, and whoever despises me will be dishonored." And the author of Proverbs: "Whoever despises a matter will be despised by it; but whoever fears the commandment is sound." And Micah says: "A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is the fear of me?" Likewise David: "The lawless man says within himself that he will sin; there is no fear of God before his eyes." And Peter says: "It is time for judgment to begin with the house of God; and if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who disobey? And if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" And Paul to the Corinthians: "That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned along with the world." And again: "The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. When they say, Peace and security, then sudden destruction comes upon them." And another also says: "Do not say, His compassion is great; he will atone for the multitude of my sins. For both mercy and wrath are with him." And again: "Do not wait to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For as great as his mercy is, so great also is his reproof. He will judge a man according to his works." And Ezekiel: "When a righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered; he will die in his sin. I will judge each one according to his way, as I find him, says the Lord." And Paul: "So then let us not sleep, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night." And he goes on: "Walk as children of light, making the most of the time, because the days are evil." And the Lord too says: "Keep watch, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. But know this: if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into. Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not know." To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
On Sloth. Sloth is yoked together with wickedness. "For, 'Servant,'

it says, 'wicked and slothful.'" Since the Lord supplies the strength, let us for our part show eagerness and cast all sloth away from us. Let us become workers in the true vine and keepers of the Lord's commandments, as true sons, and not as wicked servants or hired laborers, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain, serving their own bellies and deceiving the hearts of the innocent with smooth talk and flattery. Let us not become, as Paul says, [?] and lovers of money, deceitful workers who disguise themselves as ministers of light while being ministers of darkness. Rather, let us live in a manner worthy of our calling and our confession, living holy, righteous and godly lives, taking thought for what is good not only before the Lord but also before angels and men. For this is right, that God may be glorified in all things. Let us therefore cast sloth away from us and, as faithful servants, await the day of our Master's coming, on which the heavens will be dissolved and the earth will cast up those who have slept from the beginning of time, and the mountains and all the dry land will be thrown into terror before his face. When the Judge comes with the clouds, then trembling will seize all things, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken; for his host is exceedingly great, for mighty are the works of his word. His way is in consummation and in earthquake, and the clouds are the dust of his feet; he rebukes the sea and dries it up. For the Lord will come with his wrath like fire, and his chariots like a whirlwind, and fire will go before him. And those in the tombs will hear his fearful voice, and [?] will come forth: those who were engaged in good works to eternal life, but the slothful and worthless to eternal punishment. And they will see the dread judgment seat of Christ, where thrones are set for judgment, and fire flowing like a river before him, and books opened in which deeds are laid bare. Therefore, remembering that day, let us not be slothful and negligent in the tasks set before us, nor give our attention to present things as if they were eternal. The author of Proverbs also teaches us, saying: "If you are diligent, your harvest will come like a spring, and want will run away like a bad man." And again: "Working the [?]

she is like a worker. She makes her work a noble thing, and kings and commoners use her labors for their health." And again: "How long, sluggard, will you lie [there]? When will you rise from sleep? You sleep a little, and for a little while you fold your hands across your chest. Then poverty comes upon you, and want, like a good runner." And Jeremiah says: "We lay down in our shame, and our dishonor covered us. Woe to us, for we are wretched." And another says: "The sluggard is compared to a filthy stone, and everyone will hiss at his disgrace." And again: "The sluggard is not ashamed when reproached. For the sluggard is likened to a lump of dung." So let us cast off, brothers, as far as we are able, sloth and idleness, so that we may not be deprived of the kingdom of heaven and sent away into the Gehenna of fire. Let us listen, then, to the Apostle's advice: "Not slothful in zeal, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord." And let us sing with David: "Blessed be the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war." Let us fear the example of the man who hid his talent in the ground, so that we may not hear from the Lord: "You wicked and slothful servant." And: "Take the talent from him, and throw the worthless servant into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Rather, let us strive to hear: "Well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Not Contending with the Powerful. We are taught by the divine Scripture that it does us no good to contend with a powerful man, for we are not able to go to law with one who is beyond comparison with us. For just as full-grown fish lie in wait and make the smaller fish their food, so too the powerful find it easy to wrong the powerless. They are harsh and callous, and when they plunder the goods of the poor, they regard them as their prey. For they do not know how uncertain life is. If they did know it, they would not add what the needy lack to their own abundance, striving, as it were, to annul the command of the Apostle, who says: "Your abundance for the want of the poor." Rightly, then, does the divine Scripture exhort us to guard against such people. For it says: "Do not, being poor, reach out against the rich." "For a rich man

does wrong, and he even snorts with indignation besides; a poor man is wronged, and he will be threatened besides. For what fellowship, it says, can an earthen pot have with kettles? It will knock against them and be smashed." And the author of Proverbs says: "Do not, being poor, reach out toward the rich, and do not eat your bread with him; for he will vomit it up and spoil your fine words." And the prophet Amos says of them: "They struck the heads of the poor with their fists and turned aside the way of the lowly; they drank wine got by extortion." And the excellent teacher, the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, said: "Why not rather be defrauded? Why not rather suffer wrong? But you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and that to brothers." And he goes on: "It is already a complete defeat for you that you have lawsuits against one another. Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?" And the Lord says of the scribes and Pharisees: "They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Disobedience. Just as obedience brings about life, so disobedience brings about death. The first man, formed by the hand of God, bears witness to what I say. For if he had not disobeyed the Creator's commandment, he would not have been deprived of the tree of life; but banished from paradise, he was condemned to eternal death, he and those descended from him, hearing the words: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return." Likewise those who came out of Egypt, whose corpses fell in the wilderness, "did not listen to the voice of the Lord, and refused to walk in his law." For God commanded them to eat the manna on the day it fell and to leave none of it until the next day; and when they disobeyed and left some until morning, it bred worms and stank, and it turned, as it were, into dishonor and reproach for those who had disobeyed. O the power of disobedience! Even the manna itself became a cause of worms and stench. For it seems that nothing of the kind had happened before this, especially since it was called the food of angels, as the Prophet says: "Man ate the bread of angels." And the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, did not listen to their father's voice; and for this reason the Lord destroyed them, the sons of Eli, by the sword, and delivered the ark into the hands of the Philistines. So it has now happened in our own day as well: the Chaldeans slaughtered the people with the sword, in the midst of and all around

Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them; and he carried the cross off into exile among the Assyrians. Likewise Saul, having set aside God's commandment by his own reasoning, came to nothing, fell from the kingship and suffered a most pitiable death. And though the prophet Samuel mourned greatly for him and entreated God, it did him no good at all; rather, he afterward heard from the prophet: "Obedience is better than sacrifice, and listening than the fat of rams." So much for the divine Scripture. And indeed a disobedient disciple is like a warped piece of wood, which can never be straightened, though it is constantly corrected. And the discordant brother is like a gust of wind that sounds out of tune and ruins the new melody with its discord. And just as the wasp eats up the labors of the bees, so too the lazy brother renders useless a community engaged in virtuous deeds. And as a cowardly soldier weakens the hands of the fighters, so too a negligent monk slackens the zeal of the brothers. So let us fear, brothers, so many examples, and flee the ruin of disobedience, so that we may not be condemned along with those who went before us. For what benefit will there be for someone who has kept his body virgin, but whose soul has been defiled by a demon through disobedience? Or how will he be crowned who has mastered gluttony and every desire, but has taken no care about conceit and love of glory? The author of Proverbs also says: "A shrewd son is obedient to his father, but a disobedient son will come to ruin." And again: "Because I called and you did not obey, but made my words of no account, I in turn will laugh at your ruin. For it will be that when you call upon me, I will not listen; the wicked will seek me and will not find me, for they did not choose the fear of the Lord. Therefore they will eat the fruits of their own way." And again: "Do not be very wicked, and do not be stubborn, lest you die before your time." And again: "Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination." And another: "Whoever fails to keep his father's instruction will dwell on evil words." And again: "Whoever sows what is base will reap evil. For death meets the undisciplined." And Jeremiah says: "Turn back to me, says the Lord; and there was no one who listened." And the Apostle: "If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person and have nothing to do with him, so that he may be ashamed." And to Titus he says: "For there are many insubordinate people, empty talkers and deceivers, who must be silenced." And to the Hebrews: "We must pay closer attention, lest we drift away." Let us therefore, beloved, turn away from this death-bearing disobedience and be obedient in all things to our spiritual Fathers, so that we may hear from the Lord: "Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Obedience. Whoever sincerely obeys his spiritual fathers in all things offers to God what is according to God. Even though the obedient man spends his life in this world, he walks in procession as if he were outside it. For he has renounced his own will and carries out the will of the Lord. Such a man is counted among the confessors. More than that, he lives free of care for the whole time of his sojourn here. He is also shown to be an imitator of the Lord, since "he himself became obedient unto death, even death on a cross."
