Obedience, then, is compliance without questioning, so that one carries out what is commanded without resentment. Obedience is complete submission, stripped of one's own will. In every command it is moved to action calmly, at the superior's nod alone. Obedience is recognized as the first good among all the introductory virtues. It sets conceit aside and gives birth to humility, and it becomes the beginning of love for Christ. That is why Christ, in the plan of salvation, obeyed his own Father as far as the cross and death, so that he might lead those who have lived in obedience into eternal life. Who, then, would not call such a man blessed? Or rather, who would not strive after such a way of life? To cut off one's own will is a shedding of blood. It is counted to a man as a sacrifice, and it is the achievement of a prudent and perfect man. Isaiah teaches us this clearly when he says: "If you do not do your own will on the holy day, and do not lift your foot to work, nor speak a word in anger, then you will trust in the Lord, and you will be fed with the good things of the earth." The wise Solomon says: "I too was a son obedient to a father, and loved in the sight of a mother. They taught me, saying: Let our word be fixed in your heart." And another: "Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his own soul, but whoever despises his own ways will die." And again: "Blessed is the man who is wary of all things out of reverence. Whoever keeps the commandment will know no evil [?]." Peter writes: "Be subject, then, to every human institution for the Lord's sake. Servants, be subject everywhere to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the crooked." Likewise Paul says: "Children, obey your parents," and:

"Slaves, obey your earthly masters, not with eye-service as people-pleasers, but in the fear of God." And elsewhere: "This is why I wrote to you, to know your proven character, whether you are obedient in all things." And: "If anyone does not obey you, take note of him through the letter and do not associate with him." And again: "For your obedience has become known to all." And about the Lord: "Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered. Once made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him." And the Lord himself says: "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." [And again: "Whoever receives you receives me." And again: "Whoever hears you hears me."] To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Slander. The passion of slander is terrible, or rather devilish, as the Psalms say of it: "He will humble the slanderer." Slanderers are implacable and hateful to God. They become partners, sharers and co-heirs with those who betrayed and crucified the Truth, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ. "For I am," he says, "the truth and the life." The law therefore commands: "A single witness shall not stand against anyone for any wrong or any sin he has committed. At the mouth of two or three witnesses," it says, "every matter shall be established." Saul ignored this commandment and killed three hundred priests of the Lord on the testimony of one slanderer, Doeg the Syrian. And again: "No one shall slander his neighbor." And the author of Proverbs: "Whoever slanders a poor man provokes the one who made him." He adds: "It is a glory for a man to turn away from abuse, but every fool will get entangled in it." And David: "They spoke peaceably to me, but in anger they plotted deceits." He prays to be redeemed from the slander of men and promises to keep God's commandments. And again: "Shelter me from the slander of men and from the gang of evildoers, who have sharpened their tongues like a sword." And he adds: "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not count sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit." And another: "Whoever slanders a poor man multiplies his own evils." And the

author of Proverbs says: "A man bold in ungodliness slanders the poor." And again: "A hungry lion and a thirsty wolf is he who, though poor, tyrannizes a needy nation." And: "A king short of revenue is a great slanderer." And: "Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it." And Ecclesiastes: "I turned and saw all the slanders that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the slandered, and there is no one to comfort them." And again: "Slander drives a wise man to distraction and destroys the heart of his nobility." But the Lord "will save the children of the poor and humble the slanderer." Let us, then, guard ourselves, brothers, against slander, that utterly evil thing, and fear the bitter punishment of those who practice it. Instead, let us sing Paul's words along with Paul: "When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we answer kindly. We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, to this day." Let us not share the condemnation of Christ's hostile enemies, the Jews, who came to Pilate and said against the Lord: "We found this man perverting the nation, forbidding us to pay tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king." But he bore everything patiently, like an innocent lamb. To him be the glory forever.

On Theft. This mischief-working demon of theft first starts with small things, and as it advances it ends in great and gross ones. Indeed, everything that comes into being starts small and grows by being fed little by little, for the method of wickedness is an intricate net. Whoever is caught in part is bound tight all over if he grows careless. Making light of small things, he says: "They are nothing; it is not a sin." Then, as habit takes hold, it spreads like gangrene. For habit, as they say, is a second nature. A man who has been mastered by it is freed only with great toil, unless he comes to Christ the Master without hesitation and without shame, through prayer and fasting and almsgiving, crying out to Jesus and saying: "Set me free, Master, as you did the thief crucified with you, and Levi and Zacchaeus the tax collectors." He must also bring him tears, for tears are acceptable to him. And when God sees his repentance, he grants him a good mind, so that he no longer covets what belongs to his neighbor. So, as has been said, whoever wishes to win freedom from this lawless practice is readily and easily delivered through poverty, frugal eating, prayer and the expectation of things to come.

For whoever keeps the law is kept by Christ the Lawgiver. So let us not neglect, beloved, to be rid of such disgrace quickly. This passion is hard to shake off, because to the thief it seems very pleasant to covet what belongs to others. Thinking to hunt down what is not his, he loses what is his. Lying and slander are also bound up with theft. For the law says: "You shall not steal, you shall not lie, nor shall you slander your neighbor." Achar broke the law and the commandment and stole from the devoted things a mantle, a bar of gold and two hundred didrachmas. The people would have perished for his sin, had not Joshua the servant cried out to the Lord, who revealed the culprit to him. Joshua said: "Why have you destroyed us? May the Lord destroy you." And he received a recompense matching the theft of his lawlessness: all the people stoned him together with everything that was his, and he died. The prophet Zechariah says about such people: "The curse will enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears, and it will lodge in the midst of it." The thief also has the oath as his accomplice, so that every theft is a curse. And the author of Proverbs: "Do not set foot on the ways of the ungodly; turn away from it and pass by." For it is ungodliness to make one's own what belongs to others. He adds: "If they had walked in good paths, they would have found paths of righteousness." Paul exhorts us, saying: "Do not give the devil a foothold. Let the thief steal no longer, but rather let him labor, doing good work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need." And again: "The Lord knows those who are his." And: "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord turn away from wickedness." And he continues: "If anyone cleanses himself of these things, he will be a vessel for honor, made holy." He writes to Titus: "Slaves are to be subject to their own masters in everything, to remain pleasing to them, not talking back, not pilfering, but showing complete good faith." If Ananias and Sapphira (I mean the pair in Acts) met such an end for pilfering from their own property, how much more those who pilfer from what belongs to others? For theft is a sign of turning away from the truth, or rather of betraying the Master. It is written in the Gospel according to John: "Then one of the disciples, Judas son of Simon, the Iscariot, said: Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor? He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; he kept the money box and used to take what was put into it." But the Lord bore everything patiently. To him be the glory forever.

On Lying. [?] We see more readily that the other passions are sin. But because we keep on lying, we do not even realize that lying is grievous and ruinous. Divine Scripture forbids it absolutely, and it is more grievous than all the passions. The mouth of a man who does not lie is made holy by the truth ("For I am the truth," says the Lord). In the same way, the liar is defiled by his father, the devil, for the Lord teaches clearly that lying comes from the evil one. So whoever loves the truth plainly loves the Lord, and whoever delights in lying loves the will of the enemy. The law commands first: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor; keep away from every unjust word." And Wisdom says: "A lying mouth destroys the soul." And again: "Do not plow a lie against your brother, and do not wish to tell any lie at all, for making a habit of it leads to no good." And again: "An unjust witness kindles lies," and stirs up quarrels among brothers. Isaiah speaks thus about the people who were always lying: "With mocking lips and with another tongue." And again: "We have made a lie our hope, and by the lie we shall be sheltered." And Jeremiah: "For falsehood, and not faithfulness, has prevailed on the earth." And David: "Strangers' sons lied to me; strangers' sons have grown old and limped away from their paths." Those who are strangers to the truth limp, because they have turned aside from the straight way, that is, from the Lord ("For I am the way and the truth," says the Lord). And: "The enemies of the Lord lied to him." That is why he hated all who work iniquity. And: "You will destroy all who speak lies." And: "For iniquity lied to itself. Deceitful lips spoke lies in the heart." And the most wise Solomon says: "Two things I ask of God: do not take them from me before I

die. Put vain and false speech far from me. For lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but whoever acts faithfully is acceptable to him." And: "Whoever leans on lies will shepherd the winds, for a lying tongue hates the truth." And: "A false witness will not go unpunished, and whoever accuses unjustly will not escape." And: "A false witness will perish, but an obedient man speaks the truth with care." And again: "Do not be a false witness against your fellow citizen," that is, against your fellow believer, "and do not open your lips wide." And another: "A lie is an ugly blot on a man. A faithful witness does not lie." And again: "The simple believe every word, but the shrewd come to repentance." And again: "Faithful lips do not suit a fool, nor lying lips a righteous man." He adds: "A thief is better than one who constantly tells lies." The apostle Paul says: "Do not lie to one another. Put away falsehood and speak the truth, each of you with his neighbor." And in Acts, Peter says to Ananias: "Why has Satan filled your heart so that you lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back part of the price of the land?" He adds: "You have not lied to men but to God." And James: "If you have bitter jealousy in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth." The Lord says concerning the Antichrist: "When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own nature, for he is a liar, like his father." Now that we have heard, beloved, the grave censure of devilish lying, let us flee from it with all zeal and run to the truth, which is Christ our true God. To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Vainglory. The vainglorious man shows that he is devoted to the glory that God hates. He most gladly hunts for the praises of men and revels in them more than in [?] a feast. Such a man is judged a people-pleaser, because he loves the glory of men more than the glory of God, as the evangelist John says. Just as good things have been prepared for men through affliction, so evil things come through vainglory and pleasure. For human praise is the root of shameful desire. It is not the hearing of praise that does this, but the welcoming of it with pleasure. Vainglory and pleasure are the causes of all wickedness. This passion of vainglory takes many forms and is extremely subtle. It is not quickly detected, not even by the person being tempted. With the other passions the assaults are more obvious, and the soul (Ps. 5:7; [?] 12; Ps. 11:5 [?])

easily recognizes the battle against them and overturns it through prayer. But the vice of vainglory takes many forms, and so it is hard to defeat. It lurks alongside every pursuit: in dress, in appearance, in gait, in voice, in speech, in silence, in work, in vigils, in fasts, in prayer, in reading, in stillness and in patience. Through all of these it tries to shoot down the man of God. When it cannot lure him into vainglory through expensive clothes, it tries to tempt him through cheap ones. The man it could not puff up through honor, it lifts into arrogance through the dishonor he supposedly bears. The man it could not persuade to be vainglorious about his skill with words, it entices through silence, as though he were a man of stillness. And the man it could not make slack through costly foods, it undoes through fasting, so that he fasts for praise. In short, every pursuit gives this evil demon an occasion for war. In the end the vainglorious monk turns out like a laborer without wages: he endured the toil but did not receive the wage. For vainglory destroys the rewards of the virtues. Just as a thrown stone does not reach heaven, so the prayer of a people-pleaser will not rise to God. A prudent man hides his treasure, and the toil of his virtue. A sensible monk imitates the bee, gathering flowers outside and building the honeycomb within. Do not sell your labors for human glory, and do not betray the glory to come for cheap applause. Human glory makes its home in the dust, and its fame is extinguished; but the glory of virtue endures forever. So let us not give this passion room to master us, beloved. Let us fear the one who says: "God has scattered the bones of people-pleasers." Let us rather follow the apostle's words and say sincerely: "Am I now trying to win over men, or God? Or am I seeking to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ." And again: "So we speak, not to please men but to please God, who tests our hearts. For we never came to you with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness—nor seeking glory from men." And: "For it is not the one who commends himself, but the one whom [?]"

[?] and the Lord handed over our strength, the precious cross, to the Chaldeans, and they laid waste our [?]. So the author of Proverbs rightly says: "Better a man of no account who works for himself than one who gives himself airs and lacks bread." And again: "Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips." And the Psalmist: "God has scattered the bones of people-pleasers; they were put to shame, because God despised them." And the Apostle: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?" And to those in Crete: "Not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but whatever you do, work at it from the heart, as serving the Lord and not men." Terrible, then, as has been said, is the passion of vainglory. It worms its way into all the virtues a person practices and strives to make the monk's fruits worthless. What is worse, with the other passions, fornication and anger I mean, we naturally grieve and lament and pray to be delivered. But with vainglory we neither struggle nor grieve nor beg God to free us from it. Let us therefore, brothers, hate the passion of vainglory with a perfect hatred, so that we do not lose our labors. For it draws a person away from the service of Christ and from faith in God, as the Lord says: "How can you believe in me, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?" To him be the glory forever.

On Pride. The disease of pride is worse than all the passions. It is utterly hateful to God and wholly unfitting for human beings, but fitting for the hostile devil himself [?], in keeping with his wickedness, who through pride [?]

…fallen from heaven. For he who boasted and said, “I will set my throne above the stars of heaven,” was found with no place of rest. Instead he is paraded everywhere like a captive in a triumph. This demon of pride is the most grievous of all the passions. It wages war above all on those who are making progress, and it tries to overthrow them. A pestilent and deadly disease ruins not one member of the body but the whole of it, and so does this passion. The other passions darken the soul in part, or else trouble it. The passion of pride darkens it entirely and brings it down in a great fall. For the soul of the proud man climbs to a great height, and from there it throws itself down into the abyss. As a weight breaks a branch laden with fruit, so pride casts down a virtuous soul. And as rotten fruit is useless to the farmer, so the virtue of a proud man is of no use to God. Do not give your soul over to pride, and you will not see terrifying apparitions. For God abandons the soul of a proud man, and it becomes a delight to the demons. A proud monk is a tree without fruit and without root, and he will never withstand the blast of the wind. As a bubble bursts and vanishes, so the memory of a proud man perishes after death. And as the prayer of a humble man moves God, so the petition of a proud man provokes him. All who through pride rebel against their brother are competing with the devil. Pride is not natural to us. It is the image of the rebel demon, as Scripture testifies, for it says, “Pride was not created along with human beings.” And again: “The Lord has cast down the thrones of proud rulers.” “For the beginning of a man’s pride is to depart from the Lord,” because “the beginning of sin is pride, and whoever clings to it will pour out abomination and will be utterly overthrown.” In the law too it is written: “The soul that has acted with a high hand of pride shall be cut off from the people.” And Isaiah says: “And I will destroy all the proud.” And the Psalmist: “Therefore pride has gripped them utterly; they have wrapped themselves in their injustice and ungodliness.” And: “They have failed and perished because of their lawlessness.” And again: “The pride of those who hate you has risen up continually.” So they have used every effort to pull down your sanctuaries and lay waste your holy places. But lift up your hands against their pride once and for all, so that the proud may be put to shame, for they have dealt lawlessly with us without cause. For they are always proud, just as their fathers in the [?] transgressed greatly. But your servant David did not turn aside from your law. He did not eat with “a proud eye and an insatiable heart,” and no thought that works pride dwelt at all “in the midst of his house.” And the Proverbialist says: “The fear of the Lord hates evil, insolence and pride, and wicked ways.” He adds: “The greater you are, the more you should humble yourself, and you will find

favor before the Lord.” And: “Do not exalt yourself, or you may fall, for every proud man is hateful before the Lord and before men.” And James says: “The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” And he adds: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you.” Let us fear, then, brothers, and with all vigilance guard our own hearts from the deadly spirit of pride. When it gains mastery over the wretched soul, it is like a most cruel tyrant who has taken a great and lofty city: it overthrows the whole soul and razes it to the ground. Most pitiable of all, this accursed demon tries above all, as has been said, to overthrow the perfect, those who have climbed to the height of the virtues, and it does not even allow them to turn to repentance. How can they repent who through pride take the whole devil into themselves and make God their opponent? Let us therefore drive off the proud demon by humility. Whenever we succeed in some virtue, let us say to ourselves the Apostle’s words: “Yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” And again: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.” And the Lord’s own words: “Without me you can do nothing.” For in this way we shall be able to hear the Lord himself say to us in turn: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.” To him, the Good One, belongs glory to the ages. Amen.

Discourse 45. On Haughtiness. The haughty man is distinct from the proud man, and he also differs from the vainglorious. They are branches of a single tree, but their fruit varies. The one is bowed down in appearance, the other carries its branches aloft. The one is hollow as an empty pistachio, the other light as an empty walnut. But both are

useless. The demons who hate our souls suggest to some people that they should flatter us and give us a certain puffing up. Then they urge us to give way to it. If we grow slack through conceit and give room to haughtiness, our enemies no longer have to work at taking us captive. So let us not become lovers of glory or haughty. Otherwise sinners will build not only on our backs but on our faces too, and we will become their delight at the time of prayer, dragged away and lured by them into [?] thoughts. As the Proverbialist teaches us: “Do not be haughty,” he says, “and do not be overly righteous, and do not be excessively wise, or you may turn aside.” And: “He who makes his own house high seeks destruction, and he who is crooked in learning will fall into evils.” And again: “Everyone who is lofty of heart is unclean before the Lord.” And again: “Do not put on airs before a king, and do not stand in the places of the mighty. For it is better for you to be told, ‘Come up to me,’ than to be humbled before the mighty.” And another says: “Do not boast, and do not speak lofty things in arrogance, and let no haughty speech come out of your mouth.” And Paul says to Timothy: “Charge the rich in this present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything.” And elsewhere: “Brothers, do not set your minds on lofty things, but associate with the lowly.” And to the Romans: “You will say to me then, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ True enough. They were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand by faith. Do not be haughty, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.” Let us therefore act as David did, and sincerely sing with David: “Lord, my heart was not lifted up, and I did not walk among great things, or among marvels beyond me. But I was humble-minded, like a weaned child with its mother.” Likewise let us sing with the three youths: “For, Master, we have been made fewer than all the nations, and we are humbled in all the earth today because of our sins.” “For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will dare to say that he is clean from sins? If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will stand before you? For with you is forgiveness.” Singing this song to God with a sincere heart, let us hear from him that “whoever humbles himself will be exalted,” but the haughty will be rebuked, as the Pharisees were rebuked by the Savior when he said to them: “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men. But God knows

your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination before God.” And he also says to his disciples: “Amen I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.” And he adds: “Whoever then humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” To him be glory to the ages. Amen.

On Not Thinking Highly of Oneself. We also find in divine Scripture that thinking highly of oneself is [?] and forbidden. Such a person is ranked among the senseless, or rather among the fools. For it says: “A fool is wise in his own eyes.” So let us not hold on to this empty way of thinking, beloved. Let us rather keep to the teaching of the Spirit-bearing men, that is, to humility. Let us walk behind them, and never let our hearts be lifted up over anything at all: over our work, our ability, our giving of orders, our management of affairs, a word of wisdom, or our insights into Scripture. Otherwise we may provoke God to anger and fall into the spirit of blasphemy in our minds. It is better to keep learning, even if one happens to be very wise, for God’s ordering of things is more precious than our wisdom. It is also good to say everything through deeds. For whoever philosophizes apart from deeds and only speaks words grows rich from injustice, and his labors pass into the houses of strangers, as Scripture says. First the Proverbialist exhorts us, saying: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not be lifted up in your own wisdom.” Again: “Do not be wise in your own eyes. Fear the Lord and turn away from all evil.” And: “[Do not] boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.” And again: “Son, if you become wise for yourself, you will be wise for your neighbors too. If you turn out evil, you alone will bear the evils.” And again: “I have seen a man who seemed to himself to be wise, yet a fool had more hope than he.” And again: “A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man of understanding will condemn him.” And again: “[An evil brood judges itself righteous, but it has not washed away its filth.] An evil brood has lofty eyes, and is lifted up with its eyelids.” And James writes: “But now you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil.” Likewise Paul says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation.” And Isaiah: “Woe to those who are wise in themselves and knowing in their own sight.” And the Psalmist: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are futile.” And: “The Lord scatters the counsels of nations; he sets aside the plans of peoples, and he sets aside the counsels of rulers.”

Paul says to the Corinthians: “And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with lofty speech or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the mystery of Christ. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness, in fear and in much trembling.” And he adds: “Not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to the spiritual. The natural man does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. The spiritual man discerns all things, but he himself is discerned by no one.” And again: “Such is the confidence we have toward God. It is not that we are sufficient of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our sufficiency is from God, who has also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” And again: “I do not yet consider that I have laid hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind, I strain toward what lies ahead.” Let us then imitate the humility of the Apostle, brothers, and cast away high-mindedness about our own wisdom and understanding. Let us especially fear the Lord’s parable about the boastful Pharisee and the tax collector. For he says: “The Pharisee stood and prayed thus to himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, robbers, unjust, [adulterers], or even like this tax collector.’ But the tax collector beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner.’” And he adds: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” To him be glory to the ages. Amen.

Discourse 47. On Not Despising Anyone. It is not right to despise anyone, or belittle him, or set yourself above him, whether because he is unlearned, or ugly, or ignorant, or negligent, or a sinner, or for any reason at all. For those whom we despise, God chooses, and those whom we belittle, God brings to full stature. But if you have received a spiritual gift, a word of wisdom or of knowledge, or teaching, or prophecy, or service, blessed be God the all-rich, “God, who gives to all people and does not reproach them.” So do not be lifted up

[?] in humility and meekness, which is good and profitable to people. It is written in Proverbs: “Do not praise a man for his good looks, and do not loathe a man for his appearance. The bee is small among winged creatures, but its fruit is the chief of sweet things.” And again: “Many tyrants have sat on the ground, while one no one thought of has worn the crown.” And in the First Book of Kingdoms, concerning the sons of Jesse, the Lord said to Samuel: “Do not look on his appearance, or on the [height of his stature]. For man does not see as God sees. Man looks on the face, but God looks on the heart.” And Jesse brought forward his seven sons, the strong ones. The Lord chose not one of them, but only the boy David. Among men he was of no account, but with God he counted, for he was meek and humble. God bore witness to him afterward, saying: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart.” And in the Fourth Book of Kingdoms Isaiah the prophet said to Hezekiah: “Thus says the Lord: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you; she has shaken her head at you.” And he adds: “He shall not enter this city.” And an angel of the Lord went out and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. And David says: “I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads.” And: “I have become like a portent to many, but you are my strong helper.” And Job says: “But now I am their lyre, and they have made me a byword.” Since they made him a byword, God exalted him many times over. And the Proverbialist says: “Wealth adds many friends, but the poor man is parted even from the one he has.” These are the ways of flatterers and slaves of the belly, who look only to passing things. And “the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heard.” This too is the way of the puffed up. And in the Gospel: “Jesus,” it says, “came to his own country and taught on the Sabbaths in their synagogue, and they said, ‘Where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom that has been given to him, that such mighty works are done by his hands? Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph?’ And they took offense at him.” But the Lord, who bears no grudge, endured it all. To him be glory to the ages. Amen.

On Not Mocking. Mocking and despising are a mismatched pair yoked together. They plough up wrongdoing and reap a harvest of weeds for the fire. This happens to us because we do not see our own sins or worry about them. Nor do we keep in mind the fearful day of judgment, when we shall stand naked and laid bare before the Judge. Each of us will make his own defense and be called to account, not only for deeds but also for words, thoughts and impulses. If we were not careless about all these things, we would not be arrogant and set ourselves above those who are better than we are. My brothers, we who are Christians ought not to live like those who have no hope of resurrection. Let us rather practice mourning that is full of tears, so that it may deliver us from bitter punishment. “For blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.” Whoever mourns his own evils does not mock or sneer at another. He listens to the Proverbialist saying: “Do not mock a man who is in bitterness of soul.” And: “Whoever mocks the poor provokes his Maker.” And again: “The eye that mocks a father and dishonors a mother’s old age, may the ravens of the valleys pluck it out. For God sends the crooked down crooked ways.” And again: “A man without sense sneers at his fellow citizens, but a man of understanding keeps quiet.” And James exhorted us: “Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.” And Paul says: “Let there not even be mentioned among you shameful talk, foolish talk or coarse joking, which are not fitting.” It is more profitable, then, to be mocked than to mock. For the righteous are mocked; they are handed over into the hands of sinners [and the ungodly], as Job says. And the Hymnist says: “Those who sat in the gate gossiped against me, and those who drank wine made songs about me.” And: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.” Let us fear, then, the threat of the Lord, who says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will weep and mourn.” Let us therefore keep away from mocking anyone, for mockery comes from a lack of the fear of God. Otherwise we too may hear from the Lord: “Hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye.” And again: “The evil man brings forth evil out of the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” To Christ belongs glory to the ages. Amen.

On Not Condemning. Condemning others is worse than everything else. Those whom we think we are condemning are relieved of their burden, while we carry the load in their place and find that we are condemning ourselves. So let us be very careful, beloved, to avoid condemning anyone. It is a great disgrace for us to pry into other people’s faults and spy on them, when we ourselves are sick with incurable diseases, have sores that are hard to heal, and are in debt for countless debts. It is not good to condemn the fornicator, if he becomes chaste from now on. It is good to flee the act, but not to blame the one who did it. For he who said, “You shall not kill,” also said, “You shall not condemn.” If you condemn, you are condemned along with him, by the very things for which you condemn him. Judging and condemning do not belong to us, but to God alone, the great Judge, who knows our hearts and the hidden passions of our nature. For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will dare to say, “I am clean from sins”? Let us not, then, give up rashly and without careful scrutiny on those who fall, even if they have reached the very depths of wickedness, even if they have become empty of virtue and have been cut off far away, even if to all appearances they have wiped out the most beautiful state that belongs to their nature. For such people may well wake up one day and look up to God, and come as close to the Lord’s feet as they were once far off. There is one who slips in speech but not from the heart, and who has not sinned with his tongue? Let us then attend to what we were charged to do: to mourn and weep over our own failings, to beg God to cleanse us from our corruption, and to suffer and grieve with our kin, who share one body and one anointing with us. These are the things in which God takes pleasure. The Apostle also writes: “Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. So each of us will give an account of himself to God. Let us no longer judge one another, then, but decide rather never to put a stumbling block or an occasion of falling before a brother.” And he adds: “Therefore you have no excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. In the judgment by which you judge another, you condemn yourself, for you who judge do the very same things. We know that God’s judgment rightly falls on those who do such things.” And again: “For we know him who said: Vengeance

is mine; I will repay, says the Lord. And again: The Lord will judge his people.” James likewise says: “There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” And again Paul: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be made to stand, for God is able to make him stand.” And the Lord says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be condemned; and do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned.” [To him be] glory to the ages. … of the eyes of God [?] … To the Romans he says: “I urge [you] … [?] by fine speech they deceive the hearts of the innocent.” [?] … “[Take care] lest this liberty of yours become [a stumbling block] to the weak. For if someone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining at table in an idol’s temple

won't his conscience, weak as it is, be encouraged to eat food offered to idols?" And he goes on: "For through your knowledge the weak brother is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. When you sin against them like this and wound their conscience, you sin against Christ." And again: "Why should my freedom be judged by someone else's conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I denounced over something I give thanks for?" And the Lord declared: "Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble." And he adds: "See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father." And again: "Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks! For stumbling blocks must come." But "woe to that man through whom the stumbling block comes!" Let us therefore glorify our Lord Jesus Christ, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

Whoever reproaches his neighbor for some offense will be caught in the same nets. "For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap." He is abandoned by God because of his lack of compassion and his arrogance, and he falls into the same fault, unless he appeases God through repentance by confessing his own fault. But if the one who is reproached accepts the reproach calmly and with thanksgiving, considering himself deserving of it, God shelters him because of his humility, so that he is no longer overcome by the same sins. For a man's reproach brings grief to the heart, but it becomes a cause of purity for the one who endures it. And whatever shame a person accepts for the sake of the truth of Christ, he will be glorified for it many times over, and he will hear from the physician of our souls: "See, you have been made well; sin no more." A certain wise man also says: "Do not reproach a man who is turning away from sin," but rather "take thought for what is good in the sight of the Lord and of men." So, beloved, let us keep our hearts firmly set, so as not to pay attention to other people's faults and reproach them, lest we hear from David: "Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword." For Job's friends, too, reproached him, saying, "Where is the house of the ruler?" And again: "What then, if you die homeless under heaven?" And Eliphaz had said earlier: "Is not your wickedness great, and your sins beyond number? You took pledges from your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing. You gave no water to the thirsty, but deprived the hungry of bread. You sent widows away empty and ill-treated orphans. Therefore snares have surrounded you."

They spoke falsely when they reproached him with these things, yet not out of hatred, but so that he might be humbled by their words. For they were of one family: Eliphaz, the first of them, was his father's brother. But the righteous man bore everything nobly; though he was under so severe a blow and was being reproached, he appeased God on their behalf, and had it not been for Job's prayers, God would have destroyed them. So much for Job. For indeed, according to Scripture, "A man accustomed to words of reproach will never be disciplined all his days." Let us, then, as Christians walking in the way of the saints, say: "If an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it; and if one who hates me had spoken boastfully against me, I would have hidden from him." And this: "All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me." "But I, like a deaf man, did not hear." And blessed Peter says: "If you are reproached for the name of the Lord, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and power, the Spirit of God, rests upon you." And the apostle Paul: "For this we toil and are reproached, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Father of us all, especially of believers." And when the Lord was on the cross, those who passed by blasphemed him, shaking their heads. Likewise the chief priests, together with the scribes, mocked him, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself." And the robbers who were crucified with him reproached him in the same way. But the long-suffering Lord did the opposite: he interceded with the Father for them, saying, "Father, forgive them this sin, for they do not know what they are doing." And before this, encouraging his disciples, he said: "Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every kind of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." To him be glory to the ages. Amen.

HOMILY 52. On not repaying evil.

Having recently said a little about not reproaching others but being reproached ourselves, let us now turn our discourse to not repaying evil. If, then, we wish to be fellow heirs of Christ, let us become [?] imitators of Christ's dearest ones. Let us imitate David's gentleness, so that we too may [?] hear from God: "I have found a man after my heart." For "I have found," says [?] the supremely good God, who loves mankind [?], "a man after my heart, who will do all

my wishes." This was said of David, who bore no grudge and was good toward his enemies. Let us too, then, do nothing to take revenge on a brother who has wronged us, so that everything does not go awry for us at the time of prayer. The law commands us to look after our enemy's beast of burden. Job, too, was attested by God as one who kept away from evil. Joseph did not take revenge on the brothers who plotted against him. Abel walked along with Cain, who murdered his brother, simply and without suspicion. And in every case, the word of God plainly proclaims the saints who lived in innocence. Someone says: "Whoever repays evil for good, evil will not be removed from his house." And again: "Whoever throws a stone up high throws it on his own head." And: "Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it." And: "Whoever sets a snare will be caught in it, and evil deeds will roll back on the one who does them." And Jeremiah, pleading with God concerning Israel, says: "Is evil repaid for good? Remember how I spoke good on their behalf." So the righteous man interceded with God for them night and day, and therefore he heard from God once and again that he should not pray for them, for "I will not hear you." Yet they repaid him by lowering him into the mud of the pit. Such were always the exploits of the Jews. And Joseph not only did not take revenge on his brothers, but even wept on their necks out of great love, and said: "Do not be afraid; I will provide for you." Let us see what David, too, pleads with God: "O Lord my God," he says, "if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then let me fall empty before my enemies." And Peter exhorts us, saying: "Do not repay evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but on the contrary bless, because to this you were called, that you might inherit a blessing." And Paul says: "See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both toward one another and toward all." And again: "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." And the Lord says: "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you. And if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well. And if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak too." And: "If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two." And: "Be merciful and perfect, as your heavenly Father is." To him be glory to the ages. Amen.

On not bearing grudges.

Having finished our discourse on not repaying evil for evil, let us move on to the subject of bearing grudges. For, brothers, not only must we not bear grudges against those who share our race and our flesh; on the contrary, we must behave as Christians, doing good even to the wicked, extending great kindness to them, and showing ourselves by our deeds to be true disciples of Christ, since he himself is kind to the wicked and ungrateful. So we too ought, as far as we are able, to imitate our Lord in everything. If, then, we desire his blessedness, we ought to restrain not only anger in action but also anger in thought. For restraining the mouth in a moment of rage and not uttering frenzied words is not as great a thing as cleansing the heart of grudges and not turning over evil thoughts against a brother in the mind. For the teaching of the Gospel commands that the roots of sins be cut out. Once the root of anger has been cut out of the heart, neither hatred nor envy will be brought forth into action. Just as a passing cloud darkens the sun, so a grudging thought darkens the mind. For foxes will make their dens in a grudging soul, and wild beasts will lurk in a troubled heart. And as a respectable man avoids a disreputable lodging house, so God avoids a grudging heart; and as smoke irritates the eyes, so does a grudge-bearer at the time of prayer. Let us hear, then, what the Lord commands us, both in his own person and through his servants. Thus the prophet Zechariah solemnly charges us, saying: "Let none of you bear a grudge in your hearts over the wrong done by his brother." "Let none of you devise in your hearts the wrong of his neighbor." And another says: "Whoever bears a grudge is lawless." And again: "Whoever hides enmity contrives deceit. Do not bear a grudge against your neighbor for any wrong." But "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; and if he is thirsty, give him drink." And again: "Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then, when you pray, your sins will be released." And he adds: "Does a man harbor anger against another, and yet seek healing from God?"

And again: "Do not say, 'I will treat him so,' or, 'I will pay him back for the wrongs he did me.'" And once more: "Do not say, 'I will pay back my enemy'; but wait for the Lord, so that he may help you. For in the ways of righteousness there is life, but the ways of those who bear grudges lead to death." And James says: "So put away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness, and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls." And Paul: "Do not be children in your thinking, but be infants in wickedness." Let us flee, then, brothers, the deadly passion of bearing grudges, so that it does not estrange us from boldness before God. For no one suffering from this disease of grudge-bearing will dare to stand before God in pure prayer, since he is prevented by the Lord himself, who says: "If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." To him be glory to the ages.

On not being hostile.

To be hostile toward people of the same race and the same faith is unlawful and unfitting for those who fear God and profess godliness. For God did not ordain enmity for men except toward the serpent alone, that is, toward the one who through it deceived man from the beginning and drove him out of paradise: the devil, the murderer of men. Likewise we were commanded to be hostile to the Midianites, that is, to the unclean spirits of fornication and licentiousness, who sow evil and profane thoughts in the heart. These we must oppose with all our strength and turn away from, so that they do not make us enemies of God through friendly dealings with them, as it is said: "Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away over your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred; they became my enemies." But one must not hold enmity toward a human being, especially over bodily loss, or slander, or insult, or anything else that belongs to this present age. One should not be hostile toward a fellow man on such accounts, but rather give thanks, because such people become the agents of our salvation. For wickedness has separated us from union with God and divided people from one another. This, then, above

all, we must flee, and pursue virtue, which both brings us to God and joins us to one another. And the definition of virtue and of true wisdom is guilelessness joined with understanding. The prophet Isaiah also supports our argument, for he says, "You shall not follow the many in wickedness," speaking of unclean thoughts. And he adds: "Wash yourselves and become clean; remove the evils from your souls; cease from your wickedness; learn to do good." And the author of Proverbs says: "Do not be hostile to a man without cause, lest he do you some harm." And again: "The fear of the Lord hates evil; but the shameless man does evil with insolence." And: "The quarrelsome man delights in fights." And again: "A man with a shifty tongue will fall into evils." And David, entreating God, says: "Let not those who are wrongfully hostile to me rejoice over me, those who hate me without cause; but let those who seek my life be put to shame and confounded." And: "Turn back the evils upon my enemies." And: "In your truth"—that is, in Christ—"destroy them." And: "The Lord is my helper, and I will look upon my enemies; for in God we shall do mighty deeds, and he will bring our enemies to nothing." But he prayed these things about spiritual enemies, not about human beings. And when [?] Saul was seeking his life and pursuing him with three thousand men, and was delivered into his hands once and then twice, and those with him were saying, "Look, this is the day on which the Lord has delivered your enemy into your hand," he answered: "As the Lord lives, I will not lay my hand on the Lord's anointed." And not only this, but he even mourned him when he died, and put to death the man who brought him news of his slaughter. Likewise he mourned again over the death of Absalom, who had sought to kill him. So it is clearly shown by these examples that [he prayed] not against [?] human beings. [?] ... of James, who says, "Do not grumble against one another, my brothers, so that you may not be judged." And the Lord himself said: "But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who mistreat and persecute you." To him be glory to the ages.

On not envying.

Envy, too, is a terrible passion, diabolical and hard to cure. For it began with the devil himself, and at once leapt across to Cain, the murderer of his brother; and thereafter it came down to the Jews, the murderers of the Lord. Envy, then, as we have said, is terrible and wicked. The envious man is vexed and wastes away. Like a worm in wood and a moth in a garment, envy consumes the heart and the face of whoever falls into its hands. But the one who is envied advances, sheltered by the Lord, as Joseph did: for the more his brothers envied him, the more God exalted him, until he brought him to royal power. In the same way Saul persecuted David out of envy, as it is written: "The women came out dancing and saying, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.'" At once envy took root in Saul's heart, and he said to David, "They have given you the ten thousands, and me the thousands." And the house of envious Saul went on growing weaker, while the house of the envied David grew and became strong. And he sang: "They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love." And again: "They will curse, but you will bless." "I did not set any lawless thing before my eyes." And the prophet Habakkuk says: "Your eye is too pure to look on evil and to gaze upon painful toil." And the Apostle, denouncing teachers who were moved by envy, writes to the Philippians: "Some proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, from selfish ambition, thinking to stir up affliction for me in my chains." And exhorting them, he adds: "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as the Lord has forgiven you. Be imitators of God, then, as beloved children, and walk in love." For it is the mark of a pure soul to have speech free of envy, zeal free of malice, and unceasing longing for the Lord of glory. It is not fitting, then, for the Lord's disciples to be ruled by envy or to be disturbed, especially when we see certain brothers who are very lowly or unremarkable promoted to positions of authority. For let us listen to the Lord, who says, "Give this man your place, so that he may recline higher up." Rather, let us marvel at the just Provider, who has clearly yet ineffably decided that the lowly one should be appointed to hold first place and lead, and that we should be last. Let us flee envy, then, beloved, the offspring of the devil, so that we may not be condemned with Cain, who ended his life groaning and trembling; nor again with the wicked Jews, who out of envy at the Lord's miracles handed him over to

death, as the Gospel testifies: "When they had gathered together," it says, "Pilate said to them, 'Whom do you want me to release for you, Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?' For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy." But the Lord, who bore no grudge, endured everything like an innocent lamb. To him be glory to the ages.

On not quarreling.

A quarrelsome man is at peace not only not with his own household, but not even with strangers. Wanting to satisfy his contentious thoughts, he is always bent on mischief, constantly stirs himself up, and troubles others. Such a person is found hateful to all people, or rather most pitiable. For it is written in Genesis that Rebekah said to Isaac: "I am weary of my life because of the daughters of the sons of Heth." The passage shows by this that quarreling suits the godless, not the faithful and devout. For those who are truly devout and disciples of Christ imitate their own Master and Teacher: "He will not quarrel," it says, "nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice." Such people do not try to settle any matter whatever through quarreling and contentiousness, but through patience, prayer, obedience, and hope fixed on a single thought. For the Lord says: "I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." And the author of Proverbs says of quarrelsome people: "Do not fight with a loud-mouthed man, and do not heap wood on his fire." And: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, [lest you become like him; but answer a fool according to his folly,] lest he seem wise in his own eyes." And another says: "A hasty quarrel kindles a fire, and a hurried fight sheds blood." And again: "If you blow on a spark, it will blaze up; and if you spit on it, it will be put out; and both come out of the mouth." And James says: "For where there is jealousy and strife, there is disorder and every evil practice." And Paul says: "But for those who are self-seeking and disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury, tribulation and

…distress on every human soul that does evil.” And elsewhere: “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth.” He also writes to Titus, saying: “Avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, quarrels and disputes about the law, for they are unprofitable and futile.” So let us, beloved, as children of obedience, not become like the futile and contentious quarrelers. We have learned from divine Scripture how harmful strife is, so let us not be condemned with the lawless Jews, who always opposed the truth and said to the Master, “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.” And again, “Who are you?” To them the Lord answered, “What I have been telling you from the beginning. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.” To him be the glory for ever. Amen.

On not hating. It is written that he who loves God loves his brother also. But he who hates his brother is said to be not only hateful to God but also a murderer. For in his mind he kills his brother by the disposition of hatred. People do not see that brother's blood poured out by the sword, but God sees that he has been slain by the disposition of hatred. God renders crowns or punishments not only for each person's deeds but also for their thoughts and intentions, as he himself says through the prophet: “I am coming to gather their works, their thoughts and their imaginings.” Evil rehearsed in the thoughts emboldens the heart, but when it is put to death through self-control and hope, it is crushed. It is therefore unlawful for us to hold hatred toward one who is of the same race and the same faith as we are, and a fellow heir of the kingdom of heaven. Let us rather hate the devil, who hates us, and his works; he is the common enemy of all people, and especially of the faithful. For no one who professes faith sins, and no one who has love hates. The tree is made known by its fruit. So whoever professes to belong to Christ will be shown to do so by what he does. As it is written in Proverbs: “Everyone who hates a poor brother will also be far from friendship, but a prudent man will find it.” And John says: “Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness still. And if anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. [?]

For whoever does not love his brother, whom he has seen, how can he love God, whom he has not seen?” The law also says: “You shall not hate your brother in your mind. You shall surely reprove him, and you will not incur sin because of him. And you shall bear no grudge against the children of your people.” Likewise Paul says: “Let us consider one another so as to stir up love and good works.” And: “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as Christ has forgiven you.” And he adds: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels but have not love, I have become a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” We, then, who have put on Christ are required not only not to hate anyone, but also to love, not only our brothers and friends, but also those who hate us and are hostile to us. Even if they say or do anything against us, let us accept it all with thanksgiving, for the sake of the recompense to come. For those who are of the world are accustomed to persecuting, afflicting and slandering those who are outside the world. “For they spoke against me,” it says, “with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred.” [?] And the Lord says to his disciples: “If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.” And: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.” And he adds: “Blessed are you when people hate you, exclude you, revile you and cast out your name as evil on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven.” And again: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, so that you may become sons of your Father who is in heaven.” To him be the glory for ever.

Discourse 58. On not gloating. To gloat over anyone at all in affliction, in loss or in a fall is the mark of a vain and worthless person, or rather of one who shares with those who crucified the Lord. For they said, “Aha! You who destroy the temple and raise it in three days, save yourself!” This is unlawful. When the foot stumbles, the hand does not gloat over it; on the contrary, it tends to it, with oil or with a plaster. Since we are one body, we must not mock and gloat over our own member, but grieve and suffer with it, according to the word of the Apostle.

And we must not only refrain from gloating, but not even listen at all to talk of someone's misfortune. For those who listen to such words in that spirit reap the fruits of their own intention. And do not suppose that every affliction comes upon people because of sin. There are some who are pleasing to God and yet are tested; for the impious and lawless will be driven out, and likewise “those who wish to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted.” So also the author of Proverbs instructs us, for he says: “If your enemy falls, do not rejoice over him, and do not exult at his stumbling, lest the Lord see it and it displease him.” This is said even about an enemy. And: “He who rejoices over one who is perishing will not go unpunished.” And again: “Woe to those who delight in evil and rejoice in wicked perversity.” And once more: “Those who delight in the fall of the godly will be caught in a snare, and pain will consume them before their death.” And: “Remember the days of darkness, for they will be many.” And blameless Job says: “If I rejoiced at the fall of my enemies, and my heart said, ‘Well done!’…” And blessed Paul, writing to the Romans, said: “If some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you. You will say, then, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ True; they were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand by faith. Do not be proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.” And he adds: “Love does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.” So let us not give way, beloved, to the enemy who prompts us to gloat over our neighbor's misfortunes, lest we too fall into the same. For Job says: “You too have assailed me without mercy, so that when you saw my wound you were afraid.” Let us therefore pray, saying with David: “Do not cast me off in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me. For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who watch for my life have taken counsel together, saying, ‘God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him.’ But you, my God, do not be far from me,” “so that those who are my enemies without cause, and those who hate me for no reason, may not gloat over me.” Rather, by your power, “let those who say to me, ‘Aha, aha!’ be turned back at once in shame.” To be mocked and gloated over, then, is our portion; to gloat belongs to the scribes and chief priests. For it says, the chief priests mocked him among themselves with the scribes, saying: “He saved others; can he not save himself? Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that
we may see and believe in him.” But the long-suffering Lord bore their madness, being the lover of mankind. To him be the glory for ever. Amen.

Discourse 59. [?] On rejoicing with others. It is a great virtue, and pleasing to God, to rejoice with those who live well and make progress in God's commandments, even if some people count them as nothing. True rejoicing with others shows itself clearly in the very features of the face. For the eyes reveal the feeling of the heart, as it is written: “When the heart is glad, the face flourishes.” To rejoice in our neighbor's progress is the mark of perfect love. For many who stood at the same stage of progress and loved one another have fallen, once one of them happened to make greater progress, into the pit of envy. But he who truly rejoices with the one who succeeds offers earnest prayer to God for him without ceasing. So blessed Paul, rejoicing with some, said: “Therefore we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your endurance and faith in all your persecutions and the afflictions you are enduring, which is evidence of his righteous judgment, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God.” Likewise to the Philippians: “But even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and rejoice with you all. In the same way you also should rejoice and rejoice with me.” For just as the members care for one another, and if one member rejoices all the members rejoice with it, and if one member suffers all the members suffer with it, so we too ought to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. And: “Outdo one another in showing honor,” counting others better than ourselves. He also says to the Corinthians: “We write nothing to you other than what you read and acknowledge, and I hope you will acknowledge fully, just as you have partly acknowledged us, that we are your boast, as you also are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. In this confidence I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second joy, being confident in all of you that my joy is the joy of you all.” And it is written in the Gospel according to Luke: “When the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, she bore a son, and her neighbors and relatives heard of it and rejoiced with her.” For such is the rule of true friendship: to make the affairs of those we love our own. And

this same John who was born said to his disciples: “The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease.” For one who has perfect love counts himself less, and his neighbor greater than himself. To him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

On not grieving anyone. If he who loves his brother loves God, and he who does not love his brother does not love God either, as the apostle John says, it is clear that he who grieves his brother grieves God. For it says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed.” And: “They grieved me, says the Lord.” And again: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” And: “As you did not do it to one of these, you did not do it to me.” The passages just cited show, then, that he who serves his brother serves God. Knowing therefore, beloved, that we serve God by not grieving our neighbor in anything, let us strive in every way not to give anyone a pretext or cause for grievance against us, whether reasonable or unreasonable, so that our prayer may not become unacceptable, like a [blemished] sheep on the altar. For it says, as Wisdom makes plain: “If one prays and another curses, whose voice will the Master hear?” And again: “If one builds and another tears down, what do they gain but toil? If someone washes after touching a dead body and then touches it again, what has his washing gained him? So it is with a man who fasts for his sins and then goes and commits fornication again and does the same things: who will hear his prayer? And what has he gained by humbling himself?” And it goes on: “Do not devise evil against your friend who lives beside you and trusts in you.” “From the mouth of the fool comes a rod of insolence, but the lips of the wise will guard them.” “He who walks uprightly fears the Lord, but he who is crooked in his ways will be dishonored.” And the prophet Micah, lamenting over Israel, said: “Each one oppresses his neighbor; they make their hands ready for evil.” And the Apostle says: “If your brother is grieved, you are no longer walking in love.” And the Lord says: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’

will be liable to the hell of fire.” And he goes on: “So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” To him be the glory for ever. Amen.

On paying attention to oneself. To pay attention to oneself in all things is a great and saving matter, and pleasing to God. It is also the most general of commandments. Such a person escapes every sin and accomplishes every virtue and commandment of God. Such a person overlooks the similar faults of others and attends to his own, keeping his mind fixed on God alone. Such a person withdraws from all earthly affairs and is lifted up toward the heavenly and eternal. For all of life is like a fair: he who knows how to trade gains much, while he who does not suffers losses. It is the mark of a great and God-loving soul, then, always to pay careful attention to oneself. For such a person, reckoning present things to be of no profit, and eagerly awaiting and longing for things to come, which are beyond reach and comprehension, walks the straight road and arrives at the calm harbor of Christ. We must therefore pay close attention to what is profitable and what is not. For there are two angels with a person, one of righteousness and one of wickedness. The angel of righteousness is modest, gentle and quiet. When he enters a person's heart, he at once speaks with him about righteousness, purity, dignity, contentment, every righteous deed and every glorious virtue. So when all these things enter a person's heart, it is plain that the angel of righteousness is with him. Now the works of the angel of wickedness: first of all he is quick-tempered, bitter and senseless, and his works are evil, overthrowing the servants of God. When he enters a person's heart, you must recognize him by his works. When quick temper or bitterness comes upon someone, that angel is clearly in the person. Then comes the desire for many affairs, extravagance in many foods and in various luxuries, desire for women and for gain, arrogance and boasting, and everything else like and akin to these. All evil thoughts, too, are his. Let us therefore pay close attention to ourselves, renounce the evil angel, and follow the angel of righteousness. As the law also commands, saying: “Take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the Lord your God, and lest his words depart

from your heart all the days of your life. But you shall love the Lord your God with all your strength,” who brought you out of the iron furnace, out of slavery to the Egyptians, that is, to the world-ruler of darkness. For “Egypt” is interpreted as “darkness.” “Take heed to yourself lest, when you have eaten and are full, you forget the Lord your God” and kick against him, like the people that was once beloved but is now hateful to God. “And you shall lay my words up in your heart, and they shall be immovable before your eyes.” “Take heed to yourself that you do not forsake the Levite all the days of your life,” that is, those who now minister to the Lord. For the priests and Levites are your sureties; they bear the sins of the people. “Take heed to yourself lest there be a hidden word in your heart, a lawless thing.” That is, do not pass the days of your life with meddlesome thoughts, but without pretense. As God also declares through Jeremiah, saying: “Behold, I have set before you the way of life and of death,” that is, slavery and freedom. “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” “Pay close attention to yourselves, lest you drift away.” For the teeth of the one who eats the sour grape will be set on edge; each will die for his own sin. And Ecclesiastes says: “Thistles and snares are on crooked paths, but he who guards his own soul will keep far from them.” And again: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.” And again: “Prepare your works for your departure and make ready for the field,” and walk after me. “And you will rebuild your house,” which fell into ruin through Adam's transgression but was renewed in baptism. And the apostle Paul says: “Look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the most of the time, because the days are evil.” And in Acts: “Pay attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God.” And John says: “Children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that the Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.” And the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits.” To him, God the lover of mankind, be the glory for ever. Amen.

On gracious speech. Gracious speech comes forth from the good treasure of the heart. Unless someone cleanses his own heart for gracious speech [?], he cannot be watchful. For even if he appears to speak to his hearers, his words are unacceptable and fit to be thrown away, since they have no moisture of the grace of the Holy Spirit. So whoever wishes to benefit anyone by speaking will ask God the Word for a word when he opens his mouth, as Isaiah declares: “For the Lord,” he says, “gives me an instructed tongue, to know when I should speak a word.” And he goes on: “Listen to me, and your soul will live in good things.” And the author of Proverbs says: “Good words are a honeycomb; their sweetness is a healing for the soul.” For all words spoken for salvation produce sweetness and healing in the soul. “The one who is prudent in affairs finds good.” And: “Lips will kiss those who answer with good words.” And: “Smooth lips cover a grieving heart.” And again: “A harsh word stirs up anger, but the tongue of the wise knows what is good,” for “a healing tongue is a tree of life.” And again: “The mouth of the righteous drips wisdom, and the lips of the righteous drip graciousness.” And: “A humble mouth meditates on wisdom.” And again: “From the fruit of his mouth a man's soul will be filled with good things, and the recompense of his lips will be given to him.” And once more: “Truthful lips establish testimony, and those who wish for peace will be glad.” And the Psalmist says: “My heart has poured forth a good word.” And: “The Lord will give a word to those who proclaim good news with great power.” And: “O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise.” Paul also writes, saying: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.” And to the Romans: “For I long to see you,” he says, “that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you, that is, that we may be mutually encouraged among you by each other's faith, both yours and mine.” And again: “Exhorting each one of you and encouraging you to walk in a manner worthy of God.” If anyone, then, perceives that he has received the gift of teaching from God, he will speak with humility so as to build up others too, lest he be accused like the one who hid the talent. But he who has not yet received such a gift should keep silent and not bring forth idle words from his heart, lest he hear: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant on your lips? For you have hated instruction and cast [?]

…my words behind you?” “For the good man,” says the Lord, “out of the good treasure of his heart” (that is, out of the grace of the Holy Spirit) “brings forth what is good.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Not Swearing. On not swearing, the old law, giving laws as if to infants, commands that one should not swear at the wrong time, nor swear to deceive one’s neighbor. But our Lord and Savior commands us not to swear at all, neither at the right time nor at the wrong time. “Let your yes be yes,” he says, “and your no be no. Whatever is more than this comes from the evil one.” And he says: “To the first people, because they were stiff-necked, I commanded, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but shall pay your oaths to the Lord,’ because they were hard-hearted and disobedient to me. But to you who have believed in me, to whom I have given power to become children of God, who have been born again of the Holy Spirit, I command that you never swear any oath at all, whether small or great, so that the difference between my bastard children and my true children may be shown.” Let us therefore, beloved, revere the Master and Father who has honored us so greatly, and with all fear, as true servants, let us keep his commandment not to swear at all, so that he may never say of us too, “I have begotten and raised up sons, but they have rejected me,” and, “Foreign sons have lied to me.” Let us not, then, become reckless and contemptuous of our Master’s commandment. For what is done or said without an oath is more readily believed by men and is pleasing to God. Wisdom therefore rightly declares: “Do not accustom your mouth to oaths, and do not make a habit of naming the Holy One. For one who swears will not be cleansed of sin.” And again: “A man who swears many oaths will be filled with lawlessness, and the scourge will not depart from him.” Indeed, the talk of a man who swears many oaths not only makes the hair stand on end but is hostile to the ears. The law also says, “You shall not swear by my name unjustly.” And the prophet Zechariah: “Do not love a false oath; but love truth and peace.” Hosea also says, “And do not swear, ‘As the Lord lives.’” And Micah: “And I will be a swift witness,” he says, “against those who swear by my name.” James too writes, saying: “Above all, brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath; but let your yes be yes and your no be no, so that you may not fall into hypocrisy.” In the same way our Lord and Savior says: “But I say to you, do not swear at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet, or by Jerusalem, for it is the holy city of the great King. Nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot
make one hair white or black. But let your yes be yes and your no be no. Whatever is more than these comes from the evil one.” To Christ be glory forever. Amen.

On Keeping a Secret.
