Being entrusted with a secret belongs to those within, that is, to those who are genuine and faithful, and not to those outside. “To you it has been given,” says the Lord, “to know the mysteries of the kingdom.” If, then, someone who has been entrusted with a secret does not keep it, he has become a betrayer of the truth. It is therefore most necessary to exercise self-control with all vigilance and to keep the secret entrusted to one, so that one’s true friend may not become one’s implacable enemy, just as we are taught by the divine Scripture about not disclosing a secret. For the author of Proverbs says: “He who conceals a wrong seeks friendship; but he who hates to conceal separates friends and kinsmen.” And another says: “Have you heard a word? Let it die with you. For he who reveals a secret destroys trust.” And again: “If you reveal your friend’s secret, you will never catch up with him. For as you have lost [let go] a bird from your hand, so you have let your neighbor go, and you will not hunt him down. Do not chase after him, for he is far away.” And he adds: “A wound can be bound up, and there is reconciliation after abuse; but he who has revealed a secret has destroyed trust.” It is the mark, then, of a noble, courageous and faithful soul to conceal a secret in every way, and not to disclose what has been entrusted to it for any reason, or out of grief, as may happen. For if you bear it and hold it in for a little while, afterwards you gather the sweetness of joy from the fruit of self-control. For the faithful servant keeps his Master’s secret. The Lord says to his own disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God; but to those outside everything is spoken in parables, so that seeing they may see and not perceive, and hearing they may hear and not understand.” To him, the God who loves mankind, be glory forever. Amen.

On Not Confiding at the Wrong Time. To confide in someone at the wrong time is characteristic of an untrained and tasteless soul. For many, having thoughtlessly confided in those they should not have, afterwards fell into great and unbearable afflictions. One must therefore do everything

with circumspection and counsel, and not confide in just anyone, lest afterwards one reap fruits of grief from one’s own bad counsel. For it is good to say nothing into the ears of a fool, as Solomon says, lest he sneer at your words. Another wise man also teaches: “Do not take counsel with a fool, for he will not be able to keep a matter to himself.” And again: “Do not reveal what is in your heart to every man, nor bring every man into your house. For many are the snares of the devil.” And again: “Do nothing secret before a stranger, for you do not know what he will bring forth.” And again: “A double-tongued man reveals counsels in the assembly; but the faithful in spirit conceals matters.” And the prophet Micah cries out, saying: “Do not trust in friends. And guard yourself against the woman who shares your bed, so as not to confide anything to her.” The prophet rightly urges us to be on guard against the one who shares our bed, lest we suffer what Samson suffered. For that righteous man, pestered by his wife, told her the riddle, and it brought him great grief. In the same way his second partner, Delilah, deceiving the righteous man with deceitful words, made him an object of gloating for his enemies. And he who was conceived according to a promise, who judged Israel for twenty years, who tore open the lion’s mouth with his hands, who killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass and drank water from the jawbone, and who through surpassing strength lifted the gates of Gaza together with the bar onto his shoulders and carried them up the mountain—he, lured by a worthless woman, suddenly not only lost such great strength but also had his eyes gouged out, became a plaything for the servants of the Philistines, and ended his life together with them. It follows, then, that we should heed the Lord’s saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.” To him be glory forever.

On Truth. Perhaps, honored father Eustathius, you wonder—you and those who read the present treatise—why, though I was urged on by you and began the work by addressing you, I at once, as though forgetting myself, delivered these discourses as if to students in need of instruction. But let no one wonder at the change, or charge me with folly; rather let him commend my praiseworthy timidity. For I have not forgotten myself, but I will give my defense. I received the occasion for the present work at your urging: to summarize briefly the whole

divine Scripture, Old and New, and send it to you, because you are continually moving from country to country and from city to city on account of the Chaldean storm that prevails over the whole world. But since the Scriptures and the testimonies of the divinely inspired teaching needed some moral discourse—just as a building made of great and costly stones needs small and cheap [stones] built in along with them—for this reason I composed the plan of the present treatise in this way, not daring to address the teachings to you, but delivering them to all in common. For I know both my own weakness and the perfection of your Paternity. But now that the discourse on truth has been reached, I thought it necessary that this one be offered up to you as a divine and exceptional gift. For truly God is truth. Everyone who inquires into the things of truth must therefore first pray to come to know the real truth and to speak of it as befits a lover of truth, as the one said: “Do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth.” For truth returns to those who practice it. Just as one who speaks falsehood defiles his heart and his mouth (for lying belongs to the enemy, since the father of lies is the devil), so one who speaks the truth is sanctified in soul and body and all his members; for the truth is Christ. The prophet Zechariah too, admonishing the disobedient people, says to them: “Speak the truth, each one to his neighbor, and judge with judgment that makes peace.” And another: “Truthful lips establish testimony; and those who wish to make peace will rejoice.” And again: “Acquire truth, and do not reject wisdom and instruction; for the mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter,” that is, with joy. And David: “Lord, who shall sojourn in your tent? Or who shall dwell on your holy mountain?” And he goes on: “He who walks blamelessly and does righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart,” that is, from the heart. “For the beginning of your words is truth, and all the judgments of your righteousness are forever.” And indeed, “The works of your hands are truth and judgment.” And, “Mercy and truth shall go before your face.” And therefore, “Bend your bow, prosper and reign, for the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness.” “For in the mouth of my enemies

there is no truth; their heart is vain; their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they have deceived. Therefore judge them, O God.” The truthful Job also says, “If I have even lied against the words of my holy God.” And the author of Proverbs: “Better a poor man who walks in truth than a rich man who is a liar.” For to do what is just and to speak the truth is more pleasing to God than the blood of sacrifices. And again: “Opening my lips,” he says, “I will bring forth right things, for my throat will meditate on truth; but lying lips are an abomination before me.” And the Apostle: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another.” And, “In love unfeigned, and in the word of truth.” And John: “We know,” he says, “that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God. And we are in his true Son Jesus Christ, who is the true God and eternal life. For he who speaks the truth abides in God.” All that comes out of a man’s mouth, then, must be truth, so that the spirit which God has made to dwell in this flesh may be found true by all men, and so that the Lord who dwells in man may thus be glorified; for the Lord is true in every word, and there is no falsehood in him. Those who lie, therefore, set the Lord at nothing and become defrauders of the Lord, not returning to him the deposit they received; for they received a spirit free of falsehood. If they return it false, they have defiled God’s deposit and have become defrauders. For he who keeps [?] can gain [?] for himself; for he is kept safe by the truth. Fittingly, then, in due order, honored father Eustathius, we have dedicated to you the discourse on truth. For being always clothed with Christ, you live and move in him, and you are a true man and a most ardent lover of truth. [For now he bids me take courage to declare these things about you, who said to Thomas, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me.”] To him be glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen. Discourse 67 [?]. On Rebuking. [?]

To rebuke one’s neighbor in a godly way is pleasing and dear to God. For it is a proof of brotherly love and of a compassionate mind. But it must be done only with a sincere heart and a clean conscience, in the fear of God, rebuking with all tenderness, with the aim of turning the sinner back. One must also discern where one ought to rebuke; for a powerful man should not be rebuked out of vainglory, but rather

one should point out to him the dishonor that is coming upon him. For in this way such people accept rebuke gladly. Likewise it is not good to rebuke one who has stopped and is repenting. And if you say that you rebuke for God’s sake and out of love for your neighbor, first make your own faults known to him, and he will not be grieved at being rebuked. It is written in Proverbs: “Better are open rebukes than hidden friendship. For the wounds of a friend are more trustworthy than the willing kisses of an enemy.” And, “Better is a man who rebukes than an unjust, stiff-necked man; for when he is suddenly set ablaze, there is no healing.” And again: “He who rebukes a man’s ways will win more thanks than one who flatters with his tongue to win favor.” And again: “Do not rebuke the wicked, lest they hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you; [rebuke] a fool, and he will hate you all the more. Give a wise man an opportunity, and he will become wiser. Instruct a righteous man, and he will gain in learning.” And again: “He who winks his eye with deceit brings griefs upon men; but he who rebukes with boldness makes peace. Rebuke a friend: perhaps he did not do it; and if he did, so that he may not do it again.” And the law says: “You shall rebuke your neighbor: perhaps he did not do it. And if he did, so that he may not do it again.” And again: “How good it is to rebuke rather than to be angry in secret.” And he adds: “At a banquet of wine do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his merriment.” And again: “If you rebuke a prudent man, he will understand knowledge; for a perceptive heart is a grieving soul; but those who rebuke will appear better to them.” And Paul says to Timothy: “Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, so that the rest also may be afraid.” And again: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort.” And the Lord, our Savior, who wishes us to be saved, commands us, saying: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take with you one or two more, so that every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the Church; and if he refuses to listen even to the Church, let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector.” To him be glory forever.

On Being Rebuked. If a man is humble-minded and considers himself of little worth, he accepts with cheerfulness and goodwill the rebukes brought against him, and the penance too. Blessed, then, is the monk who

regards himself as the refuse of all. For counting himself the very least, he rejoices more in being held cheap and despised than in honor and renown. For this reason he is also sanctified by God, as Isaiah testifies: “Sanctify,” he says, “the one who holds his own life cheap.” But “he who hates rebukes is a fool,” and is in the grip of passion as well, while he who loves them is clearly free of passion. It is good, then, to welcome those who mock us rather than those who praise us, who, according to Scripture, differ in no way from one who curses. And again the same Isaiah says: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word; say, ‘Our brothers,’ to those who hate you and abhor you.” The author of Proverbs also says: “A threat crushes the heart of a prudent man; but a fool, even when flogged, does not perceive it.” And again: “He who rejects instruction hates himself; but he who heeds rebukes gains understanding.” And again: “He who accepts instruction will be among good things; and he who keeps rebukes will be made wise.” And, “He who listens to life-giving rebukes will lodge among the wise.” And again: “He who heeds rebukes loves his own soul; but those who hate them die shamefully.” And again: “Instruction removes poverty and dishonor; and he who keeps rebukes will be glorified.” And again: “Blows and rebukes give wisdom; but a child who goes astray will shame his parents.” And again: “He who loves instruction loves knowledge; but he who hates rebukes is a fool.” And David: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor chasten me in your anger”—not that he refused rebuke, but rather chastening given in anger. For he adds: “The righteous will chasten me in mercy and rebuke me.” Great and wonderful, then, beloved, is the one who is rebuked or dishonored by someone and bears it, like that modest and great Canaanite woman, who, when she heard from the Lord, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs,” was not indignant, but on the contrary humbled herself and said, “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” Hence the Lord greatly marveled at her humility and faith and said, “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” To him be glory forever. Amen.
Good, beloved, is godly shame (that is, modesty)—shame that is not for sale, not counterfeit, blameless, and that reconciles us to God. Let us hold fast to it, then, so that

we may have boldness at the coming of the Lord; for he has drawn near and is at the doors. Godly shame consists in not daring at all to lift one’s eyes to him or to speak boldly before God, because of the multitude of evils of which we are conscious in ourselves. And so, whenever we suffer some dishonor from men, let us at once think of the glory that will come from God, and accept it thankfully and with patience. For God brings it upon us for our benefit; and so we will be untroubled and undisturbed in dishonor. We ought, then, greatly to revere the Lord who bears no grudge, and especially at the present time, as it is said: “And now we cannot open our mouth; we have become a shame and a reproach to your servants and to those who worship you. For to the Lord our God belongs righteousness, but to us shame of face, as on this day, to us and to our rulers and to our kings; for we have sinned and done lawlessly and have gone utterly astray in all things, and have not listened to your commandments.” So too Jeremiah, prophesying what has now befallen us, says this: “We are ashamed, for we have heard our reproach, and dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have entered into our holy places, into the house of the Lord.” David also says: “For you know my reproach, and my shame, and my disgrace”; and, “All day long my disgrace is before me”; and, “The shame of my face has covered me.” This, then, is the good and godly shame, which leads a man to repentance and to boldness. But there is also a harmful shame, as Scripture says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace.” For many, out of shame before certain people, fall into the nets of the devil. And he goes on: “He who reveals his ungodliness will not prosper; but he who declares it and reproves it will be loved.” And again: “A righteous man is his own accuser at the outset of his speech.” And, “As long as the innocent hold fast to righteousness, they will not be put to shame. For to know the law belongs to a good mind.” And he adds: “Blessed is the man who shrinks back from everything out of reverence.” And, “Prepare your works for your departure.” And, “Do not be ashamed to confess your sins.” A man needs discernment, then, so that he may know when he ought to feel shame for the salvation of his own soul, and when he should cast it off as sinful. For there is one who out of shame makes promises to his friend, and has made him an enemy for nothing. Let us, then, beloved, hold fast to godly shame, imitating the tax collector who was ashamed to lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast and said, “O God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” so that we too may likewise obtain the forgiveness of our sins in Christ Jesus our Lord. To him be glory and power forever. Amen.

On Humility. Humility soars on high and makes a person travel through the air. For the more someone humbles himself, the more many times over God exalts him. So it was with Moses, who spoke with God as a companion: being humble-minded, he did not reject the advice of his father-in-law Jethro, even after so many appearances of God, but did everything Jethro told him. That is why God exalted him above everyone on earth. In the same way Gideon also answered Ephraim modestly, saying, "What have I done now compared with you? Is not the gleaning of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? The Lord gave the princes of Midian into your hand; what was I able to do compared with you?" And yet it was to him that God had given the victory with the three hundred men. But the righteous man calmed their anger through humility. Even before this he had said to the angel, "Who am I, or my father's house? My clan is the lowliest in Manasseh." And a certain wise man says: "The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favour before the Lord," for all the works of the humble are plain to the Lord. And the mouth of the humble meditates on wisdom, and good understanding gives favour. And the Psalmist says, "But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people." And again, "I have become like a portent to many, but you are my strong helper." The humble-minded person who has spiritual work to do, when he reads the divine Scriptures, applies everything to himself and not to someone else. If then we truly want to please God and to be joined to him in that most blessed friendship, let us present our mind to him naked, dragging nothing of the present age along with it: no tricks, no clever arguments, no self-justification. For the Divine turns away from those who approach him in this conceited manner. But if someone is God-fearing and humble-minded, not puffed up with bodily self-importance, never rash, but broken in heart and counting himself an unprofitable servant, then the grace of God looks upon him and dwells in him. For the mark of true humility is not to heap insults on oneself, but to bear insults from others nobly; and the humble person never justifies himself. Just as abundant fruit bends the branches of a tree, so an abundance of virtue humbles a person's mind. And just as

a stake supports a branch laden with fruit, so the fear of God supports the virtuous person. And the blessed Paul, to curb our pride, writes: "Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?" And again, "We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things." These words are a model of humility. And again: "For you know the grace of God, that though he was rich, for our sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich." And he goes on: "I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love." And he continues, "Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of all the apostles, unfit to be called an apostle, [because I persecuted the Church of God]." Whoever, then, wants to acquire this God-given virtue of humility, and to flee, as has been said, the vain and God-hated swelling of pride, must neglect nothing that helps to achieve it. Let his bearing, his clothing, his gait, his seat, his food, his bedding, his speech, his movements, his glance, and his dealings with his neighbour all be trained toward plainness. Above all, let him trust himself in nothing, but submit to his neighbour and serve him, remembering the Lord, who did not disdain to wash the feet of his own disciples, and who said: "For I have given you an example" of humility, "that as I have done to you, you also should do to one another. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them." To him be glory forever.

On Forgiving One's Neighbour. To forgive one's neighbour from the heart is a commandment of the Master, and it brings salvation to all people, for his commandment is eternal life. If then we forgive, we are forgiven; but if we do not, we seal up our own sins. What wise person, then, who wants to obtain forgiveness for his own countless offences, will not gladly forgive his neighbour his very small failings? And the Lord did not only command us to do this; he also showed us by his own action

how it is to be carried out. For while he was on the cross he entreated his own Father on behalf of those who had sinned against him, saying, "Father, forgive them this sin, for they do not know what they are doing." See how the compassionate and supremely good one pleads in their defence, saying, "For they do not know what they are doing." And before this, when the disciples were indignant with certain Samaritans who had not received them, and asked that they be consumed by fire sent from God, he rebuked them, saying, "You do not know what spirit you are of"—that is, the gentle and good Spirit. He teaches us the same thing through the prophets as well. Zechariah says, "Judge with righteous judgement, and each of you show mercy and compassion to his brother." And Paul says, "Be kind to one another, then, and compassionate, imitators of God as beloved children, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you." And the prophet [?] … we ought to care for one another. Fearing also the Lord's own dreadful sentence, let us forgive one another from the heart. For he said, "So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother their trespasses from your hearts." For, he says, "You wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" And in his anger he handed him over to the torturers until he should pay back all that was owed. And when Peter asked, "How often shall I forgive my brother if he sins against me? As many as seven times?" the Lord answered him, "I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven." That is why he adds, "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." And: "If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and turns back to you seven times in a day, saying, 'I repent,' forgive him." To him be the glory, to the compassionate Christ who loves humankind, to the ages of ages. Amen.

It is good, beloved, to make our way through all the commandments of Christ, since each is linked to the next as in a golden chain. "For all his commandments are faithful, established forever and ever." So whoever truly wishes to be Christ's disciple, and is set ablaze with the fire of love for him, must pass over none of his commandments, even if

one seems small or heavy. For he himself said, "If you love me, keep my commandments." And again, "Truly I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven." Yesterday, then, beloved, we spoke about forgiving our neighbour; today we remind you—or rather, we urge you—not only to forgive them but also to pray for them, since our Master and Saviour commands both. So let no one think his commandments heavy. "For my yoke," he says, "is easy, and my burden is light." And the Apostle says, "For those who love God all things work together for good." Indeed, in the divine Scriptures we find all the saints fulfilling this commandment, and all the others, in deed. Thus the prophet Samuel says to the people, "Far be it from me to turn away from the Lord by ceasing to cry out in prayer for you." And again, "Far be it from me to sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you." Yet it is plain to everyone how they had rejected and despised him by asking for a king. And Jeremiah the prophet, who suffered so many evils at their hands, was always praying for them. This is clear from what God said to him: "As for you, do not plead for them, for I will not listen to you." Likewise Moses said to God, "If you will forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me also out of your book." And not only those of the Old Testament did this, but also those of the New. So the blessed James, the brother of the Lord, who lived an angelic life on earth, was called by everyone "the Just" and "Oblias," which means "bulwark of the people." When the feast of Passover came, and many tens of thousands of Jews had gathered in the temple, they took him up onto the pinnacle of the temple and said, "We ask you, Just One, to tell the people not to be led astray after the so-called Jesus, for we all listen to you." He answered, "Why do you ask me about the Son of Man? He himself is seated at the right hand of God on high." Then the lawless high priests and Pharisees cried out, "Oh! Oh! Even the Just One has gone astray!" And they said to one another, "We did wrong to bring forward such testimony for Jesus against ourselves." And many of the people who heard him believed. The rest went up and threw him down from the height. He fell on his knees and did not die at once, but prayed for them. And one of the sons of Rechab came near, heard him, and said to them, "What are you doing? The Just One is praying for you." Then a fuller ran up and struck him on the skull with the club they use to wring out clothes, and so they killed him. In the same way the blessed Stephen too, standing in the midst of the lawless, cried out, "Look, I see the heavens

opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." They seized him, cast him out of the city, and stoned him as he called out, saying, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." So we see that the saints prayed for their enemies even to the point of death. For whoever prays for those who wrong him dashes the demons down, and is himself shown to be an heir of the kingdom of heaven. The Apostle also exhorts us to pray for all people. To pray for all means that we must pray not only for our friends but also for our enemies. If, then, we want to show ourselves imitators of the saints and true disciples of the Lord, we too are bound to pray not only for friends but also for enemies, just as he himself showed us by his own action: on the cross he entreated his own Father for those who were crucifying him, and before the cross, at the mystical supper, he prayed for his own friends and disciples. "For you are my friends," he says, and "I no longer call you servants." Then he says, "Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me." And again, "I do not ask you to take them out of the world, but to keep them from the evil one. Sanctify them in your truth; your word is truth." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Not Seeking One's Own. Just as God's commandment binds us to forgive and to pray for one another, so too we ought not to seek our own interests, but also those of our brothers, who are members of the same body, so that we do not give ourselves an occasion for harm. For God says to Moses, "Take the sandal off your feet"—that is, take off your claim to your rights, the fleshly mindset of your own will—"for the place on which you are standing is holy ground," the ground which the meek inherit. So let us too cut off our fleshly wills and hold fast to the will of God, so that we may not be accused by him through Jeremiah, who says, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water," and, "They followed their own evil wills." Let us then take careful heed, lest we ever give our brothers a muddy drink that overthrows them, through any stumbling block whatever. "For if your brother is grieved because of food," he says, "or is made to stumble [?]

and by sinning against our brothers and wounding their weak conscience, we sin against Christ." Therefore, if food makes your brother stumble, let us who are devout also say, "I will never eat meat, so that I may not make my brother stumble." This is what is said—or rather done—by the one who is truly faithful, who loves God, who loves Christ, who [?], who keeps himself blameless in everything, so that no one may be made to stumble through him and perish. Let us then, brothers, cut off our own wills for our neighbour's sake in all things, so that we may not become the cause of stumbling and ruin to those who hear us and see how we live. Blessed is the one who is wary of everything out of reverence. And the blessed Paul writes, "Let no one seek his own good, but each his neighbour's." "Give no offence," he says, "to Jews or to Greeks or to the Church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, so that they may be saved." And again, "Love does not seek its own, is not provoked, bears all things, endures all things." And he adds, "We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. For Christ too did not please himself." And again, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" And the Lord says, "My food is to do the will of the Father who sent me, and to complete his work." And the will of his Father is that every person be saved. And again, "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Not Giving In to Desire. It is written, "All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God." If, then, the sons of God love the daughters of men—that is, human glories—from these, in turn, are born the giants, the men of renown of old. That is, from such glory are born pride, arrogance, puffed-up vanity, conceit, haughtiness, and boastfulness; for pride and the other passions are as old as the ages. And God says, "My Spirit shall not remain among these people forever," because they are fleshly, given over to evil desires. So too Paul says, reproaching the Galatians, "Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being made perfect in the flesh?" It is good, then, to cut oneself off from the desires that are in the world, because every desire wages war against the spirit. For a heart that loves pleasure becomes a prison and a chain for the soul at the time of its departure, while a heart that loves toil is an open door. For the passion of desire is an offshoot

of idleness. Idleness gives birth to desire and to sloth, and indeed even to despair. If we recognized that we are sojourners on earth, and regarded present things as perishable and rushing past us like a torrent, we would not reach out for things that are not ours and last only a short time; we would instead desire what is truly ours and everlasting—that is, to be with Christ and to enjoy his sweetness and his kingdom. For those who long for him count all the things of the present age—wealth, I mean, and glory and power and bodily beauty—as dung. And the ruler of this age cannot deceive them in anything or draw them away from the love of Christ. As Solomon too says, "Desire wisdom, that you may reign forever," and, "Seek prudence, and attain understanding with knowledge," and many other such sayings are written. For Scripture forbids us to desire anything shameful or alien, so as to show, in short, the great difference between good and evil. For it says, "Put away from you every evil desire, and clothe yourself with good and holy desire." For when you clothe yourself with this desire you will hate evil desire and bridle it as you wish. Evil desire is wild and hard to tame. It is very fearsome, and by its wildness it utterly consumes people. By saying, "Evil desire is wild," it means that it springs up of itself like a wild plant in an untilled field, or like a wild animal that grazes as it pleases without any rational oversight. What sort of thing evil desire is, and good desire too, is set out precisely in the discourse that follows, so that it may be clear that we are to turn away from every evil desire and live by good and holy desire. That is why the tree of knowing good and evil shows that human beings are capable of knowing good and evil. It points to the difference between them, not so that anyone should do evil together with good in the same act, but so that in doing good one may turn away from evil, as the one says who wrote, "Turn away from evil and do good." The Law was the first to command this, saying, "You shall not covet anything that is your neighbour's." But Ahab broke this commandment and coveted Naboth's vineyard. He killed that righteous man, but brought eternal ruin and destruction on himself and his house. The people too gave way to craving in the wilderness, and there their bodies fell. And the writer of Proverbs says, "Every idle person will be given over to desires, but the hands of the strong are diligent." And again, "The giddiness of desire undermines an innocent mind." And again, "The ungodly person desires evil desires all day long, but the righteous one shows mercy and pity without stint." And he adds, "Do not let the beauty of desire overcome you, and do not be caught by your own eyes." And blameless Job, trampling

the passion of desire underfoot, says, "If my heart has followed my eye, then let grievous things befall me." The apostle Peter also says, "Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul." And Paul says, "Put to death your members that are on earth: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire. For God did not call us to impurity but in holiness. So do not let sin reign in our mortal body, to make us obey its desires; but put on our Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires." And again: "Among them," he says, "we all once lived in the desires of our hearts, doing the will of our hearts and minds." Whoever, then, wants to escape this corrupting desire, which drags a person down to the depths of Hades, must acquire the fear of God. "For the fear of the Lord," it says, "is pure, enduring forever and ever." And again, "Nail down my flesh with the fear of you." For whoever keeps always in mind death and the eternal fire, the worm that never sleeps and the outer darkness, the weeping and gnashing of teeth, and that shame before the dreadful judgement seat of Christ in the presence of angels and men, breaks down the excess of pleasure and turns all his desire toward God. Let us then, beloved, take up bodily and spiritual labours, and desire will retreat. For desires kill the sluggard, because his hands refuse to do anything. And the Lord, who loves our souls, says, "If your right eye makes you stumble, tear it out and throw it away; for it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to be thrown into the Gehenna of fire." From this may we be delivered by the grace of Christ our Lord. To him [the good God] be the glory forever. Amen.

On Just Judgment. Those who wish to judge justly will first ask God for wisdom and understanding, as Solomon did. He made this his only and his first request, and he not only received the gift but was also praised by God for asking well. Next, they will also refuse wine. For the divine Scripture says, "Open your mouth with the word of God, and judge all things soundly." And again: "Rulers are quick to anger; let them not drink wine, lest they forget wisdom and be unable to judge rightly for the weak." And whenever anyone wants to untangle a complicated matter, let him first seek what pleases God in it, and he will find a beneficial resolution. First the law commands, saying, "You shall do no injustice in judgment," and "You shall not join with the crowd to pervert judgment." And: "You shall not pity the poor man in judgment," and "You shall not pervert the judgment of the poor; you shall not show partiality to the poor, nor stand in awe of the mighty; in righteousness you shall judge your neighbor." And: "Your judges shall judge with righteous judgment, and they shall not show partiality, nor take gifts. For gifts pervert the words of the righteous." And: "The righteous man shall pursue what is right." And Jeremiah: "Do judgment and righteousness, and rescue the plundered from the hand of the wrongdoer." And another writer says elsewhere: "Whoever pronounces the unjust just and the just unjust — both are abominable to the Lord; but he who seeks the Lord will find knowledge together with righteousness." And again: "Let a man's heart consider what is just, so that his steps may be directed by God." And the author of Proverbs: "The righteous man knows how to judge the poor; but the ungodly will not understand knowledge." And again: "A prudent man walks straight ahead; and the beginning of a good way is to do what is just." And Job says: "I had put on righteousness, and clothed myself with judgment like a cloak." And again: "If my foot has turned aside from the way; and if I also [?] the judgment of my servants." So much, then, on just judgment. But it is good also to recall the saying of the Apostle: "Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law before the unjust and not rather before the saints?" And he adds: "Now it is already an utter defeat for you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather be defrauded? Why not rather suffer wrong? Instead you yourselves do wrong, and that to your brothers." And he adds: "The unjust will not inherit the kingdom of God." But let no one suppose that the law on just judgment applies only to those who judge public affairs, and lie on his back snoring without a care. For the life-giving Spirit lays this commandment on all alike. For he says also through David: "Be instructed, all you who judge the earth; serve the Lord

in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Every man, lay hold of instruction, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way." And again: "Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times." And: "If you truly speak righteousness, then judge uprightly, O sons of men." Truly, that is, and not falsely, nor in hypocrisy. "What then," someone asks, "has this to do with me, who have not been entrusted with judicial office?" I will tell you what this precept means. God, who created man, made him free to choose, open to assault, to virtue and to vice. He planted most of the senses together, as in a small plot, in the head, where they fill the rank of bodyguards, and over them he enthroned the ruling mind, like a good and just king. So virtue and vice are always on trial: temperance and licentiousness, gluttony and self-discipline, anger and meekness, vainglory and humility — in short, every virtue has a lawsuit against the vice opposed to it. If, then, the mind condemns vice and acquits virtue, it has judged uprightly and kept judgment and righteousness. But if through heavy drinking it forgets itself, it falls from justice, like Ahaziah, and [?] a sickness unto death: that is, it loses its discernment, gives the winning vote to vice, and dies the eternal death. The Lord too bears witness to this, saying: "Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? For as you go with your adversary before the magistrate, make an effort on the way to be rid of him, lest he drag you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. Truly, truly I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny." To him, Christ, the only just judge, be glory forever. Amen.

On Just Measure. All just things are dear to God and pleasing to him. For just as God loves just judgment, so too he loves just measure. Being just himself, he takes care for what is just. Fittingly, then, Scripture gives commands about equal weights and equal measures; for it is unlawful, and beyond every injustice, to keep two measures, a small one and a large one. That is why the prophet Amos, lamenting over the disobedient, says: "Woe to you who desire the day of the Lord — it is darkness — you who make the measure small and the balance unjust." Likewise Micah also says: "Shall the one with the lawless balance be justified,

and the one with a bag of deceitful weights?" The Psalmist says the same: "For the sons of men are false in the balances, so as to do wrong." And to show that this disease belongs to greed, he adds: "Together they are made of vanity. Do not hope in injustice, and do not long for plunder. If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it." And the law commands, saying: "In measures, in weights and in balances, you shall have what is just." And again it says: "You shall not move the boundaries that your fathers set." And the prophet Zephaniah: "Do judgment and seek righteousness, so that you may be sheltered on the day of the Lord's wrath." Likewise also Ezekiel, saying: "Do judgment and righteousness; you shall have a just balance, a just measure, and a just dry measure." And the author of Proverbs: "Deceitful balances are an abomination before the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to him." And again: "A large weight and a small, and double measures, are unclean before the Lord, and both shall be entangled in their own practices." Perhaps these things seem worthless to most people; but the God-inspired Scriptures declare nothing idly or in vain. The adorable Spirit made all his laws for our salvation and eternal life. Let us, therefore, beloved, guard against the passion of greed, which is a second idolatry. This is what we are taught through equal measure, as our Lord Jesus Christ also commands us in the Gospels, saying: "Give, and it will be given to you; good measure, pressed down and shaken together, will they give into your lap. For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you." To him be glory forever.

On Repentance. How sweet repentance is, my brothers! It is nothing other than a medicine of life. All the more because our sweet Master — who bears no grudge, who is good, compassionate, loving toward mankind, loving toward souls, loving toward the poor, the guardian of our salvation — always thirsts for our repentance. For he is gladdened by the tears of those who repent, he exults over confession, he rejoices over a broken and humbled heart, and with great patience he awaits our return, and does not give up until our last breath [he longs greatly for our repentance, and receives and kisses us as he did the prodigal son who repented], calling and urging each one of us, after countless lawless deeds and devilish acts, to turn back to him; as he cries out through

the prophet, saying, "After all these things, return to me." And while we are still far off he runs to meet us, and kisses and embraces our neck, spotted and stained and wholly filthy as it is; and he does not reproach us for what is past but makes promises about what is to come. And being supremely good, he not only forgives our sins but also grants the pledge of life, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and the first robe of immortality and incorruption, which we put on through holy baptism and stripped off through sin. When we sincerely repent and turn back to him with our whole heart, he gives it to us again and holds a feast, and calls together the holy powers who are his friends, showing them the drachma he has found, that is, his royal image and likeness; and carrying the straying sheep on his shoulders, he brings it in to his own Father, where, as all rejoice, [?] the dwelling in him; and he lays down his life for those who have run away. And though we often accuse him without cause, he is patient and bears with us. [And he rejoices at our return and repentance.] Since, then, brothers, we have so compassionate a Master, let us not hesitate to turn back to him quickly, nor throw ourselves into sloth and despair because of our unbearable and countless sins. For that is the devil's complete joy; that is the sin unto death of which Scripture speaks. Let us therefore come to repentance, and let it intercede for us with God. Let us too cry out with the prophet Jeremiah: "For our sins have risen up against us, for our iniquities are many before you, O Lord; act for us for your name's sake." And: "You are among us, O Lord, and your name is called upon us." And with Micah: "I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him." And with David: "I made known my iniquity and did not hide my sin," but "I said, I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart." For you, Lord, have said: "Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified." Looking, then, Master, to the ocean of your compassion, I offer you this supplication from a filthy mouth and unclean lips. Remember that your holy name is called upon me, and that you redeemed me with your precious blood; that you sealed me with the pledge of your Spirit, and brought me up out of the [?] of my iniquities, so that [?] may not plunder me

Homily 77. On Repentance. [?] hostile. Jesus Christ, help me and be my mighty helper in battle, for I am a slave of desire and am warred against by it; but you, Lord, do not forsake me, who am cast down on the earth under the condemnation of my own works. Set me free, Master, from the evil slavery of the ruler of this world, and make me your own in your commandments. My Christ is the way of my life, and your face is the light of my eyes. God, Master, and Lord of my life, do not give me haughty eyes, and remove evil desire from me. Uphold me, Christ, with your holy hand; let not cravings and lust take hold of me, and do not hand me over to a shameless soul. Make the light of your face shine in me, Lord, so that darkness may not overtake me and the one who walks in it snatch me away. Do not hand over to invisible beasts, Lord, a soul that confesses to you. Do not allow your servant, Lord, to be wounded by strange dogs. Count me worthy, holy Father, to become a lodging for your Holy Spirit and a house for your Christ. Build me up; you who guide those who have gone astray, guide me, so that I may not turn aside to the left. I long, Lord, to see your face; O God, guide me by the light of your face. Grant me, your servant, a stream of tears, and bestow on your creature the moisture of your Holy Spirit, so that I may not wither like the fig tree that you cursed; and let my tears be my drink, and my prayer my food. Turn my mourning into joy for me, Lord, and receive me into your eternal dwellings. Let your mercy reach me, Lord, and your compassion take hold of me, and forgive all my sins. For you are the true God, who forgives iniquities. And do not allow, Lord, the work of your hands to be dishonored because of the multitude of my iniquities, but call me back, Master, through your only-begotten Son, our Savior; raise me up as I lie fallen, as you raised Levi the tax collector; and bring me to life, dead as I am in sins, as you did the widow's son, for you alone are the resurrection of the dead. And to you glory is fitting forever. Amen. One who truly repents of the evil he has done must both blame himself and bravely bear the reproaches of others; for repentance means being mocked by fools and enduring it, and offering confession to God with one's whole heart. Isaiah, lamenting over the hard-hearted and unrepentant, says: "Is the Lord not strong enough to save? But because of your sins he has turned his face away from you; for no one speaks what is just, and there is no true judgment." And another says: "How good it is, when reproved, to show repentance! For so you will escape

deliberate sin." And again: "Have you sinned? Do not do it again, and pray about your former sins." And he adds: "Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent." "For the wise man, fearing, turns away from evil." And Job says: "If, having sinned willingly, I hid my sin — for I did not stand in awe of the crowds of the city, so as not to declare it before them." And in Acts Peter says to the multitude: "Repent therefore and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out, that times of refreshing may come." Let us also, beloved, as was said before, repent with a sincere heart of the evils we have done, turning to God and saying: We have sinned, be merciful; we have done wrong, forgive; we have offended, be reconciled. Cleanse me as you cleansed the harlot; justify me as you justified the tax collector; let your mercy come upon me; let your love for mankind visit me. And do not allow me to be sold to my sins, nor to fall asleep and die the bitter death of sin, but redeem me from this present evil age. Give me time for repentance and room for a defense, for "There is no peace in my bones because of my sins; for my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down. If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand? For with you is forgiveness." Let us, then, who have despaired of our life because of our sins, believe God; let us turn to the Lord our God with all our heart; let us practice righteousness for the rest of the days of our life, and serve him rightly according to his will; and he will heal our former transgressions. And we have the power to master the works of the devil. Let us not fear his threats at all, for they are as slack as a dead man's sinews; but let us fear the almighty Lord, keep his commandments, and live in him. And if we thus entreat him with groans and tears, he will say to us also through Ezekiel the prophet: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live." And again: "On whatever day the lawless man turns from all his iniquities and does righteousness, I will no longer remember his sins." "For greatly longs [?]

On Patience. 1663. [?] in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance." To him be glory forever. Amen. On Patience. Having first said a few things to you about repentance, let us now, with God's help, speak also about patience, which saves man, so far as his love for mankind allows. For repentance needs patience and cannot be brought to perfection without it. A one-winged eagle cannot fly up to the heights; but patience perfects repentance and shows it wearing its crown. And patience is not only useful in helping repentance: without it we cannot accomplish any virtue or commandment of God at all. Patience, then, is the chief of all the good things in us. And we must accept every trial and affliction with patience and thanksgiving, so that we may reach the land of promise. It is good not to move from place to place, for "let each one remain in the state in which he was called." Patience teaches toil, and bravely bears the trials that come from outside against self-control. For just as wax, unless it is warmed and softened for a long time, cannot receive the seal pressed upon it, so neither can a man, unless he has been tested through toils and infirmities, receive the seal of God's virtue. That is why the Lord said to Paul: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." When the devil left the Lord, then the angels came and ministered to him. So just as the angels were not present while he was being tempted, so too when we are tempted the angels of God withdraw for a time, though not far; and after the tempters have gone, they come to us, ministering divine thoughts, illumination, compunction, sweetness, and patience; and so the soul is refreshed after its labor. That is why Isaiah says: "Those who wait for God will renew their strength; they will grow wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not hunger." As Moses too says to the people: "For this reason he tested you and afflicted you, that he might feed you with manna, so that what was in your heart might be made known. As a man disciplines his son, so the Lord has disciplined you." And again: "And the Lord afflicted you, that he might do you good in the end." The prophet Nahum also says: "The Lord is good to those who wait for him in the day of affliction." And another: "Do not say, I will deal harshly with my enemy; but wait for the Lord,

so that he may help you; for patience will not fail the godly." So too the most gentle David endured. Lying low and being pelted with stones by Shimei, and hearing "Get out, you lawless man," he did not grow indignant. When his nephew was angered at this and said, "Who is this dog that curses my lord the king? Let me go over and strike him and take off his head," David rebuked him, saying, "Let him curse me, so that the Lord may see and repay me with good." Fittingly, then, he sang: "I waited patiently for the Lord, and he heeded me and heard my prayer." And to encourage us he says: "Be strong, and let your heart take courage, and wait for the Lord. For those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land of the living." And: "Let not those who wait for you be put to shame, O Lord, Lord of hosts." "For the furnace tests the potter's vessels, and a man is tested in his reasoning." "Woe to those who have lost patience! What will they do when the Lord visits them?" "For the patience of the poor shall not perish forever." And Zephaniah: "If it delays, wait for it; for he who is coming will come and will not tarry." And: "If the righteous man shrinks back, my soul takes no pleasure in him." And Paul: "If we endure, we shall also reign with him." And again: "For you have need of endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promises." And James: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; and let patience have its perfect work." And he adds: "Blessed is the man who endures trial, for when he has been proved he will receive the crown of life." And the Lord says: "He who endures to the end will be saved." And again: "By your patience you will gain your souls." To him be glory forever. Amen.
On the Struggle. The struggle is the fellow soldier and partner of patience; or rather, it is the beginning and the end [?]

So we have yoked the contest to endurance, because those who struggle carry off the victory over every passion of the devil, with our Lord Jesus Christ, the president of the games, giving them strength and help. The one who competes exercises self-control in all things, and he does not stop until the Lord wipes out all his enemies from before his face. Self-control, then, is twofold: in some things we must hold back, and in others we must not. We must hold back from what is evil and not do it; but we must not hold back from what is good, but do it. So hold yourself back from all wickedness, and do what is good. Keep yourself from adultery, fornication, drunkenness, lawlessness, from luxury, from wickedness, from many foods and extravagance, from wealth and boasting, from arrogance and pride, from lying, slander and hypocrisy, from bearing grudges and from every blasphemy, from theft, from defrauding others, false witness, greed, evil desire, deceit, vainglory, swaggering, and everything like these. These are the works that the competitor and servant of God must hold back from. But there are also good works which must be done and not held back from. First of all: faith, the fear of the Lord, love, concord, words of righteousness, truth, endurance; to serve widows, to visit orphans and those in want, to ransom the servants of God from their distress, to be hospitable, to be quiet, to make oneself lower than all people, to revere the elderly, to practice righteousness, to preserve the brotherhood, to be patient, to bear no grudge, to comfort those who are weary in soul, not to cast off [?] those who have stumbled in the faith but to turn them back and put heart into them, to admonish those who sin, not to oppress debtors and the needy, and whatever else is like these. If anyone keeps these and does not hold back from them, he will live to God. The competitor must also waste away the adversary in his own flesh, so that the mind does not slip, through the flesh's moistness, into the smoothness of pleasures, and so that the minds of those who struggle may be set in motion by the divine light, and may serve the divine law and delight in it, as the Apostle says. We must therefore make the mind ready, move our thinking elsewhere, peer beyond heaven, and come to be somewhere above all creation, and with burning desire and unceasing thought be bound fast

to those things which the true competitors also showed forth, and for which they were glorified in their contest. For having seen the promises from afar through faith, they endured a long stretch of afflictions, since they counted the one who had promised faithful, and awaited the bright day of the Master, on which God will display his servants, when he comes on the clouds of heaven and gathers his holy ones, the perfect competitors. We must therefore be tested and bear up: in the body under constant upsets, and in our souls under evil thoughts. So with all steadfastness and endurance we must work out the testimony of our conscience before God: "I waited and waited for the Lord, and he heeded me." For no one can acquire virtue unless he has first fought for it to the point of blood. We must resist sin even to death, like competitors and without flagging, as the apostle Paul says. And Scripture says: "Before a person are life and death, and whichever he prefers will be given to him." For devout and prudent reason is said to be master of the passions: through temperance it masters gluttony and desire; through justice, all malice; through courage, anger, [?] and fear; and this not so as to destroy them, but so as not to give way to them. For reason does not uproot the passions; it fights against them. Therefore, it says, none of you can cut out desire, but reason can enable you not to be enslaved to desire. There is need, then, of much struggle, so that we too may truly say with Paul: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness." And spurring us on to the same zeal, he said: "And if anyone competes as an athlete, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules." And again: "Do you not know that in a stadium all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run so that you may win it. I therefore do not run aimlessly; I do not box like one beating the air; but I bruise my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified." He also writes to the Philippians: "the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear of." And to the Hebrews he says: "You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin; and you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: 'My son,' it says, 'do not make light of the Lord's discipline, nor lose heart when you are rebuked by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.'" And praising others, he says: "so that we boast of your endurance and faith in all your persecutions and the afflictions that you bear, a sign of the righteous judgment of God, for which you are also suffering. For all who want to

live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted." And John says: "Do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you; we know that we have passed from death into life." And the Lord says: "Strive to enter through the narrow gate, for wide is the gate and spacious the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it; for narrow is the gate and hard the road that leads to life" — [may we be counted worthy of it by the grace of Christ our God,] to whom be glory forever.

On Concord. It is acceptable to God to take care for the unity of the Church, than which nothing among human beings is better; and to bear with everyone, as the Lord bears with us, and to put up with everyone in love. We must not, on some supposedly reasonable pretext — not to say a thoroughly unreasonable one — tear ourselves away from the body of the Church and go our own way. Rather, together let there be one prayer, one petition, one mind, one hope, in love, in blameless joy, which is Jesus Christ, than whom nothing is more delightful. So we must all run together as to one altar: one soul, though in many members, one purpose with one will, as being one body. For as a swarm of bees produces a honeycomb, so a community of brothers produces the kingdom of God; and as a trumpet rouses the eagerness of warriors, so teaching in practical virtue rouses the zeal of disciples. For the one who separates himself is like a bird that has flown from its own nest and moves from place to place, and so becomes easy prey for every fowler and hunter. For on every side the spiritual fowlers and hunters have set snares and stumbling-blocks of lawlessness for him, and the rapacious ravens peck out his eyes. In every way, then, the harmony of a brotherhood living in concord is good and well-ordered, especially where perfect love has taken root. So we find Elisha with Elijah: when he was told once and again, "Stay here," he answered with an oath, saying, "As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you." Likewise Ruth the Moabite said to her mother-in-law: "May the Lord do so to me, and more also, if anything but death parts me from you." Rightly, then, Boaz blessed her, saying: "May the Lord repay your work, and may your reward be

full from the Lord." And though she was a foreigner, she was joined to Boaz and bore the grandfather of David. And this same David says: "Behold, what is so good or so pleasant as for brothers to dwell together?" And the author of Proverbs says: "A brother helped by a brother is like a strong and lofty city." And: "Two are better than one, for they have a reward, because if they fall, the one will lift up his companion." And: "Woe to the one who is alone when he falls, and there is no second to lift him up." And: "If one prevails against him, the two will stand against him, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." And in the Acts of the Apostles it is written: "All who believed were together and had all things in common." And a little later: "The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of his possessions was his own, but they had all things in common." Blessed, then, is the monk who regards every human being as god after God. Blessed is the monk who looks with gladness and all joy on the salvation and progress of all as though it were his own. A monk is one who counts himself as one with all, because he seems to see himself unfailingly in each person. And the Apostle says: "Just as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another." And he adds: "But God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another." For this reason we ought to bear one another's burdens, and all be of one mind and one soul, compassionate, humble, doing everything in love, so that in this way too we may draw God to ourselves and our prayer may become acceptable. For the Lord says: "Truly I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them." To him be glory [and power] forever. Amen. On Thoughts. Scripture says: "He gave the law as a help."

A help, that is, to human nature for the [?] cultivation of virtue — as a farmer uses iron to prune the plant: to cut away from the flesh the natural desires for pleasure when they trouble it, and likewise from the soul the weak thoughts that disturb it, whether those that mind the things of the flesh or those that incline toward what is temporary and earthly. They spring up this way from nature, and moreover evil spirits flood nature beyond measure, as experience knows; and that is why the law was given, so that the ground [?] should not turn to waste, as under a negligent farmer, and bear no proper fruit. And the Apostle says: "I want the men to pray in every way, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing thoughts." And again: "Demolishing reasonings and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God." The Apostle's aim, then, is that we be pure of unclean thoughts, above all when we present our prayer to God; for stench does not go with fragrance, nor foul smell with perfume. The one who is carried off by his thoughts is blinded by them; for where the images of thoughts are, there assent follows. We must therefore always overturn the first assault, and destroy the sinful thoughts from the land — that is, our heart, according to the word of the Lord. And while the children of Babylon — that is, evil thoughts — are still infants, [?] the three most general thoughts of the devil against us, by which the envious demon wages war and suggests to us that of gluttony [?] ... he tried to tempt with every temptation, and so, defeated, he was driven back. The Lord became for us an example [?] in all things, that is, of rendering him powerless through fasting and prayer. For the deceitful one lies in ambush like a lion in his den, hiding snares for us and traps of unclean and impious thoughts. We must therefore [?] thoughts, as has been said, quickly turn them aside by devout rebuttal and by prayer, and especially those that defile, so that they may not defile the holy place and profane the man of God. With all fear, then, we ought to [offer] our services to God, lest we be found speaking with God with our lips while in our heart we are [carried off as captives?] to Babylon, [?] unclean things, and we hear: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." [There is] need, then, beloved, also of much watchfulness, [so that?] the mind [may go] with the voice [?], lest instead of serving the Lord we provoke him, mixing an evil reek with the incense in our prayer [?], and the [offering] of our prayer be blemished like Cain's. For

God greatly abhors unclean thoughts, or rather the heart that gives birth to them, as the law also shows. For it says, "You shall not plow with a calf and a donkey together," that is, you shall not offer prayer with a clean and an unclean thought together. You shall not bring for sacrifice a sheep that is blemished, or ear-cropped, or tail-docked, or mangy. Indeed, he will not accept even withered fruit from your hand — how much more a muddied and contemptuous prayer? For he knows our secrets, as David testifies, saying: "The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain." And David took great pains to be freed from them, saying: "Morning by morning I killed all the sinners of the land, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity." For the unclean is not permitted to enter the house of the Lord, as the law says — and we are his house, and Jerusalem is within us. And the sinners of the land are the low, crawling, snake-like thoughts that lurk in the heart. Fittingly, then, he prays, saying: "Rescue my soul from their mischief." And: "Scatter the nations that delight in war." And: "Save me from the mire, so that I do not sink; for you are my endurance, O Lord." And so the Lord says to him in his affliction: "You called on me, and I rescued you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm." We too, then, brothers, ought with outstretched hands and an intent mind to implore God, the lover of humankind, to send us help from above, so that we may conquer our enemies as Moses conquered Amalek. For it is a terrible and ruinous thing to be secretly won over by unclean thoughts. From thoughts a person is dragged down into deeds as well, and little by little is estranged from God. Indeed, whoever assents to them is condemned as though he had committed the sin. "For wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sin. For crooked thoughts separate from God. For the holy Spirit of wisdom will flee deceit and will depart from senseless thoughts," as Scripture says. And the Lord also says: "Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies." These are what the evil man has in the treasury of his heart. But let us cast ourselves down before the goodness of God, begging him every hour to cleanse our hearts, so that we may bring him gifts at the spiritual Jerusalem, and hear from him: "The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good shoots for God." To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

On Discipline. Discipline is good on every account, but above all discipline according to God. For the one who from his youth practices the life of wisdom and is trained in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, on into old age and seniority, God will never abandon. For God is not unjust, so as to forget the discipline and labor of those who endure for his name's sake. Discipline according to God will at the last speak with confidence, in great relief. If indeed the Lord often takes even good things away from us, as he did Job's wealth — "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away" — then surely the Eternal One will also take from our hand the evils he has brought upon us; for "good things and evil come from the Lord," it says. And he who brought evils upon us will himself bring us eternal gladness. We are bound, then, to accept discipline in everything with thanksgiving. For whoever does not willingly choose labors for the sake of truth is disciplined more harshly by involuntary ones; but whoever does the will of God as far as he is able will escape great labors by means of small ones. And the author of Proverbs says: "Whoever fears the Lord will receive discipline." And again: "Whoever spares his rod hates his son, but whoever loves him disciplines him diligently." And again: "Discipline your son, for so he will be hopeful. Listen, my son, and receive my words, and the years of your life will be multiplied. Take hold of my discipline, do not let it go; for a son who neglects to keep his father's discipline will ponder evil sayings." And again: "A fool sneers at his father's discipline, but whoever heeds reproofs is the shrewder." And again: "Give your heart to discipline, and make your ears ready for words of understanding." And again: "Do not refrain from disciplining a child, for if you strike him with a rod he will not die, but you will save his soul." And again: "Discipline your son, and he will give you rest and bring honor to your tribe." And again: "It is better to hear the rebuke of a wise man than to be a man who hears the song of fools."

And he adds: "Hear, children, a father's discipline, and pay attention to gain understanding. For I give you a good gift; do not forsake my law. You simple ones, learn shrewdness; you undisciplined, take it to heart. Take discipline, and not silver, and knowledge rather than refined gold." And through the prophet Zephaniah God says: "Fear me and receive discipline, and you will not be destroyed — so as to serve the Lord under one yoke." And Micah says: "Shepherd your people with your rod." And the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says: "My son, do not make light of the Lord's discipline, nor lose heart when you are rebuked by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are without discipline, then you are illegitimate and not sons." And to the Corinthians: "For if I grieve you, who is there to gladden me but the one I have grieved?" And he goes on: "All discipline seems for the present to be a matter not of joy but of grief; but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it." And David says: "Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O Lord, and teach out of your law." And: "The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he did not give me over to death." And again: "Let the righteous man discipline me in mercy and rebuke me." And: "Your discipline has set me upright to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me." And Job says: "Is not human life on earth a time of trial? And his life is like that of a hired man paid by the day." If human life on earth is a time of trial, how can one who is in the trial not be tested? For what the Saviour said — "Watch and pray, that you may not fall into temptation" — indicates [?] not being swallowed up by temptation, and [?]. For to prevail is both celebrated and glorious. And again the Lord says: "Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, will say to him when he comes in from the field, 'Come at once and sit down at table'? Will he not rather say to him, 'Prepare something for my supper, and put on your apron and serve me while I eat and drink, [?] and after that you shall eat and drink'?" [?] He adds: "Does he thank that servant because he did what was commanded? I think not. So you also, when you have done everything you were commanded, say, 'We are unworthy servants; we have done what we ought to have done.'" To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. [?]

…is pleasing to God. For there is no one who does not need a counsellor except God alone, who created wisdom. Every human being needs good counsel more than he needs to breathe the air, as the divine Scripture also teaches us. For it says: “Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel”—that is, the spiritual wine that gladdens the heart. Such a person never misses the mark, but passes through his whole life free of care. For needing counsel, especially from experienced elders, is a sign of humility and of hatred for pride. And it is plain that God gives grace to the humble but opposes the proud. As Tobit also says to his son: “Seek counsel from every wise man, and do not despise any useful counsel.” For whoever shares in good counsel walks in the [?] of the Lord's commandments, but a man without counsel is his own enemy, like Rehoboam the son of Solomon. He abandoned the good counsel of the elders and held to the counsel of the young men who had been brought up with him, and so he lost the kingdom of the ten sceptres of Israel. Rightly, then, does Isaiah lament over such people: “Woe,” he says, “to those who take counsel, but not through the Lord, who act in secret; their works shall be in darkness.” For the counsel of the wicked plans lawless things, but the godly have taken counsel with understanding. And another wise man said: “Guard your soul from an evil counsellor; for he takes counsel for himself, and will stand on the opposite side to see what will happen.” And again: “Do not take counsel with those who look askance at you, and hide your counsel from those who envy you.” It is fitting and right, then, as has already been said, that in all things we should share in the spiritual counsel of experienced elders and flee the counsels of carnal and untaught people. Otherwise we may take hold of a rod of reed instead of the support of a staff of palm, and it will pierce our hand and pour out its natural poison; and instead of a sheep we may fall in with a wolf. “For he who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be found out; for perception comes easily to the prudent.” And Solomon says: “He who leads the upright astray into an evil way will himself fall into destruction.” And again: “Son, do not let evil counsel overtake you, which forsakes the teaching of youth. For those who have no guidance fall like leaves, but safety lies in much counsel. For like a city without walls is a man who does anything without counsel.” Moses, who conversed with God, did not disdain the counsel of Jethro, but gladly did everything Jethro told him, and the great glory he had with God and with men did not make him proud. And Paul the apostle, who had Christ speaking within him, says to the Galatians: “I went up to Jerusalem and laid before them the gospel that I preach, but privately, before those who were of repute,

lest somehow I should be running, or had run, in vain.” He who says he was not taught by any man but received the gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ did not disdain to take counsel with his fellow disciples. For he did not trust himself, fearing that he might be running, or had run, in vain. We, then, who do not even know which way is right and which is left, ought all the more to do everything with the approval of our spiritual fathers. We should heed the example of the Apostle, who made use of counsel with all diligence. We should trust ourselves in nothing and not believe our own thoughts, but keep in step with the counsel and judgement of the fathers before us, so that we are never mocked by the evil demons. For they transform things as they please, especially for those who do not know their arts and who trust in their own bow and arm. Through humility the grace of the Holy Spirit will come upon us, as the Lord also taught us, saying: “When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how or what you will answer. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you must say.” To him be glory for ever—

On dreams. Some people have trusted in dreams and been turned aside from the straight path. For this reason we remind you, beloved, that you must not readily trust in [?] and many-branched dreams. For they are nothing other than the images and fantasies of a wandering mind, and the mockery of the evil demons.
