Their aim is to deceive us so that we follow their baits, and then to drag a person down into pleasure, as the apostle Jude, the brother of James, says about certain such people: “Yet in the same way these dreamers too defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones.” And Ecclesiastes comes forward, saying: “A dream comes with much trial, and a fool's voice with many words.” And he adds: “Do not let your mouth make your flesh sin, lest God be angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands; for where dreams are many, there are also vanities and many words.” And the son of Sirach says that “Dreams give wings to fools.” And he goes on: “Like one who grasps at a shadow and chases the wind is he who pays heed to dreams. From a falsehood what truth can come?” And again: “Divinations and omens and dreams are vain; for dreams have led many astray,

and those who put their hope in them have fallen.” So if a light or some fiery form appears to one of those engaged in the ascetic struggle, he must by no means accept such a vision. For it is plainly a deception worked by the enemy's evil craft. The Apostle also teaches us this clearly when he says that Satan transforms himself “into an angel of light.” It is good, then, before sleep, while lying in bed, to pray this prayer as a safeguard for the soul and a way of putting delusion to flight: “Almighty Word of the Father, self-sufficient God, Jesus Christ; Jesus, swift in your compassion, who are never parted from your servants but always rest in them; Jesus, the good shepherd of your sheep: do not hand me over to the plotting of the serpent, and do not abandon me to the desire of Satan, for the seed of corruption is in him. You, then, O Lord, all-holy King, adorable God, Jesus Christ, guard me while I sleep by your immortal counsel and by your Holy Spirit, with whom you sanctified your disciples, and deliver me from the plotting of the serpent. Grant to me, unworthy as I am, the [?] of your salvation upon my bed, and enlighten my mind with the light of the knowledge of your Gospel. Guard my soul in the love of your cross, my heart in the purity of your word, my body by your passion and your freedom from passion, and my thoughts in your peace. And raise me up at the proper time to glorify you; for you are worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.” There are also other dreams, such as those Job speaks of: “For the Lord speaks once, and a second time in a dream, as when fear falls upon one in the night.” But we, beloved, ought not to believe or assent to dreams. Even if a vision really should be sent to us by some divine revelation, let us not pay heed to it, lest we receive smoke instead of light. For in this we do not anger the Lord at all; rather he will [?] welcome us, as people who guard with fear the treasure he has entrusted to us. We had many stories that have reached me, old and new, including things that happened in our own day, about people who were mocked by dreams and fell pitifully. We might have included them in the present work for the safety of its readers. But so that we do not stray from our purpose, I will set down one single account and then end this discourse. There was a monk on Mount Sinai, a cautionary example, who had shown great abstinence and, in a cell,

had lived shut in for many years. Later, deluded by diabolical revelations and dreams, he fell into Judaism and circumcision of the flesh. The devil had often shown him true dreams, and by these he enticed the monk's darkened mind. Afterwards he showed him the company of the martyrs and apostles and all the Christians as dark and full of every shame. On the other side he showed Moses and the prophets and the God-hated people of the Jews, shining all around with brilliant light and living in joy and gladness. When the wretched man saw these things, he immediately got up and left the holy mountain. He came to Palestine and went off to Noara and Livias, the strongholds of the Jews. He told them about the [?] fantasies that had appeared to him, and then he was circumcised and became a Jew. He took a wife and openly taught [?] the Jews against the Christians. I saw him myself, as did many of the monks; it is not yet three years since his soul was torn from him in an evil death. For he wasted away over a long time, became worm-eaten, and expired. When I and some devout monks saw him, we lamented greatly. It was a pitiful sight: a man grey all over, who had grown old in ascetic discipline and toil, now flirting with women, tasting the defiled meats of the Jews, speaking indecent words, blaspheming Christ and insulting holy baptism. This was the man whom the lawless Jews called a second Abraham. Fittingly, then, did the Lord say: “Keep watch, for you do not know at what hour the thief comes.” And he adds: “But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and not let his house be broken into.” To our God be glory for ever. Amen.

On faintheartedness and double-mindedness. Brothers, let us not give the spirit of faintheartedness room to master us, lest we be condemned by the Scripture that says: “Who will bear a fainthearted man?” Instead, let us cast all our care upon the Lord, for he cares for us. Let us, then, rid ourselves of double-mindedness and faintheartedness. Let us not be double-minded at all about asking God for something, saying to ourselves, “How can I ask the Lord and receive, when I have sinned so much against him?” Rather, turn to the Lord with your whole heart and ask of him without hesitating. Then you will know his great compassion: he will not abandon you, but will fulfil the request of your soul. For God is not

like human beings, who bear grudges; he bears no grudges, and he has compassion on what he has made. So cleanse your heart of doubting, and ask of him, and you will receive what you ask; but if you doubt, you will not receive. For those who doubt God are the double-minded, and they obtain nothing at all of what they ask. But those who are whole ask for everything in faith, trusting in the Lord, and they receive whatever they ask without doubting. And if you receive it more slowly, do not become double-minded because you did not quickly receive what your soul asked for. It is surely because of some trial, or some transgression you are unaware of, that you receive it more slowly. So do not stop asking for what your soul asks, and you will receive it. But if you grow weary of asking, blame yourself and not the one who gives to you. For double-mindedness is a daughter of the devil and does great evil to the servants of God. Put on, then, the strong faith. Let us stand firm, like an anvil under the hammer. It belongs to a great athlete to be beaten and still to win. Above all, let us endure everything for God's sake, so that he too may bear with us. Let us become zealous; let us understand the times, as we await him who is beyond time: the timeless, the invisible, who for our sake became visible; the intangible, who for our sake was touched; the impassible, who for our sake suffered; who in long-suffering endured all things for us. And Scripture also says: “You who fear the Lord, wait for his mercy, and do not turn aside, lest you fall.” And it adds: “Who has trusted in the Lord and been put to shame? Or who has called upon him and been overlooked? Or who has persevered in the fear of him and been forsaken?” So do not lose heart in your prayer, lest you become like the people in Egypt, who out of faintheartedness would not listen to Moses. Hear Joshua the son of Nun saying: “Take great care of your souls, to love the Lord our God, and he will fight for you.” And it is written in Judges too: “Let us not provoke the Lord our God to anger, lest Midian come up with its cattle and destroy our crops, and we become very poor.” Let us hear Isaiah saying: “Take comfort, you who are fainthearted in mind.” For the Lord gives patience to the fainthearted and life to those whose hearts are broken. Let us too, then, with compunction, petition God together with David, saying: “I mused, and my spirit fainted. My heart was troubled; my strength has forsaken me. Refuge has vanished from me, and there is no one who cares for my soul.” But: “Do not forsake me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me.” And remove your scourges from me, for “I have fainted under the strength of your hand.” And: “Behold, I have fled far away and lodged in the wilderness, waiting for you, the life-giving God, to save me from faintheartedness

and from the storm. For my soul clings to the dust; but give me life according to your word. For I know you, good Lord, that “when my heart was despondent, you set me high upon a rock.” And: “You will give power and strength” to those who love you. Let us pay attention to what Paul also urges upon us: “Put on,” he says, “the whole armour of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.” And to the strong he also says: “Comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone.” Let us, then, always meditate on these God-inspired words with much patience, so that we never hear: “You who by this time ought to be teachers need someone to teach you again; you have come to need milk and not solid food.” It is good, then, to pray that temptation may not come upon us. But when it does come, let us accept it with patience and thanksgiving as our own and not as something foreign. Scripture bears witness that whoever believes wholeheartedly and in humility receives the gift of freedom from passion: “Today,” it says, “you will be with me in paradise.” And: “Your faith has saved you; go into the peace of freedom from passion,” and other such sayings. Even at the time of sowing, the grape begins to ripen [?]. Do not let the enemies blunt your eagerness with their various temptations, buffeting your soul. For out of afflictions the crowns are woven, and in weaknesses the power of Christ is made perfect. Rather, let us stand in prayer with a courageous mind, calling on our Master and saying: “Lord, who alone are good and loving towards humankind, who alone are kind and gentle, who alone are true and just, our only compassionate God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, and entered into his glory and yours: let the power of your majesty come upon me, your servant, and strengthen me, Lord, with the Gospel of your teaching. Yes, Master, enlighten my inmost being and all my members by your will. Cleanse me from every stain and wickedness and sin, and keep me spotless and blameless against every working of the Adversary. And grant me, in your goodness, to understand what is yours, to think what is yours, to live in what is yours, and to stand in fear of you until the last day and hour and breath. I, the sinner, call upon you, Jesus Christ, that in your indescribable mercy you may keep my body and soul and spirit safe from every snare of the Adversary. Yes, holy Father, shelter me, your servant, with your compassion, and do not forsake me, lest my enemies say, ‘We have swallowed him up.’ For you are my defender, Lord, and in you is my praise continually for ever. Amen.”

In this way, then, let us approach the good Master. Let us not lose heart in anything, but strive manfully, remembering what is written: “And he told them a parable to show that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.” And it goes on: “And will not God vindicate his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? Yes, I tell you, he will vindicate them speedily.” To him be glory for ever. Amen.

Labours undertaken for God save a person and give him the boldness to say to God: “Look upon my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins.” And: “I am weary with crying out; my throat has grown hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in my God.” Let us, then, beloved, give our body to toil together with our soul, in fasts and vigils and psalmody and unceasing prayers and the work of our hands, so that we may receive the reward “when he gives sleep to his beloved”—that is, rest. What reward? That we become heirs and sons of God. For this is “the reward of the fruit of the womb”—that is, of self-control. For such people are found to be like the apostles, especially those who practise freedom from possessions. “For like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons”—the sons of those who have shaken themselves free of the matter of this age. They are also called blessed, because they fulfil a good desire. And they will not be put to shame when they speak “with their enemies in the gate”—that is, at the time of their departure from the body, when the evil demons come, wanting to seize the soul as it leaves the body. What wise man, then, knowing these things, will not toil even to death to save his own soul? Labours undertaken for God not only save the soul, but also make the body healthy and strong. For God supplies strength in proportion to a person's resolve. But idleness teaches a thorny wickedness, for thorns grow in the hands of the idle. And: “The ways of the idle are strewn with thorns.” Such are those who do no work, but slander and babble without the fear of God. Besides this, they are also rash in incoherent talk, under the pretext

of teaching, so they claim, understanding neither what they say nor the things they so confidently assert. The Psalmist also blames them, saying: “They are not in the toils of men, and they will not be scourged with men.” For those who sin and do not repent, and are not scourged—that is, disciplined—here with men, will be punished there endlessly with the demons. For this reason we too are taught by Scripture to love toil, because it helps us in everything. For it says: “Do not hate laborious work; humble your soul greatly.” And: “Be diligent in all your works, and no sickness will befall you. For every idle man will be full of desires, but the ways of the courageous are smooth.” And David says: “This is toil before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God”; and indeed I labour for this, that I may live to the end. For you said, Master: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage”—that is, out of the [?] of the brick-making of shameful passions. It is good also to emulate the Apostle, for he says: “Brothers, remember our labour and toil; we worked night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you. For you yourselves know that we did not eat anyone's bread without paying for it.” And to the Corinthians, as he lists his struggles for godliness, he adds: “In labours far more.” And again: “I laboured more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me.” We too, then, must undertake our labours with humility and discernment, that is, by asking spiritual fathers. In this way we shall not fall into delusion and the mockery of demons. For the unclean spirits are always firing a person up to attempt what he cannot accomplish, and afterwards they sneer at him. Whenever we succeed in something, we must say and think, with the Apostle: “Not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” The Apostle is not the only model for us in everything; our Lord Jesus Christ himself showed us everything by his own example. For although he was sinless, and was God, and had no need of bodily things, he consented to do everything and to teach us everything. “For he fasted forty days”; and “he was wearied from the journey”; and he had nowhere to lay his head; and he spent the night in prayer to God. To him be glory for ever. Amen.

[?]… is good. It is also the Master's first commandment, the one that leads from slavery to freedom. For the people were commanded to go out of Egypt in haste and to reach the good land, passing from dark slavery into the light of freedom; and so they were also instructed to eat the Passover in haste. And Paul writes to Timothy, saying: "Be diligent to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed." And he adds: "For everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things." And another says: "If you see a man of understanding, rise early to go to him. And who is wise? Cling to him. Be willing to listen to every divine discourse, and do not let proverbs of understanding escape you." And again: "Meditate continually on the commandments of the Lord; guard your heart, and do not neglect the discourses of the elders, for from them you will learn understanding. Let your reasoning be with the wise, and all your discourse be in the law of the Most High. Let righteous men be your companions at table." These things, then, are fitting for everyone, but above all for those who stand outside the affairs of this life, who have chosen to be the lowliest in the house of God — or rather, whom God has drawn to himself. If, then, we grow careless through laziness, even the sins forgiven us before are undone. For just as gold being refined in the fire grows hard if it is neglected, so too the zealous person, if he is careless for a single hour, grows cold toward grace; at once the flies of sin are drawn to him and destroy the fragrance of his spiritual work. Whoever wishes to make the enemy weak, then, must cut sin away, and the enemy, stripped of his wings, is made a plaything like a sparrow. For throughout all of life the evil demons are accustomed to sharpen the swords of temptation against zealous monks who have chosen a life of stillness, and to campaign all the more furiously against the more devout and zealous, pressing them with unbearable wars, so that somehow they may be able to draw them away from prayer. The zealous person must therefore show tireless fervor in the work of prayer, so that the angels may stay with him rejoicing, and the demons may flee under the lash. For this reason the zealous person ought always to be fervent in spirit. For just as iron put into the fire is changed wholly from its own nature into the nature of fire, and becomes wholly like fire, so too the one who waits constantly upon God ought to cast off the dark stains of this life and be united to the divine fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth, and become wholly fire, so that he may be impregnable to his adversaries. The Apostle too says: "Do not lag in diligence; be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord." One who dedicates himself to God with pure thought and good deeds, then, must sing with David and say: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the

delight of the Lord." And: "But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God." And: "Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells." And: "How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord." "For blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to dwell in your courts." And the blessed Mary, the sister of Lazarus, sat at the Master's feet, staying there with great longing and listening to him gladly. And the Lord himself teaches us, saying: "Strive to enter through the narrow gate, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

DISCOURSE [?]. On Service. The one who serves ought to serve carefully, knowing that it is God's work. He must not neglect anything, nor pass it by and grow slack because of grief or irritation or some quarrel with the brothers. For everything belonging to the monastery is consecrated to God as an offering to him, and great danger attaches to it. Whoever serves carelessly is like one who despises God. "For inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me; and inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these, you did not do it to me." So if anyone serves carefully, his service goes up to God. Rightly, then, did Jeremiah say of the careless: "Cursed is the man who does the work of the Lord carelessly." And the contemptuous man is boastful and arrogant. Let us, then, who are outside the curse and within the blessing, as servants of Christ, fulfill our service with all care and diligence, so that we may inherit a blessing, as

that your labor is not in vain in the Lord." And to Timothy he says: "Be sober in all things, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry." And he says of himself: "But now I am going to Jerusalem to serve the saints; but strive together with me in your prayers, that my service may be acceptable to the saints." Let us consider, then, brothers, with what effort and longing the very apostles of the Church served the poor in Jerusalem. And he says to others as well: "For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love you showed toward his name in serving the saints, as you still do." And Peter says: "As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another." And he adds: "If anyone speaks, let it be as the oracles of God; if anyone serves, let it be as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through our Lord Jesus Christ." And the Lord says: "If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also. If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him." And again: "But I am among you as one who serves." And: "For the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Poverty. Poverty shows a monk's way of life to be pure. The monk without possessions is a high-flying eagle. The monk without possessions is free of the few things so that he may come to enjoy the many. The [monk] without possessions knows that he is a sojourner on the earth. For since he carries nothing of this passing age with him, it is plain that he longs for the everlasting goods. The one without possessions is found to be an imitator of Elijah and John, and of those who said, "Look, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?" And they will hear from the Savior: "You who have left everything and followed me will receive many times as much in this age, and in the age to come eternal life." The one without possessions lives his life on earth, but has his dwelling in the heavens. For through poverty he vies with the angels and dances with the righteous. Turning away from earthly things, he beholds the heavenly. Do you not see how great a difference there is: to leave behind things that last a short while and come into eternal goods; to leave behind the perishable and inherit the imperishable; to leave behind what is not ours and come to enjoy what has been prepared for those who love God; [to leave behind the visible and receive the

invisible, "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man"]? For whoever hates the world and mammon plainly loves the Maker of the world. Having disregarded the lesser things, he longs for the greater. Poverty, then, is the mark of a great and God-loving soul. Such a person becomes "an heir of God the Father and a fellow heir with Christ." So whoever wishes to acquire the pearl of great price, let him gladly part with all present goods, so that he may truly acquire the field in which he found the hidden treasure of life. For when someone has parted with all worldly wealth, then he finds the place where the grace of God lies hidden. It is altogether fitting, once we have come to know the way of godliness, that we should at once sell all that we possess and dispose of the money from it according to the Lord's commandment, and not disobey the saving command on the pretext of wanting to keep doing commandments continually. For first of all, from this comes that good freedom from care, and a poverty that no one can plot against. So the Apostle says, "Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood." This he says with reference to the [?] laws of the games. Wrestlers not only strip (for stripping is the beginning of the contest), but also shave their hair and anoint themselves with oil, so that they may not [?] by their hair, and also so that the oil may make their opponent's hands slip; and so they go into the contest. In the same way we too, if we long to win the crown, should strip off the old man with his deeds, shear away external things and spend them on almsgiving, and so go up into the stadium of virtue naked of every care and without a tunic. He also says to the Hebrews: "You sympathized with the prisoners, and accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy, knowing that you have for yourselves a better and lasting possession in heaven." And the Psalmist says: "If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it." He put it well in saying "if it flows," for like a channel of water the things of this world flow past us, belonging today to one person and tomorrow to another. Let us, then, sing David's words with David: "I walked at liberty, for I sought out your commandments." And: "I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz." And: "The poor and needy will praise you, O Lord." And the Lord says to the rich man: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give them to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven." And: "Come, follow me," taking up the cross. To him be the glory forever. Amen.

Homily XC [?]. On Mourning. Mourning is a companion of poverty, and it is fitting and beneficial for all of us. For it not only produces the virtues but also guards them. And after our departure from this life it becomes a cause of eternal joy for those who hold on to it to the end, and a source of consolation, according to the word of the Lord. Let us, then, ask God for this above all, that he may grant it to us unbroken for the whole time of our life. For those who love mourning and keep it with them always also persevere in prayer; such people put on the armor of light. And they hear: "Your garment is warm." But their enemies wrap themselves in shame as in a cloak. And what follows upon mourning, as has been said, is heavenly joy, delight beyond telling, and inexpressible glory. We are taught this by Ecclesiastes too, who says: "It is better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of drinking." And again: "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth." And he adds: "Do not fail to be with those who weep, and mourn with those who mourn." And the prophet Amos says: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord; and the land and all that is in it will mourn." Now this prophecy has been fulfilled in our own times. "For we have all turned aside; together we have become worthless." And Isaiah says [?]: "Leave me alone; I will weep bitterly over the ruin of my people; do not insist on comforting me." And Jeremiah: "Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night?" And he said to the people: "Let your eyes shed tears day and night." But among us there is no one who understands; for what was written beforehand has come upon us. And Daniel says: "And I set my face toward the Lord my God in fasting and sackcloth." And David: "As one mourning and downcast, so was I humbled." And: "I was wretched and bowed down utterly; all day long I went about downcast, for my loins are filled with mockeries." And Job: "The arrows of his raiders are upon me; my belly is burned up with weeping; on my eyelids is the shadow of death." Let us, then, also pay attention, beloved, and understand the lives of the holy men: how they spent their time in weeping, sackcloth and lamentation, and became, through

hardship and mourning, children and servants and friends of God. These things were written to stir us to a zealous desire for mourning, so that "our tears may become our bread day and night," and that every night we may drench our bed with tears and be cleansed of the stain that clings to us, and so become worthy to put on the wedding garment; for whoever is not clothed in the wedding garment will be thrown outside. Since we have such a good Master, then, one who holds no grudge, let us entreat him with groans and tears, so that we may be found in shining robes at his coming. For he loves our salvation. That is why he commands that the filthy garments be taken off Joshua son of Jozadak and that he be clothed in a full-length robe; for he says to him: "Behold, I have taken away your iniquities." And to us he says: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted; blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh." To God belongs the glory forever. Amen.

On "A Time for Everything." There is a time for every matter except prayer, for prayer is always in season. "For I will bless the Lord at all times," he says; "his praise shall continually be in my mouth." And: "Pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything." As for other matters, we are taught by Ecclesiastes that one must look for the right time and watch for it. For he says: "For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter: a time to keep silence and a time to speak." And: "If you have understanding, answer your brother; but if not, put your hand over your mouth." And if it is a time to speak, it is good to speak a word in season. For he says: "Let your speech always be seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person." For every word is wearisome. And: "He who increases knowledge increases sorrow." "He who is rash with his lips will fall into evils, for through an undisciplined tongue come outbursts of anger." The guileless person guards his tongue, as one who loves his own soul. For those who use flattery deceive the hearts of the guileless and lead them astray by calling them blessed. "A time to weep": that is, "Afflict your souls." And: "A time to laugh": this too means, "Keep the feast for me." For laughter is rejoicing. "A time of war": this he says of wrestling, when the devil grapples with a person, attacking him through many and varied temptations. "And a time of peace": because after he has been tempted, grace comes and gladdens the soul. "A time

of judgment the heart of the wise knows": this is when it is freed from error and the passions, and the soul says, rejoicing: "God has judged for me against my adversary." "For there is a time and judgment for every matter, and one event will befall them all." This he says concerning a person's death, because life is so uncertain. For he adds: "For man does not know his time, like fish caught in a net." And again: "I have seen all the business that God has given to the sons of men to be busy with." "Has given" is to be understood as "has permitted." It is good, then, and most acceptable, to do what has been said: "Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking on your head." That is: let the deeds of your soul and body be pure and blameless at all times, and with all your strength pour the oil of almsgiving, through the poor, upon your head, Christ. For he is our head, who says: "Whatever you did to the least of my brothers, you did to me." And through Isaiah he says: "In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you." So when the acceptable time had come, and the day of our salvation, grace, the Apostle, making this time known, says: "Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation; we give no cause of stumbling in anything, so that the ministry may not be blamed"; "but let all things be done decently and in order." Hence the Lord too, showing this, when he was accused by the scribes and Pharisees because his disciples did not fast, silenced them, saying: "Can the sons of the bridechamber fast as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days." To him be the glory, the immortal Bridegroom, Christ our God, forever and ever.

On Compassion. To suffer with one another and grieve together, to run together and labor together, is pleasing to God. For we are bound to do this as servants, attendants and ministers of God the Word, so that we may please him in whose army we have enlisted. From him we shall also receive our wages. The compassionate person has gained a merciful soul. For one who has such a soul pours forth every good thing. If he has money, he will give it away; if he sees someone in misfortune, he will weep; if he comes upon someone being mistreated, he will stretch out his hand; and he will pass over none of those who come to him. Let us strive, then, that our faith, love and endurance may be ours like

a helmet, a spear and full armor, as we are patient with one another and live in gentleness, just as God also is with us. Let us not overlook anyone who weeps, so that the tears of our prayer may not be overlooked. And if we have some gift, let us not boast, but let us show compassion to those who do not have it, and the gift will remain with us to the end. First, then, the most compassionate Job says: "I wept over everyone who was helpless; I groaned when I saw a man in distress." And: "If I overlooked the naked and did not clothe him…" And: "My door was open to everyone who came." Tobit likewise says: "I did many acts of charity. And when I saw the dead cast out, I wrapped them and buried them." And the prophet Hosea says: "Let us press on to know the Lord, for he desires mercy and [?] sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings." And Micah: "Has it not been told you, O man, what is good, or what the Lord requires of you, but to do justice and to love [?]?" It is also in Wisdom: "Rescue those being led away to death, and ransom those who are being slain; do not hold back." And James says: "If a brother or sister is naked and lacking daily food, and someone says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is that?" And Paul exhorts: "Put on, then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with one another." He also says concerning [?]: "I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie: I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh." And: "If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it." And Peter: "Finally, all of you be of one mind, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted and humble, not repaying evil for evil or insult for insult, but on the contrary blessing, because to this you were called, that you may inherit a blessing." And the compassionate Lord, wishing to show us to be sons of his own Father, says: "Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

Favoritism is next-door neighbor to people-pleasing.

We find both of these blamed and forbidden in divine Scripture. Those who show partiality always offer flattering words and false blessings to people of high rank and power, and so they set fire, as it were, to wood and hay, perishable stuff, with the fire of their own nature. Of them the prophet says, "Those who call you blessed lead you astray," and they "flatter people for the sake of gain." "For wealth adds many friends, but the poor man is parted even from the friend he has." And "the wisdom of the poor man is despised." It is not right, then, for us to act this way. All of us who have received the same faith in God ought to respect one another, and not look on our neighbour according to the flesh, but love one another in Christ at all times. Let there be nothing among you that can divide you. On the contrary, as the Psalmist says, "Rescue the poor and needy; deliver him from the hand of the sinner." "For God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they were put to shame, because God has despised them." As Scripture says, "It is not good to show partiality in judgement." And: "Do not show partiality against your own soul, and do not be ashamed to your own downfall." The righteous Job also says, "But now, having looked you in the face, I will not lie." And James says, "My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ while showing partiality. For if a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in, and you pay attention to the one wearing the fine clothes and say to him, 'Sit here in a good place,' and say to the poor man, 'You stand there,' have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?" And he goes on: "If you really fulfil the royal law according to the Scripture, 'You shall love your neighbour,' you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors." Likewise the author of Proverbs says, "It is not good to admire the person of the ungodly, nor is it holy to turn aside justice in judgement." And another says, "It is not good to show deference to a person in judgement. Whoever says to the ungodly, 'You are righteous,' will be cursed by peoples and hated by nations. But those who rebuke him will be seen as better, and a good blessing will come upon them." And Paul says, "For there is no partiality with God." And again: "As for those who seemed to be something, whatever they once were makes no difference to me; God does not show partiality to a man." And God said to Samuel about the sons of Jesse, "Do not look at his appearance or at the height of his stature, for man looks on the face, but God looks on the heart." And when the Lord himself heard someone say, "Look, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you," he answered him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father
in heaven is my brother and sister and mother." To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

On living with a few good people. It is good, beloved, to live with a few who are well-pleasing to God, rather than with many who despise the commandments of the Lord. Where there is fear of the Lord, there is also love and harmony among brothers; but where there is no fear, there is strife and jealousy. Where there is reverence for God and affection for one's neighbour, there God dwells in their midst; but where there is envy and insubordination, there the adversary exults. It is good to hold on to simplicity and innocence, and to be like infants who do not know the wickedness that destroys human life; and not to bear grudges or be lawless in malice, but to put away malice and wickedness and lawless bitterness, and to become one spirit, and to overturn evil schemes, so that the Lord of peace may dwell in all, and so that the spirit too may be whole, just as the person received it. For if someone gives a new, whole garment to a fuller and wants to get it back that way, but the fuller tears the garment before returning it, will he accept it? [?] Will he not quarrel with him and abuse him, saying, "I gave you a whole garment; why have you torn it and made it useless?" If, then, someone is so grieved over a garment and quarrels because he did not get it back whole, what do we think we shall suffer from the Lord, when we received the spirit whole and then grieved it and made it useless, by not living in holiness, so that it can be of no use at all to its Lord? For we have ruined the usefulness of the spirit. Since we live in strife and jealousy and every kind of lawlessness, it is plain that we are bringing wrath and death upon ourselves from the Lord. It is better, then, to live with a few good people than with a multitude of useless ones, if the fear of the Lord is not with them. For one righteous person is better than a thousand sinners. "For in an assembly of sinners a fire will be kindled." And: "Even if there is one stiff-necked person, it would be a wonder if he went unpunished; for mercy and wrath are with the Lord." And another says, "Do not desire a multitude of useless children; if they multiply, do not rejoice in them unless the fear of the Lord is with them. Do not trust in their life, for you will groan in untimely grief." For one righteous

person who does the will of God is better than ten thousand lawless ones. And [?]: "It is better to die childless than to have ungodly children. For through one person of understanding a city will be populated." The Apostle says, "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from wickedness." And he adds: "In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay, some for honourable use and some for dishonourable." So let all of us who are vessels of wood and clay cleanse ourselves, so that we may become useful vessels for the Master, ready for every good work, and may not hear from the Master: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire"; "Truly I tell you, I do not know you." "For the kingdom of heaven," says the Lord, "is like a net that was cast into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it up on the shore and collected the good into containers, but threw the bad away." And he adds: "So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from among the righteous, and throw them into the burning furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. For many are called, but few are chosen." "For the gate is wide and the road is broad that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it." But about the few who are devout and good he says, "For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it." And again: "Do not be afraid, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom." To him be glory for ever. Amen.

On not laughing. Laughter is not permitted to Christians at all, and least of all to monks, who have crucified themselves to the world. "If anyone wants to come after me," he says, "let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." How, then, can someone who has been pierced by the sweet nails of the cross let himself go and laugh? We were not called to distraction and laughter, so as to inherit the "woe" as the gentiles do, but so that through mourning we may come to consolation [?]. Our whole struggle is over the soul, and great is the danger to it and eternal the torment. For in Hades there is no confession; there are no tears and groans to move the Judge; there is no extension of the appointed time there, nor

repentance; there is no return after the departure from this life. After the journey from here, everything bitter will meet those who have squandered the time for repentance. That dreadful and terrifying sight of their own sins will confront them, more bitter than any punishment, and their conscience will scourge them from within, so that they continually utter those pitiable words there: "Woe is me, that I have seen this day!" For wherever such a person turns his eyes, he will see merciless angels of most terrifying appearance. In that hour of distress they will groan bitterly, when they are handed over to death and to the eternal outer darkness, to weeping and gnashing of teeth, to the undying worm, to the depths of Hades, to Tartarus, and to the most grievous Gehenna. One must keep the torments of that place before one's eyes, the torments that await sinners, and not let oneself go in laughter or distraction. Rather, one must gaze unceasingly on the grace of God, as blessed David did, who, looking to the grace of God, said, "As the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, so our eyes look to the Lord our God." And again: "Nor were my eyes lifted up." So we too ought to be sober and look to the grace of God, so that we may not die from the deadly serpents, that is, from our sins. Those who are under grace always keep their offences in mind, marvelling at the goodness of God and saying within themselves, "From how many evils God has rescued us! And what do we, the unworthy, have to give him in return [?]?" So let us not spend the days of our sojourn in laughter and distraction. Let us therefore guard ourselves with all vigilance, beloved, so as not to be caught by the Enemy in the nets of laughter; for many are the unseemly and devilish passions born of it. Laughter belongs to fools, or rather to the senseless who carry on lewdly on the stage. That is why "luxury does not suit a fool," lest he become puffed up, like the people who came out of Egypt. When they had been freed from the Egyptians and had seen the deep turned into dry ground, they turned to idolatry. Having crossed the sea without suffering any danger, they came into the land and [?]; once they were freed from bitter slavery and mourning, then they made shipwreck. Well, then, does the author of Proverbs say, "The laughter of fools is in the wantonness of sin." And again: "A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a shrewd man will scarcely smile quietly." And again: "Whoever lives wantonly from childhood will end up a servant, and at the last he will grieve over himself." And he adds: "Like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools." So let us say with Job, "If I have walked with mockers, let gloomy things befall me." Or with Jeremiah: "Lord, I did not sit in the company of those who make merry, but I

was in awe before your hand, and I sat alone, for I was filled with bitterness." James not only discourages laughter but even commands us to weep earnestly and wail. "Be wretched," he says, "and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into gloom." "For in laughter a fool does evil, but wisdom gives birth to courage and understanding." Let us become wise, then, brothers, and loathe foolish laughter, so that it may not consign us to eternal punishment, according to the Lord's sentence, which says, "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will weep and mourn." Rather, let us be found worthy of praise, hearing from the Saviour, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." To him be glory for ever. Amen.

On loving one's neighbour. Whoever loves his neighbour is far from all sin. All Scripture, Old and New alike, urges this upon us: "to love your neighbour as yourself." For the Lord showed from the law that this is the second commandment, after love for God. Jonathan the son of Saul, knowing this clearly, loved David sincerely, with a love surpassing the love of women. For as Scripture says, "Better is a small portion with the fear of the Lord than great treasures without fear," and, "Better a meal of vegetables shared in friendship and kindness than a fatted calf with enmity." And again: "Better a little income with righteousness than great harvests with injustice." "Better a morsel eaten with pleasure in peace than a house full of good things with strife." And John says, "Brothers, let us love one another, for God is love." And: "Whoever abides in love abides in God." And again: "Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling." And Peter says, "Let us keep ourselves in love, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ." And again: "The aim of our instruction is love from a pure heart and a good conscience."

And again: "Add godliness to your endurance, brotherly affection to your godliness, and love to your brotherly affection." And a little later: "Above all, keep your love for one another fervent, for love covers a multitude of sins." Paul likewise says: "[that you], being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints." And again: "Love is patient and kind; love never fails." And he adds: "Love, then, is the fulfilment of the law." And again: "Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, imitators of God, as beloved children." And: "Let us consider one another so as to stir up love and good works." And: "Above all these, put on love, which is the bond of perfection." "May the Lord make us increase and abound in love for one another and for all." And he says elsewhere: "Concerning brotherly love, you yourselves are taught by God to love one another." So let us too, brothers, love those who share our faith with perfect love, as the law of God requires of us, laying down our lives for them if the occasion calls for it. "For no one has greater love than this," as the Lord says, "that someone lay down his life for his friends." And: "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another." And: "By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." To him be glory for ever. Amen.

On hospitality. Hospitality is good and pleasing to God, especially toward those of the household of faith. Through hospitality Abraham was called the friend of God; through it Lot escaped the threat of fire sent by God; and through hospitality Rahab the harlot was saved with her whole household. Hospitality is praised by all the saints. First, the author of Proverbs says, "The blessing of the Lord is on the head of the righteous; it makes rich, and no grief of heart will be added to it." And hospitable Job, besides his other virtues, also took pride in his hospitality. "For I," he says, "was a father to the powerless, for I saved the poor from the hand of the mighty." And again: "May the blessing of the one who was perishing come upon me.

[?] and satisfy the afflicted [soul], then your [?] will rise in the darkness, and God will be with you always, and you will be filled as your soul desires." And Paul says, "Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect hospitality, for through it some have entertained angels without knowing it." And again: "Do not neglect to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased." Another also says, "Be hospitable to one another without grumbling." "For if the eagerness is there, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have." "For it is not that others should have relief and you hardship, but that there should be equality at the present time." And to Titus: "Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way quickly, so that they lack nothing. And let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works for pressing needs, so that they may not be unfruitful." And again: "Gaius, my host and host of the whole church, greets you"—that is, the one who welcomes everyone. And the Lord, calling the hospitable along with the merciful, says to them: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you. For I was a stranger and you welcomed me; I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me." To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

On love of the poor. Love of the poor and hospitality are two branches of the rich olive tree whose fruit spreads its fragrance to all. With its oil the Lord is anointed on his head and his feet, and he repays the one who anoints him with the kingdom of heaven. For the lover of the poor heeds the one who says, "Do not let almsgiving and faithfulness forsake you; bind them around your neck, and you will find favour." "Provide what is good in the sight of the Lord and of men." And: "The ways of the righteous shine like light; they go before and give light until the day is fully come." The law also commands, saying, "You shall freely open your hands to the needy, lest he cry out to the Lord against you." And the author of Proverbs says, "Do not rob the poor of his livelihood." And: "Do not grieve a hungry soul, and do not put off giving to someone in need; do not reject an afflicted suppliant, and do not turn your face away from the poor." And again: "A merciful man does good to his own soul, but the unmerciful destroys his own body." And the prophet Hosea says, "Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and keep mercy and justice, and draw near to your God continually." And Daniel says to Nebuchadnezzar, "O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by compassion to the

poor." And David says, "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever." And: "The Lord loves mercy and justice." "Blessed, then, is the one who considers the poor and needy." "The Lord will deliver him in the day of trouble." And Job says, "If I ever let the needy go out of my door with an empty bosom." And another says, "Incline your ear to the poor, and answer him peaceably and with gentleness." "Make room for every act of mercy, for each will find according to his works." And again: "Whoever has mercy on the poor will himself be fed, for he has given his own bread to the poor." "Whoever gives to the poor will not be in want." And again: "Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might." "A merciful man does good to his own soul." And: "[?] of the Lord is on the head of the one who shares." And: "The ransom of a man's soul is his own wealth." And: "By almsgiving and faithfulness sins are purged away," and "Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God, and he will be repaid according to his gift." It is good, then, out of one's own labours, which God [gives?], to provide simply for all who are in need, without hesitating over whom to give to and whom not. For God wants gifts to be given to all from his own bounty, and does not want us to decide to whom to give and to whom not. This service, performed in simplicity, is glorious before God, and whoever serves God thus in simplicity will live. "A man is a great thing, and a merciful man is precious." And the Apostle says this: "Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully." And he adds: "For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem." And the Lord says, "Sell your possessions and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in heaven. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." But also: "Take care not to practise your almsgiving before people in order to be seen by them." To him be glory for ever. On Visiting. On Visiting. Visiting is good; it ranks alongside [?] hospitality and love of the poor. "For a threefold cord is not broken"; or rather it is a lampstand of light [?], shining on those who love the poor [?] and the hospitable [?], and guiding them to eternal life. "For I was a stranger," he says, "and you welcomed me; I was hungry and you fed me; I was sick and you visited me." So whoever visits those who are sick, or in prison, or in distress, [visits] the one who for our sake became poor [?]

...visits the Word, as he himself testifies. That it is good to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and the poor who have many children, and above all and first of all those of the household of faith, is plain and undeniable to everyone. And this too is good and profitable for the brotherhood in Christ: to visit those possessed by demons and to pray over them a prayer pleasing to God, faithfully. This must not be done with a composition of many words, or with rehearsed exorcisms meant to show off and please people, so that we may appear eloquent or gifted with a good memory. Nor should we make noise like a flute at the possessed with babble and empty repetition, instead of praying in the faith of truth, as the Lord taught. For he says this: "This kind goes out by earnest prayer and by faith with fasting." So let us visit the sufferer soberly, in a spirit of humility. It is good, then, to labor alongside our suffering brothers, as has been said, through vigils, fasts and unceasing prayers. For the Lord said, "Cast out demons," together with the other healings, and "Freely you have received, freely give." "But let all things be done decently and in order," as befits people who fear God. Let us give encouragement and comfort to our brothers who are sick or suffering. But let us not be found to be like the friends of Job, reproaching our brothers with some fault or sin, as people tend to do, or secretly condemning them in our hearts, or carelessly speaking a word that stings them, and so sinning against God in ignorance. For it is written in Proverbs: "Whoever stops his ears so as not to hear the weak will himself call upon the Lord, and he will not listen to him." As Job says: "My nearest kin did not look on me; I called my servant, and he did not answer me; my mouth pleaded with my wife; I was a stranger among them." For the earth is home to every mortal. And another wise man says: "Do not be slow to visit the sick." And James: "Religion that is pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world." And the Apostle: "Remember those in prison as though bound with them, and those who are ill-treated, since you yourselves are also in the body." And he adds: "As we have opportunity, let us do good to all, and especially to those of the household of faith." And to the Philippians he says: "In the beginning of the gospel no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone; for even in Thessalonica you sent help for my need once and again. I have received everything in full and I abound; I am well supplied, having received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God." What, then, do these passages teach us? Not only to visit those in need, but also to make up what they lack,

so that the Lord may receive us too along with the others and say: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you. For I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On not hoping in man. Brothers, we must not hope in man in any matter whatever, "for cursed [?]" ... [but we must hope] in the Lord who always cares for us, because he is concerned for us. For in the divine Scripture too [?]: "In your destruction, Israel, who will help you? Where is your king? Let him save you." Likewise the Psalmist: "Do not trust in princes, in sons of men, in whom there is no salvation." "For it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man." And: "It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes." And he goes on: "Give us help from trouble," and: "Vain is the salvation of man." "For unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman has kept awake in vain." And Isaiah says of the new people: "And they will no longer trust in men, but in the one who made them." And of the old: "Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who trust in horses and in chariots," and "they did not trust in the Holy One of Israel." And the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: "God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame, so that no flesh might boast before him." And he adds: "And I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling; and my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might rest not in the wisdom of men but in the power of God." Let us cast away from us, then, beloved, the faintheartedness that gives birth to putting one's hope in man and that brings the guilty under the curse. Instead, let us hope wholly in the one who said: "Do not worry about what you will eat, or

what you will drink, or what you will wear; for your Father knows what you need." Rather, as he tells us, let us "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness," so that we may inherit heavenly things along with earthly ones. Let us imitate the Magi, who not only did not fear Herod but even outwitted him, returning to their own country by another road. And let us imitate the faith of the woman with the flow of blood, who set the physicians aside, touched the fringe of the Lord's garment from behind, and was healed at once. And let us too set our hopes on the Lord and glorify him forever.

On not trusting in one's own strength. The discourse has shown that it is unlawful and accursed to hope in man. In the same way it also threatens the one who trusts in his own strength. First, then, Moses commands, saying: "Take heed to yourself, and do not say in your heart, 'My strength and the might of my hand have gained me this power.' But you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you strength." Likewise the prophet Amos says: "The warrior shall not save his life, and the one who is swift of foot shall not escape." And Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel, said: "Let not the mighty boast in his might, for a man is not mighty by strength; the bow of the mighty has grown weak, and the weak have girded themselves with power." And in Proverbs: "A horse is made ready for the day of battle, but help comes from the Lord." And the Psalmist: "He takes no pleasure in the strength of the horse, nor delight in the legs of a man. For a king is not saved by a great army, and a giant will not be saved by his great strength." And again: "A horse is a false hope for salvation; for all its great power it will not save." "For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me"; "but you, Lord, save me from those who afflict me; put to shame those who hate me." For you alone rescue the poor from the hand of those stronger than he, the poor and needy from those who plunder him. For in you we live and move and have our being; our strength and vigor come from you; and not a hair of our head will fall to the ground without you, our Maker and Father. Since we have learned these things from the divine Scripture, then, let us never dare to trust in the power or vigor of our body, or to pride ourselves on it, so that we do not bring upon ourselves the curse pronounced on the one who makes flesh the arm he leans on. For many boast and say: "My hands feed both me and others; as long as I have my hands, I can live." These are truly the vain-minded and

the empty talkers, who forget God who made them and gives health and food to all flesh, and who trust in their own power. For whoever has cut himself off from God and credits his achievements to his own power is sick with [?]. Just as someone who steps onto a spider's web falls through it and is brought down, so the one who is confident in his own power collapses. Have they not even heard Job saying: "If I put my hand to my mouth and kissed it, let this too be counted to me as a great iniquity, for I would have lied before the Lord Most High"? And Ecclesiastes likewise, for he says: "I turned and saw that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those who have knowledge." And he adds: "Wisdom is better than weapons of war." And: "One sinner destroys much good." And the Lord says to his disciples: "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. Whoever abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit; for apart from me you can do nothing." And rightly so, for he himself is the light and the life of men, and "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On declining untimely meetings. It is very good and most profitable to decline untimely meetings and to avoid the worldly-minded, unless there is great necessity. For those who are outside the world have one disposition, and those in the world another. Just as it is an ill-matched yoking to put together the ox, the buffalo, the pack animal and the wild ass, so it is with monks and those who live in the world. The monk has no authority over himself, for he has become the slave of the one who enlisted him. He has bowed his neck to the yoke of the one who drives him to plough, without turning back, the [furrows?] that multiply the divine grain in the hollows of humility [?], those that are drenched by the showers of the

[?] ... spiritual [persons] and fellow strugglers, or to meet with brothers who need help. For such a meeting is counted as theology, and in any case one will either help or be helped. Scripture also says: "If you find a man of understanding, go to him early in the morning." And: "Who is wise? Cling to him. For whoever lives with the wise will become wise." But meeting with the world is unprofitable for us, for worldly people talk about the things of this age. Then the mind grows slack, is idled from spiritual work, and loses the tension of ascetic discipline. Then there is also the meal, and that too is different, for each displays the fruits of his own farming. That is why I have said that the life of the unmarried and that of worldly people have nothing in common and are out of harmony. Because of the harm to the soul, then, we must be ready to cut short meetings with them. For even after they have gone, the mind is weighed down both by the neglect of the rule and by the change of diet. This is why the contenders sought out the deserts: so that, being away from these things, they might converse with God without hindrance. A virgin who is kept guarded is longed for by those outside; but once she comes out, she does not please everyone and is instead criticized by many. In the same way, as long as the monk has no city and is unknown to the public, he is honored by God and the angels, and by men even more. But when he comes down from his lofty way of life and contemplation and becomes entangled in the business and meetings of this life, he becomes unapproved by God and easily despised by men. It is better, then, to desert the worldly and keep oneself shut up in one's cell, and to be saved "like a gazelle from the snares and like a bird from the trap." For to those who wish to be saved, the meetings and long conversations of worldly people are snares and traps. They draw the mind away from glorifying God and rejoicing in him, and make it chatter about their own idle talk. As the author of Proverbs says: "Much converse led him astray, and by the words of her lips she drove him aground." When people come to us for the good of their souls, however, let us meet them with a few words seasoned with divine salt, and then send them away. For they will be edified more by spiritual brevity than by worldly long-windedness. And if someone asks, "Why then did Paul prolong his speech until midnight?", the answer is, first, that he was about to set out on a journey, and second, that they were newly instructed, for it was the beginning of the preaching. Besides, Paul was full of the divine Spirit, and the Spirit spoke through him. And this is the sign of those who have the Spirit from above: first, such a person is meek, quiet and humble, and abstains from every vain desire of this age. He makes himself lower than all people. And it is not whenever the Spirit-bearer wishes to speak that the Spirit speaks;

rather, it speaks when God wishes him to speak. So whenever people come for the sake of benefit and have faith in the divine Spirit, let there first be intercession to God about everything. Then the divine Spirit fills the man, and once filled he speaks as the Lord wills; and the Lord wills that every person be saved. It is good to help inquirers with words, but it is better to work with them through virtue and prayer. Those who want to acquire the multitude of virtues, then, must not seek glory or meet with many people, as has been said. They must not go out often, nor revile anyone, even if those reviled deserve it, nor talk much, even if they could say everything well. For immoderate talkativeness corrupts the mind: it not only makes the mind idle in spiritual work but also hands it over to the demon of listlessness. When the doors of a bathhouse are constantly opened, they quickly drive the heat inside out. So too when the soul wants to talk a great deal, even if everything it says is good, it lets its recollection drain away through the gate of the voice. Silence, then, is good in every respect. For royal treasuries will be filled with gold, and the minds of true monks will be filled with rich knowledge. But if teaching is also necessary, let it be done for the correction of the soul. In teaching, then, we need integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be faulted, so that God may be glorified through us in all things. "For our weapons are not fleshly, but powerful through God for tearing down strongholds; we tear down reasonings and every height raised up against the knowledge of God." So with an untroubled soul and a meek heart, let our prayer become acceptable, like fragrant incense, to God who searches hearts and minds. And the Lord also says to his disciples: "You are not of this world, but I chose you out of the world. I will no longer speak much with you." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On stillness. Stillness is profitable because it rests from evils. And if in prayer it takes as its aids the four virtues, that is, patience and humility, vigil and self-control, nothing is a shorter way for it to dispassion. Timely silence is good, then, for it is nothing other than the mother of the wisest thoughts, since the good Spirit flees from much talking, being beyond all disturbance and fantasy. Stillness, being good, is therefore the mother of all the virtues, for it gives birth to them through unceasing and undistracted stillness before God. The monk who loves stillness is loved by God, since he too loves God and wants to converse with him alone through pure prayer; and while living on earth, he pictures the things of heaven. For his whole mind is concerned with how he may please God and become a temple of his Holy Spirit. Such a man always bows his neck to the light and kindly yoke of Christ; he looks past all visible things and longs for the invisible. Or rather, he endures as one who sees the Invisible himself. Such people rival the angels in their way of life. They always seek out the deserts so that, conversing with God in deep stillness and freedom from care, they may make their mind a spotless mirror, like the great Elijah and John, the Forerunner and Baptist of the Lord. Blessed are such people both on earth and in heaven, who count all things as refuse in order to gain Christ, and are found walking in a meek and quiet spirit. This is especially true in the times we have reached, as the prophet Amos teaches us about the present time: "In that time the prudent will keep silent, for it is an evil time." And Isaiah: "Whoever hates wickedness and shakes his hands free of bribes, whoever shuts his eyes so as not to see injustice, will dwell in a cave; bread will be given him, and his water will be sure." And he says in the person of the Lord: "On whom shall I look, but on the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?" And Jeremiah says: "Who will give me a farthest lodging-place in the desert, so that I may leave this people?" And again: "I did not sit with them as they made merry, but I stood in awe before your hand. I sat alone, for I was filled with bitterness." And David: "Lo, I fled far away and lodged in the wilderness." And: ["I made sackcloth my garment,"] "I set a guard on my mouth while the sinner stood against me; [I was dumb and humbled and kept silent even from good things. And again:] I was dumb and did not open my mouth, for it was you who did it." And: "The Lord

1747 ANTIOCHUS. settles the solitary in a house." For "a man of understanding keeps quiet." And: "A wise man will keep silent until the right time." And: "Knowing and at the same time keeping silent," as Scripture says. And Ecclesiastes: "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place." And John lived in the deserts "until the day he was shown to Israel." And the Lord, who became a pattern for us in everything, used to withdraw into the deserts and pray [?]. To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On vigil. God has given us vigil as a great and good weapon against the devil and the dark spirits of wickedness who fight in his service. Vigil is made bright and is supported by frugality, and with a sober mind it converses with God. For a full stomach and satiety of the belly are opposed to it. Not only that, but they also make the mind cowardly and feeble, easily defeated by the attacks of the unclean passions. "Let us pray, then, that our flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath," that is, while we are caught in the passions and in ease. If we are soldiers of Christ, let us be willing to travel the road of dispassion and toil, and to stand bravely against our adversary. For if we keep watch soberly in vigil, we will be able to wound him more severely. The godly virtues, that is, vigil, prayer, psalmody, humility and thanksgiving, become bows, snares and whips against the enemy. Only let us not become proud in our prayer when we shed tears. For the tears do not come from us, but from the grace that supplies them. It is good, then, to cultivate diligently the pair of sobriety and scant eating, which together strengthen vigil. This is true especially for us who have enlisted for this very purpose, so that we may please the one who enlisted us. For in many places the Lord commands us concerning vigil: "Watch and pray, so that you may escape the

…shield and spear, love for him, and the sword of the Spirit, which is his words. And let us stand against the adversary like noble soldiers, with vigils, fasts and prayers; as it is written in Proverbs: "Give no sleep to your eyes, and do not let your eyelids slumber, so that you may be saved like a gazelle from the noose and like a bird from the snare." And David says: "I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids until I find a place for the Lord." And again: "I kept watch and became like a sparrow alone on the housetop." … "For the Lord is near to the broken-hearted, and he will save the humble in spirit." And again: "At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for your righteous judgments." And again: "O God, my God, I rise early to seek you; my soul has thirsted for you." And: "I rose before the dawn, at an untimely hour, and cried out." And: "My eyes were awake before the dawn, to meditate on your words." And to his companions he said: "In the night lift up your hands toward the holy place, and bless the Lord." And the Apostle: "Persevere in prayer, keeping watch in it with thanksgiving." And again: "Pray at all times in the Spirit, and keep alert to this end with all perseverance and supplication." And of himself: "In labours, in vigils, in fasts." And he adds: "Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need for anything to be written to you. For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. When they say, 'Peace and security,' then sudden destruction comes upon them, like labour pains on a woman with child, and they will not escape." And again: "So then let us not sleep as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober." And the Lord: "Keep watch, therefore, for you do not know at what hour your Lord is coming. But know this: if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into." And again: "Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation." And again: "Blessed is that servant whom his Lord will find doing so when he comes. Keep watch, therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour." To him be glory forever. Amen.
On Psalmody. Psalmody is the work of the bodiless powers who minister to God and stand before him without ceasing, as it is said: "Praise the Lord from the heavens, all his angels,

and all his powers." And again: "Bless the Lord, all you his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word; bless the Lord, all you his powers, his ministers who do his will." But it is fitting for all people too, for "Let everything that breathes praise the Lord"; and above all for monks, who have taken up the angelic life, for "Blessed is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night." And: "You who fear the Lord, praise him; all you seed of Jacob, glorify him." Psalmody, then, is a sacrifice of perpetual offering and of praise, as it is said: "A sacrifice of praise will glorify me." And: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise." The monk is therefore bound to offer to God, perpetually and unceasingly, as a priestly service, the doxologies appointed for him: "For I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall be continually in my mouth." Let us hear David exhorting us: "Sing praises to our God, sing praises to our King, sing praises with understanding"; "Sing praises to the Lord with the lyre and the sound of song" [?]. And also: "Sing to him with shouts of joy." "My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul too, which you have redeemed." And again: "Sing to the Lord, you his holy ones." And: "Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. For his praise is in the assembly of the holy ones." And: "Let the children of Zion rejoice in their King." "I will sing and make music in my glory," "for my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze up." And: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" "So I will bless you as long as I live, and in your name I will lift up my hands; may my soul be filled as with fat and richness, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips." "For you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight" as they sing to you. But why must I set out all of David's testimonies about singing psalms, which everyone knows, or describe the grace and gladness that arise in the hearts of those who sing soberly and with compunction? Those who have experienced it know this as well, and I do not want to be judged a babbler. It is good, then, when God is remembered, to multiply our supplication, so that when we forget, the Lord may remind us. And let us stand firm at psalmody, beloved, and pray with vigour, turning away from the pressing demands of thoughts and cares. For when the demons see someone singing psalms or praying eagerly, they are accustomed to suggest to him thoughts of certain matters that seem necessary, stirring the mind to search into them, so that the mind, poured out in investigating them, may lose the sweetness of psalmody. Why does Christ perfect praise out of the mouth of the faithful who are infants in wickedness, if not surely so that through psalmody he may destroy the enemy and avenger [?]

— the avenger of wickedness, that is, the devil? So let us too, praising the Lord in simplicity, crush and destroy the devices of the Enemy. Let the psalm, then, be continuous, for when God is named he puts demons to flight. And I must remind you of something no one is unaware of: that our psalmody is called a "canon," a due.
