Just as a farmer who does not pay his due in full and in good measure is thrown into prison, hung up and flogged until [?], so also the monk, when he neglects his canon, is immediately abandoned by grace and handed over to his enemies, and falls beneath their feet. And many afflictions are brought upon him, so that he cries out: "Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? … They say to my soul, 'There is no salvation for him in his God.'" And: "Hear me quickly, Lord, for my spirit has failed." And: "Do not turn your face away from me, lest I become like those who go down into the pit," [?] "for my soul is full of evils, and my life has drawn near to Hades." When these things befall him, he will cry to the Lord in his affliction, he who neglected to render his canon to God without fail, and who is now being disciplined with hardships by God's permission. But it is uncertain whether he will hear, "In affliction you called upon me, and I delivered you." May he not rather say to him: "I do not know you [?]; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness," "for you did not listen to my voice, nor pay heed to me." "For if you had listened to me, I would soon have humbled your enemies and laid my hand on those who afflict you. Therefore I sent you away to walk according to the devices of your heart." But let us

rather listen to Paul, who says: "Let the Word dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs." And again: "Each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation. Let all things be done for building up." [?] "Through him, then, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name." And: "Present your bodies as a sacrifice [?]" … psalmody, as a canon that is owed, which we are bound to offer blameless and spotless, that is, without anger and without thoughts of resentment. For praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner. If, then, you have something against your brother and do not forgive him, [?] your prayer and your almsgiving and everything else you think you are doing will never be accepted. For you will hear from the Saviour: "Go, first be reconciled [?]

to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." Be guileless and innocent in your psalmody, like the children of the Hebrews who went out to meet the Lord with branches and palms, saying: "Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." To him be glory forever.

On Prayer. To devote ourselves to unceasing prayer is necessary and profitable for us. Let us then ask the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ to give us spiritual understanding, so that we may be sober and watchful to ask of him that his will be done in us. For this is the very thing our God and Saviour, the spiritual and true light "that enlightens everyone coming into the world," commanded us to ask. So when we call upon the holy and consubstantial Trinity with all-holy prayers, with an untroubled mind and with readiness for union with God, then we ourselves are present, and we receive the all-virtuous gifts established around it. Prayer is loftier [?] than all the virtues, since it is pure and draws near to God. For prayer is the offshoot of gentleness and freedom from anger; prayer is the fruit of joy and thanksgiving, and a defence against grief and despondency. At the time of prayer, then, one must still the mind and keep the voice silent; then one is able to pray. For prayer is converse with God. What state, then, does the mind need in order to converse with its own Master, with none of the alien thoughts hindering it? Prayer offered with mourning and in the Spirit is food for the mind, as bread is for the body. Blessed, then, is the mind that at the time of prayer converses with God without distraction. Such a mind is lifted on high like an eagle's chick, and, wholly changed by the change that God works, it becomes full of light. And when we stand to pray, let us not pray that our own will be done, as has been said, but God's, just as we were taught: "Your will be done" in me and in every matter, so that we may ask him in such a way that his will is done. For he wills what is good and profitable for the soul. But we do not always seek this. Rather, let us bewail ourselves, and with great mourning, that, impure as we are, we dare to stand before the Lord of Sabaoth. Whoever, then, wishes

to pray purely, let him first pray for the help of tears, so that through mourning he may bring the soul to holiness [?] and attain unalloyed prayer. For persistent and continual prayer, through converse with God, snatches the mind away from worldly thoughts and presents it to God, and through nearness to God fills it with reverence and gentleness. Without humility no prayer can become acceptable. "For he looked upon the prayer of the humble," it says, "and did not despise their supplication." So whoever wishes to purify his own heart, let him keep it continually on fire with the remembrance of the Lord, making this alone his meditation and his unceasing work [?]. For we must not pray at one time and at another [?], but always devote ourselves to prayer, keeping watch over the mind, even when we are lodging somewhere outside the houses of prayer. For just as someone who wants to refine gold, if he lets the fire of the furnace die down even briefly, brings back hardness into the material being refined, so too whoever remembers God [?] at one time and not at another loses through slackness whatever he seems to gain by prayer. And just as continual contact with fire [?] makes iron too hot to touch, so frequent prayers make the mind stronger for the war against the enemy. And as iron, when heated, takes on the colour of fire, so the mind is enlightened by the radiance of the fire of grace, "which our Saviour came to cast" on the earth. That is why the Lord, who wants us to be saved, speaks to us about prayer continually; and having become like us, he spent the night in prayer to God, showing us the very great benefit of persistent prayer and the great nearness to God that comes through it. One must first ask to receive the grace of prayer, as it is said, from him who gives prayer to the one who prays. For "we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself," it says, "intercedes for us." And once we have received it, let us fulfil what was commanded us by the law [?]. For Moses says: "If you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay to pay it … Keep what goes out of your lips." And again: "A man who makes a vow, or swears an oath, or binds himself with a pledge, shall not profane his word; whatever goes out of his mouth he shall do." [?] And Jephthah too, for he says to his daughter: "I have opened my mouth to the Lord about you, and I cannot turn back." And he offered her as a sacrifice to the Lord God. And another says: "Let nothing hinder you from paying a vow in due time, and do not wait until death to be justified. Before you make a vow, prepare yourself, and do not be like one who puts the Lord to the test.

And remember the wrath on the day of death." And strive in prayer, for the prayers of the upright are acceptable to the Lord. And: "The Lord hears the prayers of the righteous." And David: "Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God." And again: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High." And: "I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people." And Paul says: "Not slothful in zeal, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, persevering in prayer." And again: "With all prayer and supplication, praying at all times in the Spirit, and keeping alert to this end with all perseverance and supplication." And again: "I want the men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands without anger or quarrelling." And in Acts: "They persevered in the apostles' teaching and in fellowship, in the breaking of bread and in the prayers." And again: "But we will persevere in prayer and in the ministry of the word." And Wisdom: "When you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay to pay it, for you shall pay what you have vowed. It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay." And Job, the hater of injustice, says: "There was no injustice in my hands, and my prayer was pure." And Peter: "Be sober-minded, then, and watchful in your prayers, and resist the devil." And the Lord: "Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you receive it, and it will be yours." And when he was praying in a certain place, as he finished, one of his disciples said: "Lord, teach us to pray"; and he said: "When you pray, say: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name," and so on. And he adds: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you." And he goes on: "If you, then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!" And the Lord, so greatly longed for, wishing us to offer our prayer to God as a hidden work, says: "When you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On Compunction. Compunction gives birth to weeping and tears. But it comes only with some toil, unless through much meditation and remembrance of the fearful day of judgment, and of the requital for the sins we have committed in word, deed and thought; and of that shame before the fearful judgment seat, in the presence of angels and men and all the heavenly powers, when all things are naked and laid bare, when each of us stands making his own defence, when no one can help anyone, when hidden things are revealed which until then no one knew except our own conscience — or rather, most of which not even the heart knows, but only God, who tests hearts and minds; when "fire will go before him and burn up his enemies all around"; when some are condemned to the outer darkness prepared for the devil and his angels, and others to the eternal fire, when some are sent off to the sleepless worm and others handed over to Tartarus. But why must I recount everything in detail and weary my listeners? Considering all these things and others like them, beloved, let us come to compunction, cease from our evil deeds, and weep day and night before the Lord who made us. For where there are tears, there God is moved by entreaty. The harlot, through hot tears in a single hour, obtained the forgiveness of many debts. Tears present prayer to God and make it acceptable. Peter, through a single hour of bitter tears, was not only pardoned for the fault of his denial but was also entrusted with the keys of the kingdom of heaven. King Hezekiah, through a few tears, had fifteen years added to his life. Drops of tears are like sweet honey in the heart and fragrant incense before God. Before every petition, then, one should make good use of tears. For our Master greatly rejoices to receive prayer offered in tears with a humble heart — a heart in no way puffed up, as though we were above the many — lest we provoke still further the one who gave us the grace. For many who wept for their sins, forgetting the purpose of their tears, went mad and lost their wits. If someone possesses perfect compunction, he perceives himself receiving spiritual food from the bread of life: food of the better [?], food of heavenly longing, and of consoling groans and of compunction, and of melody, and of deeper knowledge, and of certain divine mysteries. Compunction prepares the heart to bear tearful and gentle thoughts; and so one may truly see the seeds of prayer being sown with tears in the soil of the heart, in hope of the joy of the harvest. Meditation joined with compunction and prayer begets in us the fear of God. For it says

…the law: "Whether sitting in the house or walking on the road, lying down or rising up, let them be [?] fixed before your eyes, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God." Job also says: "May my petition come to the Lord, and may my eye shed tears before him." And Hannah [?] at Shiloh and wept. She prayed to the Lord, saying: "If you will indeed look upon my humiliation and give me the seed of a man…" And the Lord heard her and granted her the prophet Samuel. And the other Anna, the wife of Joachim, weeping in her garden and asking for a child, received the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother according to the flesh of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ. And David says: "Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication; give ear to my tears, do not keep silent." And having been heard, he says: "The Lord is merciful and righteous; I was brought low, and he saved me." And: "He delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears." [?] For "those who sow in tears will reap in joy." And so: "Let us be well-pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living." And the saying "Going, they went and wept" speaks, I think, of our own captivity, for what was written beforehand has come down to us. So we too ought to weep bitterly, for ourselves and for them: first for the burning of the holy city of Jerusalem, and for the carrying off of the holy cross of Christ our God to Persia, and for those perishing in so many wars, since they are of one body and one faith with us. As the prophet Joel cries: "Lament, you priests who minister at the altar, for the whole land is in distress. Weep, you priests who minister to the Lord, and say: Spare your people, O Lord, and do not give your inheritance over to reproach, for the nations to rule over it, so that they may not say, Where is their God?" For it lies within our power to entreat the Lord, who bears no grudge, as the prophet Zephaniah teaches when he says: "He has set before you fire and water; stretch out your hand to whichever you wish. Before a man are life and death, and whichever he chooses will be given him." For who will justify one who sins against his own soul, if not hot tears shed with compunction? The good and compassionate Master always thirsts for our salvation, as the Apostle testifies when he says that "he wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." And it is written in the Gospel according to Luke: "And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, learning that the Lord was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought

an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing behind him at the feet of Jesus, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and to wipe them with the hair of her head, and she kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment." And she heard from the Savior: "Your sins are forgiven." To him be glory forever. Amen.

Homily 108. On honoring parents. Even by the law of nature we are bound to honor those who brought us into the world and to repay them. First, because through them we have seen this visible light; and then also the spiritual light, that is, the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ through baptism. We are bound to them also because of their natural affection for their own offspring; because of the toil they endure in raising them; because of the anxiety they feel night and day for them, lest anything unwelcome befall them; and because they work and labor for their children's clothing and food, and to store up something for them after their own death. What worthy repayment, then, can we give them for all this? Let us always be eager to do whatever serves their honor, their care and their rest, especially in their old age, so that they may be rekindled at the sight of their children, as Jacob was when he saw Joseph. Let us at least rival the birds called hoopoes. When their young see their parents grown old and dim-sighted, they pluck out their parents' feathers, lick their eyes, and warm them under their own wings and make a nest for them, and the parents become young again. And the young say to their parents: "Just as you made a nest for us and [?] toiled and fed us, so we do the same for you." How much more, then, should we, who are rational beings, love our own parents? Let them not groan against us, for that brings us no profit, but rather harm; and we would rightly be found to be murderers of father and mother. In the law it is written: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you and that you may live long on the earth." And: "Whoever reviles father or mother, let him surely be put to death." Likewise Isaiah: "Whoever says to his father, What are you begetting? and to his mother, What are you in labor with?" And: "I know that you are stubborn, and your neck is a sinew of iron." And another says: "Whoever honors his father will rejoice in his own children, and in the day of his prayer

he will be heard." And again: "A father's blessing makes firm the houses of his children, but a mother's curse uproots their foundations." And the Apostle: "Children, obey your parents in the Lord; for this," he says, "is right. Honor your father and your mother, which is the first commandment with promises." And again: "Let children first learn to show piety toward their own household and to make return to their parents, for this is good and acceptable in the sight of God." And the author of Proverbs: "A shrewd son obeys his father, but a disobedient son will come to ruin." And again: "The lamp of one who reviles father or mother will be put out." And again: "Whoever does violence to father or mother and thinks he is not sinning is the companion of an ungodly man." The Lord says the same to the Pharisees: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God said, Honor your father and your mother, and, Whoever reviles father or mother, let him surely be put to death. But you say, If anyone says to his father or his mother, 'Corban' (that is, a gift) is whatever you would have gained from me, he need not honor his father or his mother." These passages are enough to show that we are bound to make every return to our parents. But we must not be unaware of this either: such things are required of us not only toward our parents according to the flesh, but we owe even greater honor and reverence to our spiritual fathers, so that through them we may inherit the blessing of God. For they too toil and are anxious for us no less, and indeed far more, since the one set of parents begets us in the flesh, the other in the spirit. The Lord teaches us all this not only by word but also by deed: "He was," it says, "subject to his father and his mother." And on the cross he said to the disciple, "Behold your mother," and to his Mother, "Behold your son."

…the face of an elder." And Job: "In long time is wisdom, and in a long life understanding." And another: "Wide experience is the crown of the old, and the fear of the Lord is their boast." And the Apostle to Timothy: "Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father." But you will surely say to me: "Old men ought to be sober, dignified, sound in faith and in love," as the Apostle says. And: "Honorable old age is not length of days, nor is it measured by number of years; rather, understanding is gray hair for men, and a spotless life is ripe old age," as Scripture says. Yet it is not for us to judge this, but for God, who tests our hearts. Our part is to render to all what is due to them: "fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due," and not only to the good and gentle, but also to the crooked. And: "Be devoted to one another in brotherly love, outdoing one another in showing honor." For it is written: "Son, if you are wise for yourself, you will be wise for your neighbors too; but if you turn out wicked, you alone will bear the evil." Likewise Peter: "You who are younger, be subject to the elders; and all of you clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time." It is fitting, then, for all Christians to render what is due. We are taught this by our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ himself. In his ineffable condescension toward us he did not disdain to come to John to be baptized by him. John tried to prevent him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" And the Master said to the servant: "Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On patience and quick temper. All the virtues are praiseworthy and acceptable. But the patient man, who is slow to anger, is wise and understanding, free of boasting and gentle. Such a man is adorned on every side; by his patience he becomes a source of edification to his neighbors, and he is found to be a child of the patient God, who always bears with our failings. "Be perfect," he says, "as your heavenly Father is." For as a quiet spring offers a pleasant drink to all around it, so the patient man is of benefit to everyone. The face and manner of the patient man are always composed, and his eyes look out gently. "For a patient man," it says, "is great in understanding, but the faint-hearted is utterly foolish." The patient man is always found calm, untroubled and enduring,

always attending to his own failings and not to those of his neighbor, and anxious about how he may please God. For if someone becomes patient, the Holy Spirit dwells in him pure, not darkened by another, evil spirit; dwelling in a spacious place, it rejoices with the vessel in which it dwells and serves the Lord with great gladness. But if any quick temper comes upon him, the Holy Spirit is at once cramped, having no pure place, and seeks to depart, because it has no room to serve the Lord as it wishes. For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil in quick temper. When both spirits dwell in the same place, then, it is unprofitable and evil for the man in whom they dwell. If you take a little wormwood and pour it into a jar of honey, is not the whole of the honey spoiled? So much honey by so little wormwood! It destroys the sweetness and becomes bitter, and it no longer pleases its owner, because it has turned bitter. Do you see that patience is sweeter than honey and pleasing to the Lord, while quick temper is both bitter and useless? If quick temper is mixed with patience, then the patience is defiled, and its intercession is of no use before God. For quick temper, being evil, overthrows the servants of God by its working. When it sees people at peace, it thrusts itself into a man's heart, and he grows bitter over nothing: over worldly affairs, or about food, or because some empty trifle came up, or over some gift [?]. All these things are foolish and empty for the servants of God. But patience is great and strong, with sturdy power; it prospers, and rejoicing and free of care it glorifies the Lord, having nothing bitter in it, because it is meek and quiet. This patience dwells with those whose faith is whole. But quick temper is senseless. From senselessness comes bitterness; from bitterness, rage; and from anger, lasting resentment. The Holy Spirit, being delicate and unaccustomed to keeping company with a harsh and evil spirit, withdraws from such a man and seeks to dwell with the patient; and that man becomes empty of the righteous spirit and is wholly blinded to good understanding. The word also says: "Better is a patient man than a strong one." And: "As silver and gold are tested in the furnace, so the Lord tests chosen hearts," according to Scripture. And again: "A gentle man is a physician of the heart, and a patient man puts out strife." And again: "He who refrains from uttering a harsh word is wise." And again: "Child, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for trial. Set your heart straight and endure. Whatever is brought upon you, accept it gladly, and in the reversals of your humiliation be patient. Trust in him, and he will help you." So let us too, brothers, for the sake of

patience, sing with David: "Test me, O Lord, and know my heart; examine me and know my paths, and see if there is any way of lawlessness in me, and lead me in the everlasting way. For I have walked in my innocence. Redeem me, O Lord, and have mercy on me." And: "But you upheld me because of my innocence and established me before you forever." Solomon also says: "A patient man is prudent." And: "When a fool asks for wisdom, it will be counted to him as wisdom; and one who makes himself thoughtful and silent will seem to be prudent." And again: "A merciful man is patient." And James: "Be patient, then, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it until it receives the early and the late crop. You too, then, be patient. Take the prophets as an example of suffering and patience." And in the Gospel it is written: "When the disciples James and John saw that the Samaritans did not receive them, they said, Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did? But Jesus turned and rebuked them, and said: You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of Man did not come to destroy people's souls, but to save them." To him be glory forever. Amen.

On superiors. The divine Scripture says that "Jesus began both to do and to teach": first he did, and then he taught. Likewise he himself commands, saying: "Whoever does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven." One who has been entrusted by God with souls needs to strive hard on behalf of those he governs, knowing that he will bear the danger and give an account for them no less than for himself; for "from the one to whom they entrusted much, they will demand all the more." The shepherd, then, ought to be all mind and eye, so that not one of the flock entrusted to him becomes unacceptable through his negligence: scabby with evil thoughts, or mangy through consenting to them, or lame through unseemly walking, or with a cut ear through disobedience, or blind through evil looking, or mauled by beasts and left a carcass through evil deeds. Knowing, as has been said, that he will give an account for them, he ought to keep close watch over his flock and, like an excellent physician, bring to each of them the help suited to each ailment.

For a skilled superior will not let a disciple be wounded, and if he is wounded he will heal him quickly. You, then, superior, arm your disciples with protective weapons, and put on them the breastplate of the promise of the good things to come; fence them about with the shield of true faith, and put on them the helmet of hope in Christ; shod their feet with the teachings of the Gospel, and gird their loins with words of self-control; put a sword in their hand, the sharpest anger against the passions, and set them in array against the phalanx of passions and pleasures. And do not stir up anger against a disciple who has sinned. For it is not right to wound him yourself with another wound before you have treated him; rather, correct what has gone wrong with forbearance. The physician treats the illness but is not angry with the one who fell ill against his will; and as the physician cuts without anger, so the teacher should reprove without mixing anger into his reproofs. Nor again should he keep silent about what needs to be said because of those who contradict, lest the harm done to one spread to the many. [?] be patient, and not seek his own advantage but that of the many, that they may be saved. Nor again should you accept one under your obedience who says: "Give me leave for a time to try this or that thing [?] and to carry it out." For one who speaks this way is plainly doing his own will [?] and setting aside the covenant of obedience. One must also expect this, and endure it: he who eagerly nourishes those subject to him in the word of God should prepare his inner self for spiritual scourges and nobly bear every trial. For it happens that the teacher is even handed over to dishonor, bearing trials on behalf of those who have been spiritually helped. "For we," he says, "are dishonored and buffeted by the thorn, but you have become strong and glorious." The man of God, then, must be adorned [?] in every good work and word, and do all things decently and in order, as a model for those trained under him. For a superior (hegoumenos) is called hegoumenos because he goes ahead in deeds. The name by itself does not bring anyone into the kingdom of heaven, nor does an idle word benefit the hearer; it is effective [?] action that shows the true shepherd. "For whoever does one of the commandments and teaches it will be called great in the kingdom of heaven." But one who undoes the commandment through inaction and teaches with a fruitless word "will be called least." Indeed, he will pay the penalty of the hireling who runs away while the wolf tears his flock to pieces and scatters it. He must therefore be discerning in everything, and give his orders gently, not by compulsion but willingly; and when he is not obeyed, he must be patient

and forbearing, so that he may not hear from David: "He who frames mischief by decree," and from Solomon: "The heart of the ungodly is merciless," but may hear instead: "You shall know well the souls of your flock," and: "You shall set your heart on your herds," and: "[?] the lives of his cattle." He must not [?] their failings either. "For, son of man," he says, "I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. If the watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet, and the one who hears does not take warning, his blood will be on his own head. But if the watchman sees the sword and does not give warning, and the sword takes someone, I will require his blood from the watchman's hand." Having learned, then, superiors, of the danger that hangs over you on behalf of your pupils, watch over the Lord's rational flock with the wakeful eye of the mind, and like Jacob be scorched by the heat by day and the frost by night, and let sleep depart from your eyes, so that not one of the sheep is mauled by beasts. Take care that you do not hear: "Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep from their hand. For the shepherds did not seek out my sheep; they fed themselves, but did not feed my sheep." And through Jeremiah: "The shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture… Therefore, behold, I will punish you for your evil deeds." This ministry, then, belongs to a perfect and devout man, one who can strive, so that he knows how to lead a brotherhood skillfully, as the Scripture says: "I have appointed you leader; do not be puffed up. Take care of them, and then sit down; and when you have fulfilled all your duty, take your place at table." And Gideon says to his three hundred fellow warriors: "Watch me, and do likewise." Likewise Abimelech took a load of wood, put it on his shoulders, and said to the people with him: "As you see me doing, do the same yourselves." And the Psalmist says of Joseph: "He made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct his princes as he himself was, and to teach his elders wisdom." And Paul: "Admonishing everyone in all wisdom, that we may present everyone perfect in Christ Jesus; for this I toil, striving." And to Timothy: "Attend to reading, to exhortation, to teaching; persevere in them." To the Ephesians: "Remember," he says, "that for three years I did not cease night and day to admonish each one of you with tears." And again: "I coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands served my needs and those of the people with me. In everything I have shown you that by toiling in this way we must help the weak." So too, then, a superior [?] a model [?]

…let him be [?] to the flock in all righteousness and holy conduct, living in holiness and righteousness, holding to whatever is pure, whatever is honourable, if there is any virtue, if any praise, if anything of good report. Let correction for others' benefit come from him. Let him uphold his office with all spiritual diligence and take care for the unity of the members, for nothing is better than that. Let him bear with everyone in love, and carry everyone, as the Lord also carries him. Let him pray for everyone without ceasing. Let him ask for spiritual understanding, so that he can discern what is profitable. Let him be watchful and concerned for everyone, and bear the failings and the illnesses of all like a perfect athlete. For where the toil is greater, the gain is great too. If he loves the good disciples, he deserves no credit for it. Rather, he should bring the more disobedient into submission with gentleness. Not every wound is healed with the same plaster: fits of fever must be calmed with cold compresses. Let him be wise in all things as serpents are, and innocent as doves are. Let him attend to the things that appear before his face, and ask that the unseen things be revealed to him, so that he may lack nothing but abound in every gift. For the times demand that he stand nobly like a pilot against the winds, the heavy seas and the squalls stirred up by the spirits of fornication, and guide the storm-tossed into the harbour of God's will. The Lord too says: 'If anyone among you wishes to be greater, let him be the slave of all and the servant of all.' And: 'Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves.' So let him be, as has been said, a pattern of humility to all who are under him, as the Lord says: 'The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.' And again: 'But you, do not be called teachers, for you have one teacher, the Christ.' To him be glory forever. Amen.
On Renunciation. Whoever renounces the world ought to withdraw in his mind from the things that are seen, and to fix his gaze on the things that are unseen. For the

things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. This is why it is called renunciation: in renouncing earthly things, we pledge ourselves to heavenly ones. We leave our homeland here behind and seek the Jerusalem above. We desert those whose minds are set on the world and compete alongside the spiritual. So if we want to acquire virtues, let us practise self-control, endurance and humility, and above all of these, constant prayer, and we will more easily achieve what we are striving for. A man who wants to build a house first gets all the materials ready for completing it. In the same way one must also prepare his own house, that is, the dwelling of the Trinity. For 'I and my Father,' he says, 'will come and make our dwelling with him.' And: 'The Spirit dwells in you.' To reach the goal of a virtuous life, the necessary things are self-control, endurance, humility and prayer. For it is toils and struggles that produce an unbreakable and unceasing [?] righteousness. And the labours are nothing compared with the greatness of the glory of endurance, which virtue brings forth, just as the Lord declares: 'In this world you will have tribulation.' Clearly the present life is the arena of contests and struggles, while the life to come is the place of prizes. So let us love the Lord sincerely, so that he may give us what he promised to those who love him: 'What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered into the heart of man.' Let us strive to conquer the flesh and its mind. By the Spirit of God let us conquer Satan the dragon, in Christ who strengthens us. Let us take up the cross and follow Jesus, who gives the victory. Let us strive, then, to run straight and with confidence, so that we may win the prize of the upward call in Christ. For everyone who runs with full assurance, and not uncertainly, wins the crown of renunciation and the wealth of purity, which costs much toil and brings a rich reward. So Peter writes: 'Like newborn infants,' he says, 'long for the pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow.' That is, long for the undefiled faith, which makes a person grow and gives him light in good works. And Paul says: 'Put on the whole armour of God, so that you can stand against the schemes of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness.' And again: 'Above all, take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the Evil One. With all prayer and supplication, pray at all times, and keep alert for this very purpose with all perseverance and supplication.' If you struggle like this, you will truly be able [?] to have the image of Christ formed in you in all things: in your life, your conduct, your purpose,

your prudence, your self-control, righteousness, long-suffering, forbearance and godliness, in holiness, continence, faith and hope, and in perfect love toward God. Those who are truly sincere contestants exercise self-control in all things and live by every virtue and every commandment of God. As the Apostle says: 'We who live are always being handed over to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal flesh.' 'For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven, since once we have put it on we will not be found naked.' The monk has no authority over himself in anything, and no will of his own. 'For I live,' he says, 'no longer I, but Christ lives in me.' And again: 'The unmarried man cares about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord and complete his work, so that he may be saved for ever.' Those who are carnal cannot do spiritual things, and those who are spiritual cannot do carnal things. So whoever wishes to practise this angelic way of the solitary life must acquire the prudence of the serpent and the innocence of the dove. Then he will understand in everything what the will of God is, what is good, acceptable and perfect, and God will be glorified in all things through our God-fearing order and our sincere way of life. Those who see us will recognize that we are a blessed and holy seed, sons of the living God, in every word, in modesty, meekness, behaviour and attentiveness. Therefore let us not resemble worldly people in a single word or in any way at all. Let us resemble instead the God-fearing teachers of our religion, in all knowledge, prudence and righteousness. So guard the lamp of your purity with all care. Emulate the way of life of Christ's friends. Be like John, the forerunner of Christ, the pure messenger of the Lord, and like John who leaned on the Lord's breast, whom the Lord loved because he was pure. Paul, Barnabas and Timothy finished the course and the contest of purity without stain, as true imitators of Christ. You will also find that the life of Elijah, of Elisha and of many others was like this, pure and blameless. If, then, you wish to imitate them effectively, imitate the elders: 'Consider the outcome of their way of life,' it says, 'and imitate their faith.' And: 'Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.' Those who imitate Christ are able to imitate [?] him, and such people are also blessed. The Lord said to someone, 'Follow me.' He replied, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' The Lord said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead.' He also said to another, 'Follow me.' He replied, 'Lord, let me go and say goodbye to those in my house.' And he said

to him: 'No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven.' And he adds: 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.' And: 'If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me.' To him be glory forever. Amen. On Obedience. Whoever wishes to live under obedience must renounce his own wishes and put on the saving wishes of our Saviour. He must take up his cross, as the Saviour said, and walk after him. So whoever wishes to be under obedience should leave his dead wishes to the dead and hold fast to the living ones among the living. Whoever wants to live under obedience must put himself to death to this temporary life and hold to obedience without question, so that he may enter into the life that is truly eternal. Whoever chooses to run the way of the Lord's commandments, to reach the broad place and to be made bright, must become like a garment at the fuller's. The fuller beats, tramples and scrapes the garment, and it is whitened and made white as snow. In the same way, the one who lives under obedience is insulted, reproached and belittled by many, and so he is cleansed and becomes like refined silver, gleaming bright. Whoever longs to advance to perfect obedience must leave behind everything useless and lay hold of what brings benefit. Let him become a true disciple of Christ, so that he can say with Peter: 'Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?' Let us therefore leave behind our grovelling wills, brothers, and keep the lofty commandment of our Saviour, which leads us up to the Jerusalem above. For the Lord says: 'Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever hears me hears the one who sent me; [and whoever rejects you rejects me].' Disciples must therefore love their teachers as fathers and fear them as rulers. They must not, because of love [?], despise them or grow slack

in their fear of them. It is also written in Wisdom: 'He who honours his father atones for sins.' And: 'He who fears the Lord will honour his father, and will serve him as a master.' And again: 'Honour your father, so that a blessing may come upon you from him.' And again: 'With your whole heart glorify your father.' And Paul says: 'Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over our souls as men who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no profit to you.' And again: 'Let every soul be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and the authorities that exist have been appointed by God. So whoever resists authority opposes what God has ordained, and those who resist will bring judgment on themselves.' And again: 'As slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will as to the Lord and not to men, knowing that you will receive your reward from the Lord.' And to Titus: 'Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, and not to answer back.' And Peter says: 'Be subject to every human institution for the Lord's sake, for it is the will of God that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people.' And the Lord says: 'I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of the Father who sent me.' To him be glory forever. Amen. Homily 114. On Keeping the Commandments. Keeping a commandment brings a person into the land of life, while breaking it brings death. We learn this precisely from divine Scripture. If we had not broken the commandment in paradise at the beginning, we would not have heard, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall return,' and the world would not have been held by the tyrant for so many years. No one who despised God's commandment has lived rightly. Saul disobeyed God's commandment, lived out his days in grief, and in the end lost his kingdom as well. The sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, did not obey their father's voice. They handed the ark of God over into the hands of foreigners, and they themselves [died] most pitiably [?]…

[?] …'Why will you die, O house of Israel?' And the Law says: 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. You shall carefully keep the commandments of the Lord your God.' And again: 'You shall be holy [?] men to me, if you walk in my ordinances and keep my commandments. I will walk among you, and I will be your God, and you will be my people, says the Lord.' So if we too do his will, walk according to his commandments and love what he loves, we become his temple. Whoever has love for him and for his neighbour will be far from all sin and will be loved in return by God. But if we despise him, he knows how to punish us when we disobey his holy commandments. So let our good God not be grieved with us: he who is compassionate, merciful, holy, pure, undefiled, immaterial, the only one, the one, unchanging, sincere, guileless, without anger, God higher and loftier than every name that we can speak or conceive, Jesus Christ. Let him rejoice with us when we live nobly. Let him be glad when we live purely. Let him rest when we conduct ourselves with reverence. Let him feast when we love him, practise self-control well and are temperate. If we begin to carry out God's commandments fervently, then grace enlightens all our senses so that we perceive it. It burns up our own thoughts like fire and sweetens our heart in a peace of unfailing friendship. It makes us ready to think spiritual thoughts and no longer to think according to the flesh. It is also written in Proverbs: 'Son, do not slip away, but keep my counsel and understanding, so that your soul may live. And walk confidently in peace in all your ways, for the Lord will be with you in all your ways.' And again: 'Keep the commandments, do not forget them, and do not disregard the speech of my mouth, nor turn aside from the words of my mouth. Do not forsake it, and it will hold fast to you.' And again: 'Son, incline your ear to my sayings and keep them in your heart, for they are life to those who find them and healing to all flesh.' And in Ecclesiastes: 'Whoever keeps a commandment will know no evil thing. Whoever keeps a commandment guards his own soul. Whoever keeps a commandment, he is in health [?].' And he adds: 'Blessed is the man who will listen to me, and the person who will keep my commandments.' And Paul says to Timothy: 'I charge you before the Lord to keep the commandment spotless and beyond reproach.' And to the Corinthians: 'I praise you because you remember me in everything and hold fast to the traditions just as I handed them on to you.' All of divine Scripture teaches us this: we are bound not only to keep God's commandments without wavering, but also to preserve intact, with all reverence, the commands of our fathers, teachers and superiors. The Lord also says: 'You are my friends if what I command you'

'you do.' And again: 'If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love.' To him be glory forever [?]. On Meekness. Meekness is service to the Divine. Moses was the meekest of all men, and for this reason he was called the servant of God and was counted worthy to see God beyond all the prophets. 'Not so,' it says, 'with my servant Moses: with him I will speak mouth to mouth.' Certain men once rose up against him and Aaron, contending for the high priesthood and the rule of the nation. Moses rose above all ambition and love of power, and yielded the leadership of the people to God as the better leader. When they gathered against him again, reproached him over what had happened before, threatened him and very nearly struck him, the meek man cried out [?] for the salvation of the good [?], and himself pleaded with God on their behalf, saying: 'If you will forgive them their sin, forgive it. If not, blot me too out of the book you have written.' Then there is David, the meekest of men. His own son plotted against him, openly showed his hatred by what he did to his father's wives, and sought to kill him. Yet David, truly meek, righteous and forbearing, mourned for him. Likewise, when Shimei cursed him and threw stones at him, he did not become angry with him. His servants were furious and wanted to kill Shimei, but David said to them: 'Let him curse David.' It was fitting, then, that he said: 'Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness.' The minds of these divine men are examples enough for those who wish to imitate their meekness and forbearance. Then they too will hear from the Lord, along with them: 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land of the meek.' For meekness according to God is a work pleasing to God and has real substance [?]. 'For on whom shall I look,' he says, 'but on the one who is humble, meek and quiet, and trembles at my words?' A calm sea is a delightful sight, but nothing is more delightful than a peaceful state of soul. In a calm sea dolphins leap and play, and in a peaceful state of soul fitting words resound. James also says: 'Put away all malice and filth, and in meekness [of heart] receive the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.' And the hymn-writer [?]

David says: 'The Lord lifts up the meek, but brings sinners down to the ground.' And: 'He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach them his ways.' And another says: 'The Lord will save a humble people, but will bring low [?] the proud [?].' And our good Lord says: 'Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.' To him be glory forever. Amen. On Being Wronged and Not Doing Wrong. The old law commands us not to do wrong. The new law urges us to be wronged and to give thanks. Or rather, the [Lawgiver?] of the law [raises?] man to [?] and holy adoption as a son. 'Be merciful,' he says, 'as your heavenly Father is merciful.' So whoever wishes to win a splendid victory must do more than bear being wronged nobly. He must also give more than the other wants to take, and by the abundance of his own generosity go beyond the limits of that man's wicked desire. Whoever wishes to become a disciple of Christ will show his teacher's lessons in his deeds. 'When he was reviled,' it says, 'he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten.' Otherwise he will have to hear: 'Why do you call me "Lord, Lord," and do not do what I say?' The true disciple chooses to be wronged rather than to do wrong, and to be gentle in the face of other people's anger. Toward the arrogant he is humble; toward the savage he is gentle [?]. He does not become like them in [?], but by his forbearance, as an imitator of [?] Christ, he [?] bears the [?] of those who want to wrong us, and prays for them. Then, through our repentance [?] and through our giving back what they took from us, they may be released from the charge of greed. For this is God's will: that we should win over the greedy man himself, not the thing he greedily took. Whoever is wronged by others escapes sin, and will find help like that given in [?] affliction. Whoever has shared in holy knowledge and tasted the sweetness of God ought never to go to law, nor bring any lawsuit at all against anyone, even if someone takes away the very clothes he is wearing. Otherwise, what difference is there between God's nurslings

…and the people of this age? For the law commands: "You shall not wrong your neighbor"; and: "The wages of the hired laborer shall not stay with you overnight. You shall not speak evil of the deaf, and you shall not put a stumbling block before the blind." And the author of Proverbs says: "Do not oppress the needy, for he is poor, and do not dishonor the weak at the gates, for the Lord will judge their cause." These things the old law said, since it was speaking to infants who were still imperfect. But the law of Christ, being perfect, gives its commands to the perfect, who share in the perfect food. For the Lord says: "Pray for those who persecute you and abuse you." This commandment the true disciples of Christ, Stephen and James, fulfilled at once. One was being stoned and the other thrown down from a height, and both prayed for those who were killing them. It is also told of James the brother of John that, when the man who had accused him saw him being led away to his death, he repented, fell down before him and said, "Forgive me." James paused a little and said, "Peace be with you," and kissed him. At once the man proclaimed himself a Christian in a loud voice, and being condemned together with the one he had accused, he won the prize of the upward calling along with him. Peter also says: "What credit is it if you endure when you sin and are beaten? But if you endure when you do good and suffer, then, when they slander you as evildoers, those who abuse your pure conduct in Christ will be put to shame." And he adds: "The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment." And David says: "He executes justice for the wronged and gives food to the hungry." Therefore I too say: "I hated and abhorred injustice, but I loved your law." And since, Master, it is your commandment to suffer wrong and not to do wrong, "they repaid me evil for good. But I prayed: My God, rescue me from the hand of the lawless and the unjust." And Paul says: "Why not rather suffer wrong? Instead you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and that your own brothers. Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?" And elsewhere: "Brothers, remember the former days in which, after you had been enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproaches and afflictions, and sometimes becoming partners of those who were so treated." And the Lord says: "If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two. If anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. For blessed are you when people hate you and exclude you on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

Homily 107. On Thanksgiving. According to the Apostle, we are bound to give thanks in everything, whether we are comforted or afflicted. For the Lord, who provides for our souls, brings afflictions for our benefit. He is like an excellent physician who applies sharp cauteries to the disease so that the patient may be made whole. He is also like an affectionate father who disciplines his son when he sees him misbehaving and encourages him when he sees him careless or downcast. So our good Master and Father deals with us: because he loves his children, he brings everything upon us for our benefit, whether comfort or discipline. We ought therefore to give thanks all the more in afflictions, as true sons and not illegitimate ones. Christ is Master by nature and Master by the divine plan, since he made us when we did not exist and redeemed us by his own blood when we were dead in sin. What thanksgiving, then, can we unprofitable servants render him? For if we give thanks only in times of prosperity, we are found to be like the ungrateful Jews. When they were eating in the wilderness while the Lord worked miracles, they said, "This is truly the prophet," and wanted to seize him and make him king. But when he said to them, "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life," they said, "What sign do you show us? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness." The saying fits us well, then: "They will give thanks to you when you do them good." And of such a person it is said: "He will never see light." So let us not be like the ungrateful. Instead, as disciples of grace, let us become an example of it through our thanksgiving, so that they too, seeing the light of our thanksgiving, may be able to leave the darkness of ingratitude that holds them. For the command "In everything give thanks" covers every situation [?]: whether a person is cheerful or despondent, afflicted or rejoicing, he is bound to give thanks. Such was the great Job. He lost all his possessions and even his ten children, who were buried together when the house collapsed during the feast, and yet he gave thanks and said: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord." And not only this: he also sat on the dunghill amid the rot of worms, and when he heard his wife say, "Speak some word against the Lord and die,"

he silenced her, saying: "Why have you spoken like one of the foolish women? If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the bad?" This is how a truly thankful person is recognized: he gives thanks to the Lord even when misfortunes change his lot [?]. The mark of the ungrateful person is blaming fate in afflictions, grumbling, resentment, self-justification, and the like. But David, who was patient and open-hearted in afflictions, rose from the ground and worshiped the Lord when he saw that the child had died. At another time he said: "Who am I, my Lord, Lord, that you have loved me this far?" And again, singing hymns, he said: "All my bones will say, Lord, Lord, who is like you, who rescues the poor from the hand of those stronger than they?" And again: "O God, what great things you have done for me! Who is like you? You have held my right hand, guided me by your counsel, and received me with glory." Therefore: "I will exalt you, my God, my King [?], and bless your name forever, and I will give thanks to you, because you heard me and became my salvation. For you rescued me from every affliction. I remembered you, Master, and was glad." And: "Blessed are you, O God, who have not turned away my prayer, nor your mercy from me." Isaiah also says: "I will bless you, Lord, because you were angry with me and had mercy on me." And Zechariah says: "For if there is anything good, it is his, and if anything beautiful, it is from him." And Paul says: "Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of Jesus Christ, giving thanks through him to God the Father." And again: "For what thanksgiving can we render on our behalf?" So let us also give thanks unceasingly to God the Father, because he did not spare his only-begotten Son but gave him up for us all. Let us give thanks to the Son, because by his own blood he redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us. And what praise or what thanksgiving can we render him for all the good things he has richly given to us, the lowly? Let us give thanks to the Holy Spirit, who spoke in the Law, in the Prophets and in the New Testament. He enlightens our darkened minds to understand and carry out his commandments, and he opens our mouths to confess and give thanks for his goodness. The evangelist also says: "At that time Jesus answered and said: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for such was your good pleasure." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

Homily 108. On Joy in God. The joy that is celebrated in song belongs to those who have gained perfect love for God. Such are all who are filled with the Holy Spirit and rejoice in him: the apostles, the prophets, the martyrs and the perfect ascetics. They regarded persecutions, afflictions and tortures as joy, and counted everything in the world as rubbish so that they might gain Christ. Fire, wild beasts, swords, hunger, cold and all the rest gladdened them because of their love for God. As Isaiah declares: "They shall be redeemed and gathered by the Lord; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads, and gladness and joy shall overtake them." And again: "Joy upon their heads. Everyone who sees them will recognize them, that they are a seed blessed by God, and they will rejoice in the Lord." And again: "Behold, those who serve me shall eat and drink, and they shall rejoice and exult with gladness." And Zephaniah says: "He will bring joy and praise upon you in his love." And Nahum says: "Celebrate your feasts, Judah, pay your vows to the Lord, for the one who breathes into your face has come up." And Christ said to the apostles: "Receive the Holy Spirit." And David says: "I will rejoice and exult in you." And: "This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it," meaning the day of Christ's resurrection. And: "Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul." And: "My soul will exult in the Lord; it will delight in his salvation." And: "For my heart was glad and my tongue exulted, because you will fill me with joy in your presence." So may one be filled with such joy through love for God, for the joy of the righteous is love for God. Then he also urges others, saying: "Come, let us exult in the Lord." And: "Serve the Lord with fear and with gladness." And: "Delight in the Lord," that is, enjoy his sweetness. "For eat honey, my son,"

he says, "for it is good, so that your throat may be sweetened," and "he will give you the desires of your heart." For the Lord says to the disciples: "If you love me and keep my commandments, ask my Father for whatever you wish, and he will give it to you in my name." And again: "Let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice." And: "Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous." And: "The righteous will rejoice in the Lord." And: "Let Israel rejoice in the one who made him, and let the children of Zion exult in their King. For those who dwell in you are like people who all rejoice." And another says: "For those who serve me will be called by a new name, which will be blessed on the earth, and they will find joy and gladness on it." For all who serve him in fear and exult in him with trembling are sons of the living God. The author of Proverbs also says: "Grief does not mingle with joys." For "pain, grief and sighing have fled from the chorus of the righteous." And: "In the day of prosperity, live in good things." And again: "An eye that beholds good things gladdens the heart." And: "When the heart is glad, the face flourishes." "For if your eye is sound," he says, "your whole body will be full of light." And: "Good news fattens the bones," as the soul of Paul also said: "I rejoice and rejoice with you all." And: "A glad heart brings good health." And the Apostle says: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice." It is also in the Gospel: "It was right to make merry and rejoice," says the father, "for this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found." To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Not Being Anxious. Anxiety about the affairs of this life belongs to a faithless and faint-hearted person. For then we no longer hope in God, who cares for us, but in ourselves, and we worry about ourselves. If we do not trust the good God with the visible good things that he provides for us, how will we trust him with the invisible things which he has promised? [?] …and all these things will be added to us, according to his word. It is more profitable for us to despise what is not ours and to long for what is truly ours, by which I mean incorruption and immortality. For when we become incorruptible and immortal, we shall be filled in all-pure contemplations with his visible manifestation, which will shine around us with most brilliant splendors, as it shone around the disciples at that most divine Transfiguration. And we shall share in his intelligible illumination

with a mind free of passion and matter, and in the union that surpasses mind, through the unknowing and blessed intuitions of his most radiant rays, in a more divine imitation of the heavenly minds. For, as the divine word has said, "we shall be equal to the angels and sons of God, being sons of the resurrection." So the Preacher rightly declares: "Sweet is the sleep of the servant, whether he eats little or much." And he adds: "There is a sickness which I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his own harm. That wealth perishes in some evil trouble, and all his days are spent in darkness and mourning, in much anger and sickness, and his toil is for the wind. For as he came naked, so he will depart. And often God does not give him the power to eat from it, but a stranger eats it. For the poor man knows how to walk before the living." And another says: "Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for you do not know what the next day will bring forth." And again: "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what will happen to you. Our life will pass away like the traces of a cloud, for our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no turning back from a man's end." And David says: "Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you. For I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging for bread. They will not be put to shame in an evil time, and in days of famine they will be satisfied. I will richly bless her provisions, and I will satisfy her poor with bread." And Peter says: "Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you." Likewise Paul says: "The Lord is near. Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God." And again: "God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that, always having all sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work." And the Lord says: "Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will wear. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of heaven, and all these things will be added to you." To him be the glory forever.

On Firstfruits. As for firstfruits, we are bound in every way to offer to God what comes from God: from our own labors, from the strength that he himself supplies, and from the things by which he provides for us and cares for us. As the Scripture says: "Honor the Lord from your just labors, and give him the firstfruits of your fruits of righteousness, so that your storehouses may be filled with an abundance

of grain." And the law says: "You shall not appear before me empty-handed." And: "You shall bring the firstfruits of your produce to the house of the Lord your God." And: "Do not disobey him, for my name is upon him." And: "You shall not delay the firstfruits of your threshing floor and your winepress. He shall offer them to the Lord as a gift of firstfruits." And: "You shall offer a sacrifice of your firstborn." And: "The priest shall make atonement for his sin, and he shall be forgiven." And again: "The leaders brought their gifts before the altar." And Ezekiel says: "All the people shall give the firstfruits to the prince." This is why Tobit said: "I gave the firstfruits of my produce to the priests for the altar." And another says: "Do not appear before the Lord empty-handed, for all these things are to be done because of the commandment. Give to the Most High as he has given to you, and he will repay you sevenfold. Glorify God with a generous eye, and do not stint the firstfruits of your hands. With every gift show a cheerful face, for the offering of the righteous enriches the altar." And David, the keeper of the commandments, says: "I will enter your house with burnt offerings; I will pay you my vows, which my lips uttered. I will offer you burnt offerings of fatlings, with incense and rams; I will offer you oxen with goats." And another urges: "Bring to the Lord, you sons of God, bring young rams to the Lord." And: "Take up sacrifices and enter his courts." And: "Make vows and pay them to the Lord our God." And again: "All who are around him will bring gifts," that is, those who draw near to him. And the Apostle says: "…that I may be a minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, serving the gospel of God as a priest, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Spirit." All of us, then, as I have said, owe firstfruits and tithes to God, and let no one plead poverty. For no one is found poorer than the widow who offered the two small coins and was accepted above all the rest. Above all, monks are bound to offer firstfruits and tithes to God. These are not only the visible ones, that is, from what they receive from others for their support and from the work of their hands, but also spiritual sacrifices, in which [?]…

…humbled [?]. If you offer yourself to God as a whole burnt offering in this way, you are cleansed of the leprosy of the unclean passions and become an altar and temple of the Holy Spirit. Then you hear: "Go, show yourself to the priest," that is, to Christ, "and offer the gift which Moses commanded" you, the Jew in spirit, "as a testimony" to the adoption you have received. To him be the glory forever. Amen.

On Propitiation. The priest must first propitiate God for himself, and only then for the people. This is in keeping with the commandment of the Lord, who says: "First clean the inside of the cup, and then the outside." For how can anyone propitiate God for another unless he has first done so for himself? This is also the law, as Moses says to his brother Aaron: "Offer your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and your household; then offer the gifts for the people and make atonement for them." Clearly, it was only after Aaron had cleansed himself and his household that he lifted up his hands and blessed the people. And Ezekiel says this about the priests: "No priest shall drink wine when they enter the inner court." And the Apostle says: "Just as the high priests first offer sacrifices for their own sins, and then for the sins the people commit in ignorance." And: "For the law appoints as high priests men who are subject to weakness." And again: "For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed on behalf of men in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can deal gently with the ignorant and the wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness, and because of this he must offer sacrifices for sins for himself as well as for the people." So, as has been said, the one whom God calls to offer gifts and sacrifices for the people must first cleanse his own soul and body of the whole old man. Only then may he dare to offer intercessions to God for others. He must also imitate the great high priest Zechariah, the father of the Forerunner. "For he was righteous," it says, "walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. And while he was serving as priest, he entered the temple to burn incense, and the whole multitude was outside, praying at the hour of incense. And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar, and said: Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard
[?] “…and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John, and you will have joy and gladness. For he will be great before the Lord God.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

On the high priesthood. According to the account handed down by tradition, the high priesthood embraces all the sacred things that belong to it, and it holds the highest rank of all: to be established directly about God and to be illumined by the first manifestations of God that come from him. For the hierarch must be an inspired and divine man, filled with all sacred knowledge and understanding, as Paul writes to Timothy: “The bishop, then, must be above reproach, sober, self-controlled, orderly, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent, not greedy for gain, but gentle, peaceable, free from the love of money.” Likewise to Titus: “For the bishop,” he says, “must be blameless, as God’s steward, hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, just, holy, disciplined, holding fast to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.” And he says to the Ephesians: “Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the Church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.” That “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” is plain [?], for in our times there is a famine of hearing the word.

Therefore let us pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest: [?] such laborers as rightly handle the word of truth; laborers such as the apostles, and those like them, to whom Paul said, “Are you not my work in the Lord?”, fellow workers with the Lord [?] in the gospel, working for the salvation of people. “For God does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live.” This is why he also said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel, and you shall hear a word from my mouth [?] and warn them. When I say to the lawless man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you do not…

“…his righteous deeds that he has done [shall not be remembered], and his blood I will require at your hand, because you did not warn him.” And: “If you warn the righteous man not to sin, he shall surely live, and you will have delivered your soul.” And he adds: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” And what does the Lord say to Peter? “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” See the force of the saying: he did not say, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound on earth,” but, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven,” so that when you excommunicate someone, or debar him, or depose him, you may regard the matter with fear, as calling on God to cast his vote with you, as doing it with the One in heaven as witness; and so that the one debarred or deposed may tremble, as one cast out of the kingdom of heaven. See what you are doing, he says, O priest: whatever [?] you bind, expect to render account for it above. The binding is not without accountability if you bind unjustly, for you are to appear before the tribunal of the holy angels. Therefore do not impose the binding in anger and passion, not as avenging yourself but as vindicating virtue. For God vindicates the one who has been unjustly bound, [even if?] he disregards the binding [?]. He, then, who sincerely shepherds the flock of Christ is called the mouth of God, for he says: “If you bring forth the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth.” This is the mark of the true shepherd: that he lay down his life for those in his charge. [If he shrinks from this?] [?], he will suffer the punishment of the hireling who fled because of the wolf, and he will hear from the chief shepherd: “The shepherds did not seek out my sheep,” and “they fed [?] them,” and, “I will require my sheep at their hand.” We find something of this kind in Irenaeus. For he says of John the Theologian that, seeing a very gifted young man who had been instructed and baptized by him, he said to the bishop of the city, “I entrust this one to you,” and went away. The bishop took great care of the boy and brought him to great progress. But later, as he gradually neglected him, the young man turned aside from the straight road, so that he became a robber chief. When the Theologian came back, he demanded the deposit from the bishop. The bishop, thinking money was being demanded, was at a loss how to answer, since he had received nothing from him. Then John says to him plainly, “Give back the young man whom I entrusted to you.” The bishop wrung his hands and said, “He is dead,” and told him what had become of him. The apostle, with a great cry of grief, struck his head and said, “A fine guardian of our brother’s soul I left you!” And at once he went out to [?]…

[?] …of his. But when the young man saw him, he began to flee; and John cried out, “Wait, child, for your father! Have pity on my gray hairs!” And he came and fell down before him, his right hand stained with blood; and the evangelist kissed his hand, saying, “Your sin is upon me, child. God will require your soul from me.” And having turned back again, he became a chosen vessel. Behold, this is truly the shepherd laying down his life for the sheep, so that when the Lord of the sheep comes, he may rejoice over him and be glad over the sheep. And he will rejoice if all are found sound and none of them has fallen away; but if any of them are found fallen away, woe to the shepherds. And if the shepherds themselves are found fallen, what will they say to the Master of the flock? That they fell because of the sheep? They will not be believed. For it is an incredible thing that a shepherd should suffer harm from sheep; rather, they will be punished for their lie. Knowing, then, that they must give a very strict account for them, as leaders of the Church and holders of the first seats, let them carefully secure themselves together with their flock, so that they may be shown to be well pleasing to God. For in the man of God there is no fleshly mind, but all the saving fruits of the Spirit, those in whom God dwells and walks. By these they shine as lights in the world, truly holding fast the word of life and being the boast and glory of godliness. For hierarchy is a sacred order and knowledge. The aim of hierarchy, then, is likeness to God and union with him, as far as is attainable, having him as guide of all sacred knowledge and activity; gazing unswervingly toward his most divine beauty, and being stamped with it as far as possible, it makes its own initiates divine images, mirrors most clear and spotless, able to receive the primal light and the original ray, and in turn to shine it ungrudgingly upon those next in order, according to the ordinances of the divine source. For it is not lawful for those who perform the sacred rites, or for those who are sacredly initiated, to act in any way contrary to their own sacred ordinances. So whoever speaks of hierarchy means in general a sacred ordering, an image of the beauty of the divine source, which performs the mysteries of its own illumination in hierarchical orders and forms of knowledge, and is led up, as is lawful, toward its own source. For the perfection of hierarchy is to be led up, each according to its proper capacity, to the imitation of God, to become God’s fellow worker, and to show the divine activity shining forth in oneself as far as possible: to be illumined and to illumine, to be purified and to purify, to be perfected in divine things and to perfect others, so that everyone who sees you may recognize that you are a seed blessed by the Lord, truly an honored seed, “a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession,” heirs of incorruptible and unfading promises, “which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” and keep his commandments.

And Peter too says: “Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have it; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not as lording it over your charge, but becoming examples to the flock; and when the chief shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.” And the Lord says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
